events.title: Chip stocks slide after Broadcom boss likens AI investing to ‘casino’
events.summary: Asian markets fall and Samsung shares tumble after its Chinese rival CXMT claims strong progress South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index tumbled 6.25% as investors dumped chip stocks, while other Asian markets were also lower. Japan’s Nikkei fell 1.8% and the Taiwan exchange lost almost 2%, with the country’s chip maker TSMC down by a similar amount. Samsung Electronics shares dropped 7.4% on the South Korean exchange, while the memory chip maker SK Hynix was down 10%. In Japan, the chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron fell 7.15% while SoftBank Group, an OpenAI investor, lost 8.5%. US stock futures point to a mixed open on Wall Street after the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite slipped 0.4% on Monday. The US chip maker Micron Technology slid 3.9% while Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom also fell. Crude oil prices dropped amid escalating tensions in the Middle East. AI shares have been on a rollercoaster in recent months, amid concerns that companies are spending eye-watering amounts on AI infrastructure, funded by debt. The latest sell-off came after the South China Morning Post reported on Monday that CXMT had made good progress on new Dram architecture that would boost memory density. Investors are worried that it could challenge Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron, the world’s biggest memory chip makers. CXMT, which had an impressive debut on the Shanghai stock market in late July, makes Dram chips , which store the data that other AI chips draw on for their calculations. Hock Tan, the chief executive of the US chip maker Broadcom, said the AI boom had attracted investors that do not really understand what they are betting on. “A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in,” he said at a conference in Singapore, in comments reported by Bloomberg . They “set very extreme expectations only to find out that it’s almost like they are in a casino”. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning AI companies such as ChatGPT maker OpenAI are still loss-making. Tan said OpenAI’s annualised revenues of $50bn (£38bn) at the end of September suggested a viable business model but offered little guarantee on long-term profitability. “For now it’s still losing money because they’re spending a lot on training,” Tan said. “So frankly, it doesn’t tell anything at this point except that there is a lot of potential revenue growth out of providing frontier generative AI models.” He noted that a sizeable portion of AI labs’ enterprise revenue came from pilot projects. “When you are a kid you go to a video arcade, you play,” he said. “Your parents give you $10 of tokens, you finish it in 10 minutes and you haven’t learned anything.”

events.title: IMF raises UK growth forecast in boost for chancellor - business live
events.summary: Introduction: IMF upgrades UK growth outlook for this year Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets, and the world economy. The International Monetary Fund has increased its growth forecast for the UK this year, but has said that it expects a modest slowdown in 2027 as higher energy prices take effect. The upgrade will be welcome news for the chancellor, John Healey , who will arrive in Bangkok later this week to attend the IMF’s annual meetings for the first time. The IMF , which publishes its World Economic Outlook twice a year, has predicted GDP growth of 1.3% for the UK this year – up 0.3 percentage points from its most recent update in July. However, the IMF also warned that high oil prices and rising interest rates meant growth was likely to “edge down” in 2027, “as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”. It cut its UK growth forecast for next year modestly to 1.2%, from 1.3%. The IMF singled out the UK as among the countries where core inflation – which excludes volatile commodities such as energy – is not expected to return to the 2% target until late next year. It expects average inflation in the UK to be 3.3% this year, and to remain at 2.8% in 2027 – a challenge for Healey and the prime minister, Andy Burnham , who are promising to offer voters a “breathing space” from rising costs. It comes just weeks ahead of Healey ’s first budget on 28 October. He is expected to focus on plans to devolve more tax revenues to mayoralties, as well as measures to help households cope with higher energy bills ahead of the winter. The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) warned this week that the budget would be a “work of fiction” unless Healey explained how he would deal with what it said were £35bn of future spending pressures. The IMF’s growth upgrade follows from the fact that UK GDP has been stronger than expected in early 2026, at 0.6% in the first quarter and 0.5% in the second quarter. 7am BST: Reach trading statement, Marston’s trading statement, Bellway full-year results, Whitbread interim results 8am BST: Worldpanel by Numerator UK grocery inflation report 9.45am BST: Nikhil Rathi to face questions from the Treasury Committee 12pm BST: JP Morgan, Citigroup and Wells Fargo Q3 earnings 12.30pm BST: Goldman Sachs Q3 earnings 18m ago Kingfisher appoints Sebastian Gundel as new CEO 1h ago UK grocery inflation rises to 2.5% 2h ago IMF economic counsellor tells UK to 'stay the course' 2h ago Introduction: IMF upgrades UK growth outlook for this year UK government bonds are rallying this morning, after the IMF said it had increased its growth forecast for the country this year. Yields (which fall when bond prices rise) are down by about 5 basis points for the 10-year gilt, and down by 4 basis points for the 5-year. There have been some dramatic moves in the global band market recently, largely thanks to the persistently high cost of oil. Last week, the yield on 30-year UK bonds hit 6% for the first time since 1998, before easing slightly later in the day. Its yield has since fallen back to about 5.81%. Kingfisher appoints Sebastian Gundel as new CEO Kingfisher, the owner of DIY retailer B&Q, has appointed Sebastian Gundel as its new chief executive. Gundel, who was most recently chief executive of the German home improvement company OBI, will start on 1 February 2027. It is a privilege to be appointed chief executive officer of Kingfisher. I have long admired the strength and diversity of Kingfisher’s retail banners, its scale and its strategic ambition. The industry is evolving rapidly, creating significant opportunities across trade, digital, marketplaces, services and new customer propositions. I am much looking forward to working with the team to build on those opportunities and create sustainable long-term value.” Kingfisher’s current chief executive Thierry Garnier , who has been in his post since 2019, will remain in the job until the end of the year. He is leaving to take the helm at Ahold Delhaize – one of Europe’s largest supermarket chains. It has been an honour to lead Kingfisher, and I am proud of what our teams have achieved together. Sebastian brings deep sector expertise, a strong customer focus and a proven track record of performance. I am confident that he will successfully lead Kingfisher through its next chapter.” European stock markets have opened tentatively higher this morning. The UK’s FTSE 100 is leading the pack so far, up by almost 1% – its best performers are the chemicals company Croda International , up 3.6%, and JD Sports Fashion , which is up 3.1%. Premier Inn owner Whitbread is up 2.9% after it urged its shareholders to vote against an activist investor demanding a seat on its board. The Stoxx Europe 600 is up by a modest 0.3%. The German Dax is up 0.2%, while the French Cac 40 is up by 0.4%.

events.title: Palestine weekly: Gaza marks year of ‘ceasefire’ with more Israeli killing
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? A year after Gaza’s ceasefire, Israeli attacks persist as settler violence disrupts West Bank’s oil harvest. The Gaza “ceasefire” marked its first anniversary on October 10, but more than 100 humanitarian and human rights organisations said it exists “in name only” . Islamic Relief noted that Israeli forces have killed or wounded a Palestinian in Gaza on average every 90 minutes since the ceasefire took effect. list 2 of 3 Northern Israel explosion kills at least 1 person, injures 19 list 3 of 3 Israeli academic and Al Jazeera contributor Ori Goldberg dies at 50 Gaza’s Health Ministry put the toll since the truce at 1,493 killed and 5,299 wounded as of October 12, up from 1,460 a week earlier; the cumulative death toll since October 2023 stood at 74,382. Among the Palestinians killed in Gaza over the past week: Four Palestinians were killed in a drone strike near Panda Mall in western Gaza City on Saturday, which Israel said targeted members of Hamas’s Nukhba force . Also on Saturday, eight-year-old Shahd al-Najjar was killed by Israeli fire that struck her inside her tent in western Gaza City. Seven-year-old Jihad al-Ghandour died of wounds from a separate shooting near Jabalia camp north of Gaza City on Sunday. A child and his mother were killed Thursday when Israeli warplanes struck a home in Gaza City’s al-Sabra neighbourhood after an evacuation warning. A drone strike on a charging point west of Khan Younis killed four people on Sunday, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported. Two more men were killed in a strike near a mosque in al-Mawasi in the south on Monday. In statements describing attacks, Israel’s military claimed several of those killed this week were Palestinian fighters. The Israeli military said two men killed near the Jordanian Field Hospital were Islamic Jihad operatives; Wafa identified one as a recently released former prisoner. It separately said a civil defence worker killed while responding to the wounded near Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza had been a Hamas sniper; Hamas rejected the claim, and it has not been independently verified. Gaza’s health system continued its collapse: Gaza’s Ministry of Health said that 44 percent of essential medicines are completely out of stock. A Physicians for Human Rights Israel report found that a year into the ceasefire, not one of Gaza’s 36 hospitals is operating at full capacity. More than 18,500 patients need medical evacuation and more than 1,000 have died waiting, according to the joint NGO statement. The Health Ministry said this week that no patient had been permitted to leave through Rafah crossing in the last week. Israeli forces have also continued pushing the so-called Yellow Line demarcating Israeli control further into residential Gaza City neighbourhoods this week, triggering fresh displacement. One year into the ceasefire, the Board of Peace – Gaza’s transitional oversight body – has failed to meet most of its central commitments : no international stabilisation force has deployed, aid trucks are entering at roughly a third of the agreed rate, and Israel now controls nearly two thirds of the Strip — well above the roughly 50 percent it was supposed to retain before further withdrawal and a future handover of control to Palestinians. Olive harvest under coordinated assault The Palestinian olive harvest – traditionally a time of family and celebration – gathered pace as Israeli settlers and soldiers intensified efforts to disrupt it. Harvesters were killed, attacked and blocked, while isolated families faced dayslong settler sieges. On October 7, Ali Hassan Yasser al-Bazzari, 44, was shot dead when settlers and soldiers opened fire on olive pickers on farmland between Burqa and Ramin, northwest of Nablus in the occupied West Bank. At least 16 others were wounded during the pogrom, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa. The Palestine Red Crescent Society said Israeli forces assaulted ambulance crews trying to reach the wounded olive pickers and briefly detained three paramedics. Soldiers later raided the nearby village and made arrests, while the settlers who carried out the attack marched past unimpeded. The Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission recorded 19 settler attacks on Friday alone , another 12 on Saturday and 18 more on Sunday, according to Wafa. The Israeli rights group Yesh Din had already documented 109 harvest-related settler incidents across 75 Palestinian communities in a 10-day period between September 27 and October 6. The commission says settlers and soldiers have destroyed roughly 50,000 trees so far this year. The attacks followed a familiar shape village to village, according to Wafa and field reports from local residents and activists: Settlers in Qusra stole a farmer’s olives before bulldozing more than 50 of his trees.

events.title: Drone attack sinks ship off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, PM says
events.summary: Two ships were hit in the attack, including the Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3, which sustained damage. Two ships have been hit in drone attacks off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, with one of them sinking, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said. The Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3, which was sailing under a Maltese flag, was hit by three drones and damaged about 18 nautical miles (33km) off Bulgaria at about 1:30am on Tuesday (22:30 GMT on Monday), Radev said. list 1 of 3 NATO says will do ‘anything and everything’ if alliance is attacked list 2 of 3 Russia and Ukraine trade strikes amid doubt over ‘energy ceasefire’ list 3 of 3 Trump insists energy ceasefire holds as Ukraine reports new Russian strikes Radev said its 15-man crew, seven of them Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis, was rescued. Five crew members received medical assistance, and no one was seriously injured. He added that one crew member from the ship that sank was also rescued. Radev called the incident “absolutely unacceptable”. “Another attack in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters,” he said in a televised address, adding, “I am due to speak with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.” Radev said there was no clear evidence of who carried out the attack, but “the outcome benefits” Russia and that the Russian ambassador would be summoned over the incident. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned the attack on the ships. “The Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine,” she said. “This is unacceptable. I strongly condemn the drone attacks on merchant ships near Bulgaria’s coast. Putting the lives of the crew in grave danger and threatening security in the Black Sea,” she wrote on X. “We stand with Bulgaria and thank its rescuers for their swift response. Those responsible should be held accountable,” von der Leyen added. As a member of the NATO military alliance, Bulgaria holds a strategic position on the Black Sea, where Russia and Ukraine have vital ports. The incident comes as concerns grow over hybrid attacks involving Russia. Last week, drones hit two ships off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast , causing one to sink. All 10 crew members from the ship that sank remain unaccounted for .

events.title: UK growth forecast upgraded but energy prices and rates to hit in 2027
events.summary: Published 13 October 2026, 03:00 BST The UK economy is forecast to grow by more than previously expected this year before higher energy prices and interest rates hit growth in 2027, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has said. The organisation's latest report, which is closely watched by the government, said the UK economy would expand by 1.3% in 2026, up from the 1% it predicted in July, before slowing in 2027. Economies across the world have proved more resilient to the energy price shock caused by the US-Iran war, the IMF said, but it warned the economic fallout from the conflict remained "highly uncertain". Chancellor John Healey said the government would look to "provide some breathing space" for households in the Budget. Healey is making the final preparations to Andy Burnham's new-look government's tax and spending plans, which will be announced on 28 October. Government borrowing costs have surged, placing pressure on the chancellor to ensure his plans are credible in the eyes of financial markets, which the UK relies on to borrow money. But IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro told BBC News on Tuesday that the UK's process of managing its debts is now leading the major G7 economies. "As you know, the UK has already started the consolidation process and it is the country that basically stands out, along with India", she said. The organisation said the UK is one of the only major economies on course to stabilise levels of national debt. The UK is also projected to have the lowest annual borrowing in the G7 in 2031. Asked if the UK was one of the countries the IMF was telling to reduce borrowing, Tenreyro said that the country had begun the process already and should "stay the course". The head of the IMF has previously called on the world's advanced economies to cut borrowing and reduce debt levels. While the IMF's forecasts are closely watched, the figures are only a prediction, a best estimate, of what will happen in the future. Forecasts often turn out to be incorrect due to world events. The reversal of downgrades to economic forecasts made at the start of the US-Iran war, mean the UK is expected to have the second-fastest growing economy in the G7 along with Germany. But growth is estimated to slow in 2027 to 1.2% due to higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weighing on household spending and business investment. Healey acknowledged that wars in the Middle East and Europe were "hitting people in the UK and around the world", but added that "Britain's economy is showing strong international resilience". When the economy is growing, businesses tend to invest more, more jobs are created and people, on average, tend to feel better off. The opposite can occur if the economy stagnates or shrinks. Sir Howard Davies, former deputy governor of the Bank of England, told the BBC the IMF's growth forecast was "better than it might have been", but noted that for 2027 it remained "more pessimistic". In March, the official forecaster, the Office of Budget Responsibility (OBR), predicted growth of 1.6% next year, while the IMF is now expecting 1.2%. The OBR is currently working on a new forecast, which is the one that the chancellor will base his Budget decisions on. Sir Howard said the UK was "a bit of a sideshow" when it comes to the global economy and that the IMF was more focused on how much the US is adding to its debt pile. "That is what is putting pressure on interest rates all over the world and that is what is affecting us as well. Unless the US does something about its deficit, we can expect interest rates to be higher, which of course increases our debt interest costs," he said. He added that the IMF was giving the UK credit in its forecast for tax rises which it might not end up actually putting through. Economists have suggested Healey faces having to find £35bn to avoid cuts to public spending while meeting defence promises in his first Budget. On Tuesday, the Resolution Foundation called on the chancellor to "make repairs" to the public finances, but said well-targeted support was needed for those "struggling to heat their homes". Andrew Griffith, Conservative shadow chancellor, said if Healey "reaches for more tax rises" in his Budget, "he is choosing slower growth and working people will pay for it". Burnham has pledged to create "good growth in every postcode" as part of his plans to giving nations and regions more control, but his strategy has faced criticism inside his own party. The IMF said households are likely to continue feeling the pinch of rising prices, with inflation expected to average 3.3% this year and remain above the Bank of England's 2% target in 2027 at 2.8%. The Bank itself has predicted inflation could rise above 4% at the beginning of next year - making it more likely that interest rates will rise.

events.title: CNBC Daily Open: 'Boring' trumps disorder and volatility
events.summary: The IMF warned that mounting debt, persistent inflation and AI-related borrowing could trigger a “disorderly” spike in sovereign bond yields. The fund raised its 2026 global growth forecast as AI investment offsets part of the Middle East energy shock, but cautioned that the world economy’s resilience is approaching its limits. Asian technology stocks tumbled, with SK Hynix, Samsung and SoftBank hit by concerns over AI financing and growing Chinese competition. DBS CEO Tan Su Shan touted Singapore’s stability and predictability, arguing that “boring is not bad.” Trump defended temporarily easing restrictions on Russian diesel despite bipartisan concerns. Hello, this is Hui Jie writing to you from Singapore. Welcome to another edition of CNBC's Daily Open. Many modern investors lack enthusiasm for "boring" — but "boring" is perhaps preferable to a disorderly market environment. The International Monetary Fund warned Tuesday that mounting debt and inflation could trigger a "disorderly" spike in sovereign bond yields. The global economy, meanwhile, is proving more resilient than expected as the AI investment boom offsets some of the energy shock from the Middle East conflict. The IMF, however, says this resilience is approaching its limits. In this context, DBS Bank CEO Tan Su Shan's assessment of Singapore as a predictable market where — "boring is not bad" — sounds rather timely. Some warning lights are flashing on the global economy dashboard. The IMF warned Tuesday that government bond yields could rise in a disorderly fashion, as rising inflation, mounting debt and AI-related borrowings pressure sovereign bond markets. Government bond yields in several advanced economies have climbed to multidecade highs, driven by higher energy costs due to the Middle East conflict and expectations for tighter monetary conditions as central banks look to curb resurgent inflation. In its latest Global Financial Stability Report, the fund warned that conditions could deteriorate, flagging the potential for "a sharp rise in sovereign bond yields." The IMF warned last week that global public debt had reached near its highest level since World War II and was on track to soon exceed 100% of GDP. A sharp rise in yields would mark down asset values through higher discount rates, including for AI-related assets, and erode the value of government bonds posted as collateral. It's not just the bond market. Silvana Tenreyro, economic counsellor and director at the IMF research department, warned that "the global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits." While the IMF sees a softer-than-anticipated slowdown in the global economy this year, partly thanks to the AI investment boom, it says this is also adding to inflationary pressures and financial fragility. "This is a large, front-loaded demand shock" that sees massive investment pouring into sectors such as semiconductors, data centers, and power generation, before any broad productivity gains have materialized, it said in the report. The IMF warned that in a scenario where AI productivity gains fail to materialize, U.S. equities could fall 20% and global growth could end up 1.1% below its baseline estimates by 2028, with Asia 1.7% lower. Against that backdrop, Singapore's predictability may be becoming a selling point. DBS CEO Tan Su Shan described the city-state as open, predictable and "almost kind of boring." "In this huge time of volatility, 'boring' is not bad, right?" she told the DBS Asia Future Forward conference. Tan said Singapore's stability and DBS' regional network could help companies diversify supply chains and pivot between markets as trade and geopolitical risks mount. On the markets front , Asian tech stocks suffered a spillover effect from the U.S. as major names like Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Softbank Group all fell during the trading session. The fall was mainly due to worries over artificial intelligence financing and intensifying competition denting sentiment. Over the weekend , China's ChangXin Memory Technologies announced significant progress in developing a new chip architecture, designed to increase memory density by packing more data into a smaller space. "Investors are jittery and looking for excuses to take profit on AI-related stocks that have outperformed this year, especially memory stocks," said UBP's senior equity advisor Vey-Sern Ling. However, Ling said that while the Chinese memory makers can potentially become a threat to global demand-supply balance over time, they continue to face short-term technology hurdles, especially for more advanced memory like HBM. U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday defended last week's decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel fuel exports after the announcement drew bipartisan criticism . Trump, in a Truth Social post , said "I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!

events.title: Tech stocks slide as Wall Street chip rout spreads. SK Hynix, SoftBank and ASML slump
events.summary: Technology stocks tumbled Tuesday as a sell-off in U.S. semiconductor shares spilled into Asian and European markets. China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, reported progress on a new chip structure, intensifying chip competition. Intel and Broadcom CEOs have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the artificial intelligence boom. Technology stocks fell Tuesday after a sell-off in U.S. semiconductor shares sparked worries over artificial intelligence financing and intensifying competition. European chip stocks sank in early morning trade, with semiconductor equipment maker ASML down 3.3%, and STMicroelectronics and German chip maker Infineon both down 5%. Dutch firms BE Semiconductor and ASM International were both around 4% lower at the open. In Japan, shares of tech-focused investment giant SoftBank Group sank 8.5%. The group, which has significant exposure to the global AI industry, led a broader retreat in Japanese semiconductor and electronics shares. Tokyo Electron , a major supplier of chipmaking equipment, dropped 7.2%, while Advantest , which makes semiconductor testing equipment, declined 2.9%. Other Japanese technology stocks also came under pressure. Lasertec fell over 5%, Disco lost 4.7% and Renesas Electronics shed 5.9%. The declines followed a weak session for technology stocks on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.44% on Monday. U.S. memory chipmaker Micron Technology slid 3.9% as investors assessed intensifying competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT , which reported progress on a new chip structure. Over the weekend , CXMT announced significant progress in developing a new chip architecture, designed to increase memory density by packing more data into a smaller space. "Investors are jittery and looking for excuses to take profit on AI-related stocks that have outperformed this year, especially memory stocks," said UBP's senior equity advisor Vey-Sern Ling. "In reality, while the Chinese memory makers can potentially become a threat to global demand-supply balance over time, in the short run they continue to face technology hurdles, especially for more advanced memory like HBM," Ling told CNBC via email. Phillip Wool, chief market strategist at Rayliant Global Advisors, said CXMT's breakthrough marked a significant milestone for Chinese chipmakers , demonstrating their ability to overcome technology restrictions and potentially challenge established players sooner than expected. But he cautioned that the market reaction appeared disproportionate to the immediate competitive threat, given that CXMT has yet to demonstrate large-scale production and continues to lag Samsung and SK Hynix in market share. "More importantly, we're not even talking about HBM here, and the Korean chipmakers are still unquestionably dominating that space, with very little threat at all from the likes of CXMT or anyone else for the foreseeable future," Wool said. He said the sharp sell-off reflected broader anxiety over the AI trade rather than a fundamental shift in the competitive landscape. "I read that more as a sign of how vulnerable AI sentiment is at this moment," Wool said, warning that volatility could persist as investors reassess chip demand and how long semiconductor manufacturers can sustain their pricing power. The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the AI boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply. Investors are also looking ahead to a busy week of corporate earnings and U.S. inflation data, which could provide fresh clues on the outlook for interest rates that often have an inverse correlation with growth stocks.

events.title: As 'Cockroach' protests grow over alleged voter fraud, Modi defends India as ‘mother of democracy’
events.summary: Protests in India demanding the removal of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, for alleged fraud have intensified. On Monday, thousands of people reportedly joined leaders of Indian opposition parties in their march to the Supreme Court in Delhi to file a petition against the Election Commission. Over the weekend, authorities cracked down on protestors by resorting to mass detentions, which led to the United Nations Human Rights Office flagging concerns. Experts said the scale of the protests does not pose a threat to the stability of India at present, but crackdowns could broaden the unrest. Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday defended India as a " mother of democracy ," as protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter fraud are intensifying. "A wide range of issues are debated openly, and diverse perspectives are discussed by the people," Modi said, speaking at a Bloomberg New Economy event. His comments coincide with a severe crackdown by authorities against protestors demanding electoral reforms. Earlier today, key members of the viral pseudo-political movement, Cockroach Janta Party, were detained for protesting without permission . CJP, whose leaders were detained by authorities over the weekend as well, had sought permission from Delhi Police on Monday to launch fresh protests at the Jantar Mantar grounds in the capital. However, the government then barred the use of the site for protests. On Monday, thousands of people reportedly joined leaders of Indian opposition parties in their march to the Supreme Court in Delhi to file a petition against revisions made to the voter list by the Election Commission. Names of 130 million people have been struck off from the voter list after the commission began conducting "special intensive revisions" (SIR) to update voter lists across the country last year, as per several local media reports. Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the opposition in India, said the huge crowds were a sign that people were not going to be "intimidated" by the government . "There are no parallel protests. It's one protest, and it's a protest where everybody is standing together," Gandhi said, dismissing concerns over the absence of members of the Cockroach Janta Party who had called for protests over the weekend. "Delhi is once again flooded with people standing up to save democracy ," Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the viral pseudo-political movement, CJP, said in a post, reacting to the crowd amassed for the march led by Gandhi. Over the weekend, Indian security forces reportedly clamped down on protests in the capital city, detaining young people, several opposition party politicians, YouTubers, lawyers and a few journalists. The Delhi police, which is under the control of the Indian home ministry, did not respond to an email seeking comments. Experts told CNBC that while the scale of the protests does not pose a threat to the stability of India at present, crackdowns could broaden the unrest. "If security forces keep taking heavy-handed approaches, this will create a more volatile environment that could make protestors angrier and galvanize even larger groups of marchers," Michael Kugelman of the Atlantic Council told CNBC. He added that at present the scale of the protests was not significant enough to impact "capital flow and investor behavior" but warned that "heavy-handed tactics that generate violence and volatility" by the state could change it. The United Nations Human Rights Office on Saturday raised concerns over mass detentions and called on Indian authorities "to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled." On Sunday, India's Ministry of External Affairs responded to the UNHR's comments, calling them "unwarranted" and claiming they constituted an "unacceptable interference in the internal affairs of India." The crackdown during the latest protest has been "significant and massive" compared to earlier reactions to farmers' protests or uniform civil code protests, Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at Teneo, told CNBC. He added that there is a higher chance that the broad-based retaliation to the police crackdown could lead to more demonstrations. The CJP had first called for a nationwide protest on Oct. 2 , seeking the removal of the election chief after an investigative report by the Indian Express showed discrepancies in the functioning of the Election Commission and reports of deletion of millions of voters. On Sept. 26, following reports of the voter deletion, the Election Commission of India launched a special drive across India to enroll voters who have been left out of the rolls . It has downplayed discrepancies as highlighted in the Indian Express report and maintains it is "committed to ensuring that no eligible voter is left out of the voter list .

events.title: Despite his $200 million success, Matthew McConaughey spent a weekend in the desert reading 20 years of bad reviews—he says some of them had ‘a point’
events.summary: Matthew McConaughey has an Oscar, an estimated $200 million net worth and a hefty catalog of 20 years’ worth of reviews—good and bad. Despite his clear career success, he collated all the worst things ever written about him, went to the desert for a weekend, and read every one. “I took them on as a thick book… not all the positive, the negative ones—and I sat with them,” McConaughey said in a recent interview with Build or Break .  “It’s all I took, and I spent two days looking at them, and it was hard.”  And he learned from the tough experience that there are two kinds of critics—and only one is worth listening to. “Some of the reviews, what I learned is that, from the very first sentence, this person has it out for me. It didn’t matter if they saw the movie or not. They just don’t like me. They were going to write a negative review,” McConaughey explained.  Not every bad review was out to get him, though. Some were still critical, but actually useful. “I was like, ‘This person got a point.’ They’re actually a fan of mine, and they didn’t get from my performance what I was actually hoping they would’ve got. Where did I fail in achievement?” That he says is constructive criticism.  “They were looking at the work and objectively criticizing it. Applauded some things, but also applauded some things that shined a light on where I came up short.” His next question was simple: What can I learn from that? “Some are going to write bad about you or wish you the worst no matter what, because they just don’t like you from afar, don’t like your success or what have you,” he added. “Some are really good critics or write constructively about what you did wrong—and you can learn from it.” And it’s a lesson you can carry into every discipline. No matter how good you are, there’s always room to learn more. But first, you have to separate the feedback that’s real from the noise. Taking criticism is even now a job interview test—and one CEO says candidates who ‘get offended’ aren’t a fit McConaughey’s team told Fortune the trip to the West Texas desert near Marfa came around 2018 or 2019, while he was writing Greenlights . By then, he’d been in the business for more than two decades, since his 1993 breakout in Dazed and Confused , with major hits like Interstellar and True Detective already behind him. And he’s hardly the only big name who keeps taking feedback on board. Ozark actor Jason Bateman said in an interview with Esquire last year that he also reads all the reviews for his television shows and movies because they shape how he shows up for the people on the other side of the silver screen who are paying to see him play. “I am doing these projects for public consumption, so it matters to me what the public thinks about them,” he said. And at the top of the business world, there’s no resting on your laurels either.   Despite growing a $5.5 trillion company from the ground up, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is still hard on himself. After more than 3 decades of climbing to the top, he still works seven days a week and says he’s “always in a state of anxiety” that Nvidia could go under. “Nobody suffers better than I can,” Huang recently said in conversation with the Korea Society. “In order to do something incredible, you have to suffer. It’s not a walk in the park. If it’s a walk in the park, anybody could do it.” He’s even admitted he’s “still working on being a good CEO.” And he’s no softer on his staff. The billionaire boss says he criticizes everything they show him . “You can’t show me something without me giving you some criticism,” he told CNA. Huang said he believes feedback works best when delivered immediately, and with improvement (not punishment) in mind. “Just like a Taiwanese parent, once the feedback is given, you’re back to loving the person again,” Huang said. “And so, I’m always critical of everybody’s work so that I can help them be better.” Ralph Lauren CEO Patrice Louvet doesn’t believe in sugar-coating feedback either. “Sometimes people need to be hit by a 2×4 across the forehead, because it doesn’t always register right,” he told LinkedIn’s This is Working podcast.  The French-born Fortune 500 exec said that addressing weaknesses sooner rather than later can help businesses—and careers—thrive. One CEO thinks the ability to take feedback on board is so important that he’s testing for it in the interview room. Gagan Biyani , the CEO of the education platform Maven and a cofounder of Udemy, has started giving candidates critiques live in the interview, sometimes in front of a full panel. He calls it the “most telling part” of the process, and it’s often what decides whether they get the job. “If this is their nightmare, [the] candidate freezes up or even gets offended,” Biyani added it highlights straight away that they are ‘not a fit’ for the company. “If this is exciting, they are more likely to join.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: This 39-year-old quit 80-hour consulting weeks to make underwear for his struggling family business. He credits ‘sweaty feet’ for record profits
events.summary: When Lawson Glidden gets back from a hike in the woods around Ashland, N.H., he doesn’t always head home. Sometimes he heads to the sock department. “If my sock doesn’t fit just right, then when I get back from my hike, I go to the sock department, and I check in on our QC boards and make sure that the foot is fitting correctly,” he told Fortune . Glidden, 39, is president of Minus33, a maker of merino-wool base layers, underwear and socks, and the latest incarnation of a textile business his family has run in Ashland since 1916. He wears what he sells, more or less head to toe. “We make this polo, we make the underwear I’m wearing,” he said on a video call. “… We don’t make the pants or the shoes. That’s all we don’t make right now.” He also has opinions about what he sells. “They are the best socks on the planet,” Glidden said. “I say that because not only am I incentivized to say it and I believe it, but also because it’s true.” The numbers he cites aren’t modest either. Since he joined the company in 2018, Glidden said, profits have roughly quadrupled, and revenue is up about 2.5 to three times. The company’s PR pitch to Fortune billed this year as one of its highest-profit years. Minus33 is privately held, and Fortune could not independently verify the figures. That’s a long way from where the family stood two decades ago. At its peak in the 1990s, Glidden said, the family’s mill was a $50 million operation with about 300 employees. By around 2002 it was, in his words, “a zero-dollar, three-person company.” Glidden tells the story of how it got back up — and of nearly everything else — at length. At the end of the interview, he made an offer: “If you ever want to talk again, I can talk for days.” ‘If you put moose on it’ When Glidden left tech consulting and came home in 2018, the first thing he did was buy sock machines and learn to program and run them. Minus33 started manufacturing in the U.S. in 2019. “I program and designed them all myself,” he said. He thought socks were a solved problem. Then he got the machine. “You’re like, wait a second, everybody else, they could have been making this good sock the whole time, and they just chose not to,” Glidden said. “I had the same sock-making machine as everybody else.” There are a lot of ways to make a sock, he said. You can stuff it with synthetic material for durability. You can make it bigger, because a bigger sock looks meatier on the shelf and, he says, studies show it sells better. Or you can make it fit. His socks hug the foot “like a second skin that eliminates all the friction,” which lets him use less nylon and more wool, he said. He claims a pair has lasted the entire Appalachian Trail, worn every fourth day, without a hole. The tradeoff is that they look smaller on the shelf, and plainer. Glidden is fine with that. The alternative, as he describes it, is some “business analyst sitting in New York, you know, saying, oh, if you put moose on it, it’ll be better. I don’t know.” “We’re not as stylized or pretty as everybody else, but I think that’s fine,” he said. “I made them for myself. I’ve got sweaty feet, and I just kept making socks until I no longer got blisters and I was comfortable all day.” His advice to other founders follows from that. “Use your product every single day,” he said. “If you use it every single day, then your customer’s complaints become your complaints. And therefore you’re just going to fix it yourself.” ‘I live where people go on vacation’ Ask Glidden about his business, and he may start with the trees. Ashland, a town of fewer than 2,000 people, sits roughly at the geographic center of New Hampshire, in the state’s Lakes Region. Squam Lake is five minutes away, he said. His favorite snowboarding mountains are 25 minutes away. Boston is an hour and a half down the highway. And the foliage, he informed Fortune in early October, is “the best foliage in the world right now.” “Yes, I live where people go on vacation,” he said. He spent about eight years in Worcester, Mass., including his time at Worcester Polytechnic Institute, and doesn’t plan on going back. Down there, he said, it’s houses, then some trees, then houses. “But up in New Hampshire, it’s a house, an entire forest of trees, another house, an entire forest of trees, and I just don’t know if I could go back,” he said. “I can’t give up on my trees.” Before he came home, he was a senior technical consultant for a regulatory-software company, doing database work for big telecom companies that needed to report data to the government monthly instead of yearly after a change in the law. He was working 80-hour weeks. One year he did the math and figured he’d spent the equivalent of a full month — 24 hours a day, 30 days — on airplanes. In 2018, his father called and asked if he wanted to come work at the family business. He did. Two years later, he was president. Asked whether being a fifth-generation member of the founding family gave him an inside track, Glidden didn’t argue. “I do have an inside track,” he said. “But like all generational companies, they start up here, and then they go down.” Broadcloth, cashmere and a shotgun In 1916, his “dad’s dad’s dad’s uncle,” as Glidden puts it, bought up buildings in Ashland and started the L.W. Packard Mill. For roughly 82 years it made wool broadcloth — in the same building where Glidden works today — and sold it to garment makers in New York who turned it into suits and overcoats. In the 1990s, Glidden’s father, a textile engineer, took the business into cashmere, a fiber that cost about “a hundred dollars a kilo,” Glidden said, and that few companies were willing to risk processing. “We became a $50 million company in the ’90s because my father took the technology to basically make cashmere,” he said. Then the bottom fell out. As apparel production moved overseas, the New York customers disappeared. “Everyone that bought wool from us … and sewed it into beautiful suits and pea coats and stuff, they stopped doing that, and therefore they stopped buying from us,” Glidden said. The suppliers that had processed wool and cashmere and shipped it in bulk to the U.S. pulled back too. The company was cut out from both ends. Ashland had plenty of company. events.title: I built a family business from scratch to $200 million. Now I’ve become its bottleneck
events.summary: In 2003, my father, my sister and I founded Kormotech, a Ukrainian family-run company producing cat and dog food; in 2008, I became its CEO. I made decisions quickly, trusted my intuition and didn’t believe in lengthy approval processes. Over 23 years, the company has grown into a business with revenue of $210 million , and we’ve become one of the world’s top 50 pet food manufacturers. When, in 2021, we set ourselves the goal of becoming a global company, I realized that my management style, which had helped Kormotech grow, was now holding it back. I had become the bottleneck in my own business. In the spring of 2022, at the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, we began looking for independent directors for the supervisory board. It wasn’t the best time for a major transformation, but we had only two options: to globalize or to disappear in the face of the new challenges posed by the war. The board began its work in early 2024. We gave the independent directors the majority of the votes – five out of nine – meaning they had the right to block even my decisions.  Agreeing to this was easier than actually sharing power and relinquishing some control. It was only once the board was running that I realized what this meant in practice. Here are three things it taught me. The owner must evolve alongside the company When we were just starting out and looking for a way to get into supermarkets, there were five of us. We didn’t even have an office, and we’d discuss how to do it over lunch at our first factory. We operated like a startup. I knew every member of the team; we’d stay late coming up with new ideas, and back then, building a management system wasn’t on the agenda.  We acted quickly, even when decisions seemed risky. For a young company, this was a competitive advantage over multinational corporations. Eventually, we captured over 30% of our home market, overtaking Nestlé Purina and Mars. Today, Kormotech employs 1,500 people across five countries, including the U.S. I can no longer afford to make all decisions as quickly and unilaterally as before, because they affect far more people and processes. What once made me a strong CEO is something I now have to consciously learn to rein in. When you’re both CEO and owner, it’s a whole new level of complexity, because changing your management approach means, in part, changing yourself. A willingness to share power means a willingness to hear the word “no” Being prepared to hear “no” from the board is the key condition under which it makes any sense at all. If the owner wants to retain the ability to override the board’s decisions at any moment, then it is an advisory panel, not a supervisory board.  Recently, we were preparing to acquire a Ukrainian company; the term sheet had already been signed, and the lawyers were finalizing the agreement. But the board blocked it. Naturally, I wasn’t pleased: I was ready to move on, but I had to return to the negotiating table. In the end, we agreed on significantly better terms than those initially proposed. For me, this confirmed why the board needs the right not only to advise the CEO, but also to stop them. The hardest thing to accept is that people who didn’t build this company alongside you can see things you don’t. Sometimes I even regret that I didn’t come up with certain ideas proposed by the board myself. But that’s precisely why it’s needed: not to rubber-stamp the owner’s decisions, but to broaden the boundaries of their experience. The owner must step back from day-to-day management in time My sister and I each have two daughters, and the eldest have already said they don’t see themselves taking on day-to-day management at Kormotech. I’m not going to try to persuade them – I didn’t want to get into the business myself until I was twenty-four; back then, I wanted to open a nightclub. But we’re a family business, and naturally we’re thinking about handing it over to the next generation. I’m not going to leave my children a folder of instructions saying “do it the way Dad did.” On the contrary, the company must be able to develop in the future without being tied to my way of running it. At the moment, I’m wearing three hats at once – owner, member of the supervisory board and CEO. For a family business, this is a risk, because it makes the company too dependent on one person, and as long as I remain irreplaceable, the problem isn’t solved. Over the next few years, Kormotech should be led by a hired CEO, while I step back from day-to-day management. It is quite likely that this person will prove to be stronger at this than me. If that happens, it will mean that I, as the owner, have done my job properly. events.title: Binance weighs stock access in markets including Hong Kong and South Korea, says co-CEO Richard Teng
events.summary: Binance is considering offering exposure to stocks from markets including Hong Kong, South Korea, Taiwan, and Brazil as the world’s largest crypto exchange pushes beyond digital assets and seeks to become an all-in-one trading platform , co-CEO Richard Teng told Fortune . “We are weatherproofing ourselves,” Teng said on the sidelines of TOKEN2049 in Singapore. “A lot of our users say: ‘Hey, I want to have exposure to, let’s say, the top 10 Hong Kong stocks, top 10 Korean counters, top 10 Taiwanese, Brazilian counters.’ We’re looking at what our users demand and giving them that.” In 2026, Binance introduced trading in tokenized U.S. stocks and commodity derivatives, including precious metals and oil. The exchange also rolled out pre-IPO perpetual futures contracts settled in USDT, a U.S.-dollar-linked stablecoin, giving traders the ability to speculate on the expected valuation of private companies like Anthropic. Sitting behind this shift is a slump in digital asset prices . Bitcoin and other cryptocurrency prices remain far below the highs reached in October 2025. Coinbase, for example, posted a net loss of $359.5 million in Q2 2026, its third consecutive quarterly net loss, as transaction revenue declined. Several cryptocurrency exchanges, including Binance, are transforming themselves from apps devoted to coins like Bitcoin and Ethereum into platforms that can handle different asset classes . Coinbase rolled out traditional stock trading, perpetual futures, and prediction markets on its platform last December as part of its push to become an “everything exchange.” OKX last week revealed plans to both offer tokenized shares in dozens of U.S. companies (through a joint venture with Intercontinental Exchange), as well as launch a new app for U.S.-dollar-linked stablecoins . Traditional financial companies are embracing digital assets, while crypto platforms must accept clearer rules to attract institutional money . “The first 3% of [crypto] adopters didn’t need certainty, and they didn’t want certainty,” Teng said. “But for crypto to go mainstream, we need not just retail investors, but also sophisticated institutions that want clear rules and regulations they can operate within.” Teng casts tokenized stocks and round-the-clock trading as ways to give investors outside major financial centers greater access to global markets . “Many people are still constrained by the geography that they are born in,” Teng said, pointing to how those born in emerging markets in Africa or Latin America may still lack access to U.S. stocks, despite the U.S. being the world’s largest capital market. “If we tokenize U.S. stocks, these people can get exposure to companies around the world they may not have had access to previously.” Today, though many more individuals are banked, roughly 1.3 billion adults globally still lack access to a formal bank account, according to a 2025 World Bank report. Binance, therefore, acts as a so-called shadow bank for savings, yield generation, and cross-border payments, while allowing access to global stocks with low entry thresholds. Later this month, Binance will roll out Binance AI Pro, an AI-powered crypto trading assistant that automates market analysis, strategy execution, and position management. Teng expects more trading to shift to AI agents as investors grow more comfortable setting the parameters that guide them. “It has been a great leveler,” he said. “But the nature of trading will be different.” Where ‘clear rules and regulations’ come from Binance tapped Teng to serve as its CEO in November 2023, after founder Changpeng “CZ” Zhao came under regulatory scrutiny in the U.S. after failing to register as a money-transmitting business and breaching sanctions laws. Following the criminal plea, Binance paid $4.3 billion in penalties and forfeitures, while Zhao personally paid a $50 million fine and served a four-month prison sentence . (He was later pardoned by U.S. President Donald Trump) Teng started his career on the traditional side of the finance sector , with roles at the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the country’s central bank, and the Singapore Exchange. He credits his time at both those institutions for his perspectives on risk and growth. “If you look at many different regulatory agencies around the world, the key focus is just to mitigate risk, but if you do that to the extreme, that means very minimal or no growth,” Teng explains. At MAS, Teng said he had the dual task of both regulating and growing the financial services sector. “It’s not only about looking at the risk dimension of the ecosystem, but also how you mitigate and manage it in order to support growth,” he adds. Teng was first exposed to the world of blockchain and cryptocurrencies in 2017 during a visit to the U.S. when he was serving as CEO of the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of the Abu Dhabi Global Market, an international finance center in the United Arab Emirates.  Teng grew to believe that cryptocurrencies could broaden financial access in emerging markets. “I was blessed to be born and bred in Singapore, where we had access to multiple banks and investment platforms, but many people around the world were not as fortunate.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Cyber attack hits hundreds of French supermarkets, heating fridges to 122°F and sparking fires
events.summary: Hackers targeted hundreds of French supermarkets, causing refrigerators and freezers to overheat. The attack sparked fires and spoiled food across supermarkets in the region. European Commissioner for Agriculture and Food Christophe Hansen warned that "the weaponization of food has become a reality." Hackers targeted hundreds of French supermarkets in a cyberattack that reportedly caused refrigerators and freezers to overheat, spoiling food and sparking fires. Fridges at French supermarket chains Carrefour, Monoprix, the Les Mousquetaires-owned Intermarché, and Coopérative U, among others, all saw fridges heat up to as much as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) overnight, Reuters reported on Monday. Coopérative U's CEO Dominique Schelcher confirmed that cyberattacks had affected "refrigeration production facilities of several stores." "Attacking equipment that is essential to the preservation of fresh products and the food supply of the French people is extremely serious and unprecedented. It is unacceptable," Schelcher said in a LinkedIn post . CNBC has reached out to Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarché, Coopérative U, and E Leclerc for comment but did not immediately hear back. Felix Aime, a senior cyber threat intelligence analyst ​at Sekoia Threat Detection and Research, said the attack affected several European countries including Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium, per the Reuters article. "I strongly condemn the cyberattack targeting food products at @intermarche @CooperativeU @Leclerc," European Commissioner for Agriculture and Food Christophe Hansen said in a post on X on Monday. "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponization of food has become a reality."

events.title: Emir says Qatar has shown resilience in the face of ‘exceptional events’
events.summary: Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani says Qatar has demonstrated its strength and cohesion. Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani has told the Shura Council that the region has faced “exceptional events”, during months of instability amid the United States-Israeli war on Iran . Speaking in the capital, Doha, on Tuesday, Sheikh Tamim said Qatar’s response had shown its resilience. “Our country and the region have faced exceptional events that have once again proven the cohesion of state institutions,” the Emir said. Qatar has found itself caught up in the war, which began on February 28 and has triggered a global energy crisis. The Gulf state has been directly attacked by Iran on several occasions, including in March, when Tehran struck Qatar’s Ras Laffan gas facility , the world’s largest liquefied natural gas (LNG) production site. Sheikh Tamim said Qatar had been able to absorb the consequences of the regional instability due to policies implemented before the war, stressing that Doha’s preference was to resolve conflicts through peaceful means and dialogue. However, the Emir maintained that the Gulf Cooperation Council’s (GCC) security was non-negotiable. “The security of Gulf Cooperation Council states and the preservation of their sovereignty are matters that cannot be compromised on,” he said. The war on Iran has disrupted global supply routes, particularly the Strait of Hormuz, which Tehran has effectively blocked since the start of the conflict. Sheikh Tamim said efforts to safeguard maritime routes must be increased. “Efforts must be doubled to secure navigation in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz and to protect energy facilities and civilian infrastructure,” he said. Reporting from Doha, Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi said Sheikh Tamim had used the address to reiterate Qatar’s preference for ending wars and resolving disagreements through peaceful dialogue, while reaffirming the country’s commitment to the Palestinian cause. “He highlighted how the attacks on LNG facilities have effectively hurt Qatar’s capacity, it has hurt Qatar’s economy directly,” Basravi said. “He also cautioned and said that ‘we should not be like we were before this crisis going forward’. Certainly, a signal that will be taken seriously by those in this chamber; by people heading up institutions.” “If you read between the lines, the signal is clear, that they will lean into non-carbon related industries.” Sheikh Tamim said Qatar has invested more than $60bn across a variety of areas, including infrastructure projects, public-private partnerships and private sector investment. Rashid Al-Mohanadi, vice president of the Center for International Policy Research, told Al Jazeera that Qatar has a history of “turning crises into opportunities”. “In the last 10 years, Qatar has been through many challenges and usually the output is we become more resilient. The hope is that after this war, which has been very challenging on the population [and] on the economy, that Qatar will turn out stronger and more resilient,” Al-Mohanadi said.

events.title: Malaysia’s Firefly cancels flights to Singapore over haze from Indonesia
events.summary: Move comes as haze from Indonesian fires makes Singapore and Kuala Lumpur the world’s most polluted cities. Firefly, a Malaysian low-cost airline, has extended the suspension of its flights between Kuala Lumpur and Singapore through Wednesday as smoke from fires in Indonesia continued to blanket the region. The announcement came as IQAir, an air quality monitor, ranked Singapore and the Malaysian capital Kuala Lumpur as the world’s two most polluted cities on Tuesday. list 1 of 2 Central Colombia forest fire threatens tourist town of Villa de Leyva list 2 of 2 ‘Nature can recover’: Inside the race to rescue world’s crisis-hit wildlife Firefly said in a statement that flights between the Sultan Abdul Aziz Shah Airport (SZB) near Kuala Lumpur and the Seletar Airport in Singapore (XSP) have been cancelled up to Wednesday due to “weather and haze conditions”. It called the action a “proactive safety measure”. The fires, mostly on the Indonesian islands of Sumatra and Borneo, are the country’s most intense in 11 years. They have been spurred by El Nino, a weather pattern expected to be among the strongest in four decades. IQAir, a Swiss air quality monitoring company, said Air Quality Index in Singapore stood at 199 on Tuesday and 183 in Kuala Lumpur. Readings above 150 are generally considered unhealthy, and those above 300 are classified as hazardous. Firefly, a subsidiary of Malaysia Aviation Group, which includes Malaysia Airlines, first announced the flight cancellations on October 10, citing “low visibility” due to the haze conditions. Firefly said that affected passengers were being rebooked on Malaysia Airlines flights between Kuala Lumpur International Airport and Singapore’s Changi Airport, subject to seat availability. The Singapore government has reintroduced subsidised care for haze-related illnesses, as it last did in 2015, when smoke from Indonesian fires hung over the region for weeks. In Malaysia, schools reopened in most states on Tuesday as air quality improved slightly, but they remain closed in three states, one federal territory and several districts. Malaysia’s foreign minister, Mohamad Hasan, said on Monday that he would press for stronger regional mechanisms when foreign ministers of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) meet next month. “We already have an ASEAN mechanism for natural disasters, but haze is not included or classified as a natural disaster,” he told reporters in Sepang, according to Bernama, Malaysia’s state news agency. The Philippines, which chairs the bloc this year, confirmed that the issue would be on the agenda. “It’s in the agenda,” Dominic Xavier Imperial, a spokesman for the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs, said of the November meeting, which will precede the 49th ASEAN summit in Manila. Mohamad, the Malaysian minister, said Indonesia had deployed about 60,000 personnel to fight the fires, but thick smoke had grounded 34 aircraft, including planes and helicopters. Remote terrain and limited water supplies have also hindered the effort, he said, and cloud seeding is not possible without suitable rain clouds. He acknowledged Indonesia’s efforts but urged more effective action, citing the toll on Malaysian communities.

events.title: IMF raises its forecast for world growth this year but warns of risks from AI boom and debt
events.summary: The International Monetary Fund has slightly upgraded its outlook for the world economy for this year, but it's forecasting growth at a still sluggish 3.1% BANGKOK -- The International Monetary Fund on Tuesday slightly upgraded its outlook for the world economy for this year, while warning of growing risks from rising debt, including borrowing related to artificial intelligence. The IMF says it expects the global economy to grow at a 3.1% pace this year. That's up from its July forecast for 3.0% growth and well below the 3.5% expansion in 2025. Growth in 2027 should rebound to 3.4%, it said in its latest Economic Outlook. The report, released as world economic and financial leaders gather in Bangkok for the fall meetings of the IMF and World Bank, predicts that growth in the United States will remain steady at 2.3% in 2026 and 2027. Collectively, advanced economies will grow 2.1% this year, up from 2.0% in 2025. But growth is forecast to slow to 1.9% next year, it said. The forecasts are based on a nearly 41% increase in oil prices this year, at an average of $96 a barrel. Global inflation is foreseen at 4.7% in 2026, falling to 4.1% next year. They also are based on the assumption that shipments of oil and gas through the Strait of Hormuz will resume by March, and that the boom in AI demand will moderate. The boom in artificial intelligence is offsetting damage from sharply higher prices for oil and gas, IMF economists say, but it also carries risks. Its benefits are not shared equally: the U.S. and China account for more than three-quarters of net demand for imports of computer chips and other AI-related equipment, the report said. “The outlook is highly uneven,” Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF's director of research, told reporters in Bangkok. Growth is increasingly concentrated, with 32 countries accounting for 95% of global growth, the report said. That compares with 54 countries as of April. “The global economy is not simply slowing or accelerating; rather, growth is being reallocated across countries according to their exposure to the war-induced supply shock and AI-related demand strength,” it says. Athanasios Vamvakidis, deputy director at the IMF's Monetary and Capital Markets Department, said an AI-related correction in stock markets is just one of the risks. Rising bond yields are another evolving problem, along with cyberthreats that could disrupt financial systems, he said. AI's effects on employment are another key focus of the meetings in Bangkok, which IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva described during an event Monday as “a slow moving tsunami, but a tsunami nonetheless." Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded 8 people, including 2 kids, pregnant woman, killed at home: Police Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer "The impact over time on jobs globally we estimate to be around 40% — jobs either augmented or downgraded or eliminated. And we are already seeing some of this impact,” she said. Last week, the IMF chief urged countries both rich and poor to do a better job of improving their national finances , urging policymakers to do more to tame mounting levels of debt. That's especially true at a time of high borrowing costs, Tenreyro said. Countries that are somewhat insulated from the energy shocks of the Iran war and that are benefiting from rapid adoption of AI are managing to keep growth on track. But developing economies and emerging markets more vulnerable to higher costs for oil and gas will see growth slow to 3.7% this year from 4.5% in 2025, the report says. It forecasts they will regain momentum next year, expanding at a 4.4% annual pace. The situation is much worse in the Middle East and Central Asia, where those regions' economies are expected to contract this year before recovering to a 6.3% rate of growth in 2027. The 21 European countries that share the euro currency are expected to grow by 1.1% this year and 1.2% in 2027. China , the world’s No. 2 economy, is expected to expand 4.5% this year, down from 5% in 2025, in line with the government's official target. India is once again forecast to be the world’s fastest-growing major economy, advancing at a 7% clip, down from a sizzling 7.7% last year. The IMF is a 191-nation lending organization that works to promote economic growth and financial stability and to reduce global poverty. At the meetings in Bangkok, finance ministers and central bank governors will assess the state of the world economy and discuss strategies to support financial stability and sustained growth. events.title: Imran Khan’s PTI braces to fight federal takeover of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
events.summary: Islamabad says the PTI failed to lead the fight against armed groups, but analysts question the takeover. Islamabad, Pakistan – The Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party of jailed ex-Prime Minister Imran Khan is planning to legally challenge the federal government’s Sunday takeover of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, a province that the party governed. Sheikh Waqas Akram, the PTI’s central information secretary, told Al Jazeera that the party would challenge the imposition of emergency laws – suspending civil liberties – and governor’s rule in the province in court on Tuesday. A petition had been drafted by a legal committee headed by PTI Secretary-General Salman Akram Raja, but Akram did not say whether it would be filed in the Supreme Court or the Federal Constitutional Court. list 1 of 4 Can Pakistan’s Sohail Afridi win freedom for ex-PM Imran Khan? list 2 of 4 What do emergency and governor rule in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa mean? list 3 of 4 Pakistan suspends Imran Khan’s party-led provincial government list 4 of 4 Pakistan imposes emergency rule in ​province governed by Imran Khan’s party The federal government’s moves have emerged as Pakistan’s latest political flashpoint, with competing narratives from the government and the PTI, at a time when the party was in the middle of a delayed march towards Islamabad, aimed at pressuring authorities to release former PM Khan, who has been jailed for more than three years. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Monday justified the government’s moves by arguing that federal rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was needed for Pakistan to effectively combat “terrorism” in the province that shares a porous border with Afghanistan. “No war can be won, however many resources you bring, whatever you do, until the government there leads it,” Naqvi said in Peshawar on Monday. On Sunday, President Asif Ali Zardari imposed emergency rule and governor’s rule, suspending the PTI government in the northwestern province. The party has governed Khyber Pakhtunkhwa since 2013. Sohail Afridi , the suspended chief minister, and some members of his cabinet have been taken into preventive custody, Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry confirmed on Monday. Afridi had been leading the march towards Islamabad seeking to free Khan, and despite the setbacks to the party, PTI leaders said the protest was still on. “The long march has not ended. But a historic crackdown against the party has begun,” Akram said. According to the proclamation signed on Sunday, the provincial government had “failed to demonstrate the ownership, will and intent to adequately deal with the menace of terrorism”. “The federal government’s position is clearly described. ‘A deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism’ as communicated after cabinet meeting. That’s the constitutional premise needed for imposition of emergency,” Aasiya Riaz, joint director of the independent political think tank the Pakistan Institute of Legislative Development and Transparency (PILDAT), told Al Jazeera. However, Hassan Abdullah Niazi, an adjunct faculty member at the Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS) and a lawyer based in Lahore, disputed that premise. “If all of this was true, then KP would be in a state of anarchy, but we know that is not the case. It had a functioning legislature and executive that commanded the confidence of the people, hence this entire exercise is an unconstitutional move against provincial autonomy,” he told Al Jazeera. A more detailed case was set out last month in a 14-page white paper presented in Islamabad by Ikhtiar Wali Khan, a political adviser to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif from the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PMLN). The paper pointed to rising police deaths, staff and equipment shortages in the provincial counterterrorism department, and spending priorities. However, Akram rejected the charge that the PTI had failed to lead the fight. He said the provincial government had paid 1.83 billion rupees ($6.6m) from its own funds to the families of more than 900 soldiers, police and paramilitary personnel killed fighting armed groups, a contribution he said no other province had made. Naqvi said at a news conference in Islamabad on Sunday that the federal government had been involved in negotiations with the PTI on a proposed “sit-in” by the party in support of Khan. “We have no problem with the sit-in. Do the sit-in as eagerly as you like; we have no issue with the sit-in. Our issue is entirely terrorism-related, and we want to get you on board on that,” he said. Taimur Jhagra, a PTI leader and former provincial finance and health minister, said the talks with the government that the party had agreed to were meant to focus on Khan . “It’s absurd that a negotiation about a protest movement to give Imran Khan Supreme Court-ordered medical and visitation rights becomes a negotiation about terrorism strategy,” he told Al Jazeera.

events.title: Visa gets Beijing's green light for bank card business after 40 years of working with China
events.summary: Visa said Tuesday it received China's approval to begin the process of establishing a local bank card clearing business. Mastercard and American Express have already gotten the approvals in the last several years. Visa's CEO became chair of the U.S.-China Business Council in June. BEIJING — U.S. credit card giant Visa announced Tuesday it had received approval from the People's Bank of China for setting up a bank card clearing business in the country. The news comes as the U.S. and Chinese presidents plan for their third meeting this year. "This marks an important milestone toward the company serving China's domestic payments market," Visa said in a statement. "For more than 40 years, Visa has been an active contributor to China's dynamic payments landscape," Visa CEO Ryan McInerney said. "We look forward to taking the necessary steps in the process, pursuant to the PBOC's regulations, to begin operating domestically in China." McInerney joined U.S. President Donald Trump's business delegation to Beijing in May and subsequently became chair of the U.S.-China Business Council in June. The Visa CEO also led a trip to Beijing in early September . "The timing is notable," said George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice, The Asia Group. "Beijing chose to approve visa's license just ahead of the APEC Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen next month, where Xi [Jinping] and Trump are expected to meet again," he said. "The move suggests that Beijing is keen to demonstrate tangible progress for American businesses before Trump's next visit to China." Trump told Fox News after his Beijing trip in May that he brought up Visa's request to gain China market access. After the summit in September, China said it would approve applications from all foreign financial institutions to operate in the country . Mainland China has kept a tight grip on its financial sector, favoring domestic players and restricting cross-border capital flows. Visa previously said it had applied with the PBOC in May 2020 to operate a bank card clearing institution. The company has worked with Chinese banks for dual-branded cards, for which China's UnionPay processes transactions domestically and Visa processes overseas payments. In January, Visa said the mainland China-issued cards could be linked to Apple Pay for use overseas. Rival Mastercard 's joint venture in China said it started processing payments in 2024 after getting the PBOC's approval to begin bank card clearing preparations in February 2020. American Express was the first, receiving its processing license in June 2020 after getting the PBOC nod back in 2018 . Mobile pay dominates daily consumer transactions in China, primarily facilitated by Tencent's WeChat and Alibaba-affiliate Ant's Alipay.
