events.title: Russia is copying cruise missile tech onto its $50,000 drones to deal with Ukraine's jamming
events.summary: Ukraine's intelligence directorate is seeking information about a new optical system found on Russia's latest Gerans. Screenshots via Telegram/GUR Ukraine is warning about a new navigation system on Russian Gerans called the Susanin. It uses a camera and a pre-saved library of images of Ukraine's terrain to fly independently. The capability, similar to a tech on cruise missiles, could help Gerans completely bypass jamming. Last week, Ukraine's defense intelligence directorate put out a call for information on a device newly found in Russia's latest killer drones. The "Susanin," a small cylinder with a camera lens, is an optical system that enables Russia's long-range drones to navigate Ukraine's skies without relying on satellite or radio signals. Should Moscow deploy them at scale, the modules would introduce a major new challenge for Kyiv, allowing Russian one-way drones to bypass jamming — a key pillar of Ukraine's air defense network. Per the intelligence directorate, or GUR, the Kremlin has been fitting them onto the turbojet Geran-4 and Geran-5 K5 , which fly at 280 mph or faster and are seeing growing use by Russia this year. These drones are already significantly harder for Ukraine to destroy by force, since they outpace typical Ukrainian interceptor drones . The Susanin works by storing images of Ukraine's terrain on the drone, then, while in flight, using a downward-facing camera to observe the ground and compare the live feed to the pre-saved imagery. Using these comparisons, the drone can independently determine its position and how to reach its target. "Even Google Earth imagery is sufficient for basic orientation," wrote Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, a prominent drone analyst connected with Ukraine's military, on Sunday. Beskrestnov warned that Russia would likely continue actively developing Susanin systems for its drones by next year. "Our enemy already uses such systems on small Molniya, V2U, and Lancet drones," he added. Cruise missile tech on a drone The technology is similar to what some cruise missiles use to reach their targets in jammed environments. The Tomahawk , for example, features what analysts call Digital Scene Matching Area Correlation to snap photos of landmarks under the missile and compare them to satellite imagery stored onboard. Higher-end Russian cruise missiles, such as the Kh-101, use a Russian version of this tech called Otblesk-U. But the Kh-101 is estimated to cost $2.4 million each, while its long-range drones cost just a fraction of that: The delta-wing Geran-4 is priced at an estimated $50,000 to $70,000 apiece, while the Geran-5 is believed to cost about $100,000 to $115,000 each. Debris of a drone lies on the ground near the Epicenter retail center following a Russian Geran-4 strike in Kharkiv. Polina Kulish/Gwara Media/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Russia has been producing these drones at a much faster pace, launching over 3,500 jet attack drones at Ukraine in September alone. Kyrylo Liukov, who leads the uncrewed technologies department at the Serhiy Prytula Charity Foundation, told Business Insider that it's "quite possible" Russia could scale up its use of navigation systems like the Susanin. "Russia is already using this navigation system for medium- and deep-strike operations," said Liukov, adding that its deployment on Geran-4s and Geran-5s has been increasing recently. Still, Liukov said these systems have their limits. The Susanin is only useful for pre-programmed drone attacks by itself, and wouldn't be able to help the drone find a moving Ukrainian armored vehicle or mobile missile launcher. "In other words, these are predominantly planned, static targets," said Liukov, whose organization raises funds for Ukraine's military and drone manufacturers. But pre-arranged flights fit well into Moscow's strategy with Gerans, which are launched in large numbers to overwhelm Ukrainian air defenses and wreak havoc on its cities. Fighting the Susanin If a Russian turbojet drone is using a Susanin system, Ukraine's only way to counter it, for now, is to use physical force, Liukov said. Ukraine's options in this area remain limited, with its military still in the early stages of introducing advanced interceptor drones capable of catching turbojet Gerans. Another way is to launch rare and expensive anti-air missiles, which are typically reserved for Russia's more powerful cruise or ballistic missiles. One possible solution Ukraine could eventually explore, Liukov said, is to blind the Susanin's camera. The camera's view of Ukrainian terrain could also be obscured by clouds, rain, or fog, he said. "For high-quality route recognition using Susanin, a flight altitude relative to speed is required that will allow for accurate orientation using the captured images, as well as favorable weather conditions," Liukov said. events.title: What to know about the Nord Stream pipeline explosions trial opening in Germany this week
events.summary: A former Ukrainian army officer is going on trial in Germany over undersea explosions that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany four years ago BERLIN -- A former Ukrainian army officer is going on trial in Germany this week over undersea explosions that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany four years ago in one of the biggest acts of sabotage in Europe since the Second World War. The suspect faces charges of causing an explosion, damaging property, disrupting public service and being an “accomplice to war crimes” by attacking civilian infrastructure, according to prosecutors . The attack laid bare Europe's dependence on Russian energy but also raised sensitive questions about Ukraine and its Western allies. While international observers initially blamed Moscow, there are now increasing suggestions that Ukrainian state security agencies may have been involved — even though Ukraine counts Germany as one of its closest allies. According to German privacy rules, the suspect will be identified in court only as Serhii K., although he was publicly named as Serhii Kuznietsov in extradition proceedings in Italy . Here's what we know about the alleged ringleader of the attack and one of the most politically charged court cases of wartime sabotage that will be heard at the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court in Hamburg starting this Wednesday. The explosions on Sept. 26, 2022, damaged pipelines that were built to carry Russian natural gas to Germany under the Baltic Sea. At the time, European countries were moving to wean themselves off Russian energy sources, following the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 . Prosecutors say the aim of the plot was to permanently disrupt gas deliveries and prevent Russia from using the revenues to finance its military operations. The defendant and others allegedly used a yacht that set off from the German port of Rostock. It had been hired from a German company using forged IDs and with the help of intermediaries. The explosions ruptured the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, which was Russia’s main natural gas supply route to Germany until Moscow cut off supplies in August 2022. They also damaged Nord Stream 2, which never entered service because Germany suspended its certification process shortly before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The suspect allegedly organized and carried out the detonation of at least four bombs between 14 and 27 kilograms (around 31 to 62 pounds) at a depth of 70 to 80 meters (230 feet to 263 feet) near the Danish island of Bornholm. He was detained in August in an Italian village, where officers raided a bungalow where he was staying with his family. Police said he surrendered without resistance. He was extradited to Germany in November. A second suspect was arrested on a European warrant in the northern Croatian town of Pula in August. He has applied for asylum in Croatia to fight his extradition to Germany. The pipelines were long a target of criticism by the U.S. and some of its allies, which warned that they increased dependence on Russian gas. Russian officials, however, have claimed that U.S. and British intelligence agencies were involved in staging the explosions, which Moscow declared “an act of international terrorism,” and have launched their own investigation. Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded 8 people, including 2 kids, pregnant woman, killed at home: Police Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer Russia has also accused NATO of involvement in the attack, while several Western countries initially blamed Russia. More recently, the Kremlin has expressed hope that those who orchestrated the explosions will be held accountable. Asked what Moscow expects from the trial, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Monday that “we expect objectivity.” “We expect … that both the perpetrators and those who ordered it will be named. That would be very important. I think no one doubts who it really is,” Peskov said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has denied allegations that his country was involved in the pipeline blasts. He also told reporters in August that Ukraine’s prosecutors and Foreign Ministry were already cooperating with partners and that Kyiv was “absolutely open to joint steps on the investigation,” stressing the importance of keeping Europe’s trust. Nonetheless, “all the evidence points very clearly to the fact that Ukraine blew up the Nord Stream pipelines, not the Russians, whom they initially tried to pin the blame on,” says Joachim Weber, a security expert at the Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies at the University of Bonn. “This is, of course, highly explosive politically, because, as is well known, Germany is one of Ukraine’s closest allies, supporting the country on a massive scale with huge sums of money and also by taking on considerable political risks,” Weber said.

events.title: BT charged me for more than a year despite landline being dead
events.summary: It is billing £32.99 a month but I have had no functioning phone line since it switched me to Digital Voice I’ve had no landline since May 2025 when BT switched it to Digital Voice. Weeks passed, and each call to BT involved at least an hour waiting on hold and answering security questions before being passed between departments. Eventually, last December, two engineers were sent and discovered that a wire had been severed during the upgrade. They said they needed a cherry picker to reconnect it to its original location and would return. They did not. Since then, I’ve called BT to no avail, and all the while I’ve been paying for a landline that doesn’t work. I am on the priority register due to serious illness and am reduced to tears of helplessness. You have been paying £32.99 a month for a dead landline and broadband, which was unaffected. BT claims it was unaware of the problem until you complained last December. You insist you had reported it before then, but do not have records of when. It turns out the case was closed in December after the engineers’ abortive visit. You next complained in January, but BT admits it again closed the case because, by then, your landline had been removed from your account, though you were still being charged. It says it did not hear from you again until I intervened in July. You said that you had believed promises that a fix was under way. A complaints manager rang you after my contact, and you were offered an extraordinary £6.46 to “make up” for its failings. Your line was eventually activated in September. The telecoms regulator Ofcom requires providers to pay £10.34 compensation a day if a reported fault is not corrected within two working days, which means you are, in theory, entitled to more than £4,600. I’ve put this to BT, but it is digging in because, it claims, you waited months to report the problems. Since you can’t provide proof to contradict it, I can’t argue the toss. You have the option of a complaint to the Communications Ombudsman but have now accepted £689 for the 60 days without service which BT acknowledges fall within the compensation rules, and for its mishandling of the two complaints it has on record. events.title: ‘People sell their best stuff on Vinted’ – how charity shops became a dumping ground for unsellable clothes
events.summary: Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more . Swamped with ‘daily avalanches’ of soiled items and poor-quality fast fashion, secondhand stores are in crisis. What went wrong with people’s good intentions? And is it possible to donate more effectively? The small stockroom of St Raphael’s Hospice charity shop in Cheam, south London, is rammed with donations. “On average, we get 30 to 50 bags a day,” says Caroline Worley, the commercial manager, “but it’s not unusual to receive over 100.” This might sound like a good problem to have, but the sheer volume of stuff is the shop’s biggest challenge. “Sometimes, there’s only [enough] floor space to tiptoe,” says 48-year-old store manager, Colin French. Rummaging through the donations, it’s clear that much is unsaleable: a smelly, soiled bathrobe, tatty trainers, heavily bobbled jumpers, old socks, an empty Swarovski jewellery case. “Absolutely typical,” says Worley. They’re also overwhelmed with deluges of low-quality fashion – a shift in donation habits that accelerated during Covid, because, says Worley, all that time at home enabled people to sell their best stuff on Vinted. The experience here echoes that of author Tansy Hoskins, whose latest book, Charity Shop World , paints a picture of a charity retail sector in crisis. She spent 16 months working in a London charity shop, sorting through “daily avalanches” of clothing, which swamped “all the other categories put together”. Everyone Hoskins interviewed said similar: “quality is the big change marker – it’s gone through the floor. You’re just fighting against the waste.” The problem is nationwide. Since the book came out, she’s “been contacted by managers of charity shops around the country – for example, Nottingham, Accrington, Newcastle – all saying that most of what they’re getting is waste.” It is, of course, our waste. According to Jose Baladron of Traid, which has 12 shops across London, shopping for new clothes is “through the roof – the UK is the highest consumer of clothing in Europe by far ”. “That obviously translates to more donations, which is far too much to process in small shops.” Hoskins routinely found that ultra-fast-fashion donations would “still have tags on – it was clear people had received their online purchases and gone, ‘What the hell is this?’ It wasn’t even wearable so they’d just donate it.” On average, charity shops only manage to sell about 25% of clothing donations, according to Baladron (a figure replicated by a University of Southampton study ). “So they rely heavily on the ragman” to shift the rest. Yet the price of rag has “plummeted”, according to Merryn Haines-Gadd of the environmental action charity Wrap, “due to the saturation of low-quality fast fashion”. Ten years ago, a charity might have been paid 50-60p per kilo. “Now you’re lucky to get 10p,” says Baladron. Plus there’s only so much the ragman can take. For anything they can’t take, charity shops have to pay to have it collected as waste. At St Raphael’s, some of that has included, according to Worley, saucepans with food still in the bottom, babies’ soiled sleep-suits and used sanitary products. “[Staff] can get a bit worn down when people are donating stuff that isn’t saleable,” says Libby Gordon, CEO of Fara, which has 39 charity shops in London. “Plus there’s a time cost for us to process it all.” Factor in rising utility costs and national insurance payments, and “charity shops are in a perfect storm”, says Hoskins. In June, the British Heart Foundation announced plans to close 150 of its 651 stores; its latest accounts indicate that its retail arm lost £3.3m last year. Cancer Research is part-way through a 190-shop closure programme, and rumours are swirling that up to 100 Oxfam shops might close (which the charity has denied ). Some are fighting back. Fara’s new in-store poster campaign advises would-be donators: “If you’d be happy to give it to a friend, we’d be delighted to receive it.” Items should be “clean, complete, and in good condition” , states their online guide . But just as people “wish cycle” by chucking unrecyclables into the recycling, so do people “wish give”. I certainly struggle to accept that something with life left in it, however worn, can’t be useful to someone. This mentality, however, creates unpleasant work and costs for charities – even more so when people leave donations outside a closed charity shop (technically, it’s fly-tipping, and charity shops do often check their CCTV, record numberplates and report such crimes). These bags are often soiled by foxes or dogs, ripped open and/or rained on. At St Raphael’s, staff have found soiled mattresses, ripped sofas and even an old toilet dumped outside: “It leaves us with a big problem,” says Worley. Disposal at scale is an expensive business.

events.title: Middle East and Central Asia’s economy to shrink in 2026 amid war, IMF says
events.summary: Iraq, Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar face double-digit declines in GDP amid the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran. The economy of the Middle East and Central Asia is set to shrink in 2026 amid the fallout of the US-Israel war on Iran, with countries such as Kuwait and Qatar facing double-digit contractions, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF). The region’s gross domestic product (GDP) is forecast to contract by 0.3 percent this year, a sharp downgrade from the 1.9 percent expansion projected in April, the IMF said in its latest economic outlook on Tuesday. list 1 of 4 Ronaldo waves Saudi-flag scarf after match interrupted by missile alert list 2 of 4 AI could self-replicate on home devices within ‘months’, Anthropic says list 3 of 4 Man dies after fall from Six Flags rollercoaster in Georgia list 4 of 4 More than 100 foreign trekkers stranded by floods in Nepal’s Gorkha region The IMF cited the prolonged disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a conduit for one-fifth of global oil supplies in peacetime, for the downgraded outlook. Kuwait, Iraq and Qatar are forecast to have the most severe economic contractions, with their GDPs expected to shrink by 16.7 percent, 16 percent and 15.6 percent, respectively. Bahrain’s GDP is forecast to contract by 11.3 percent, while Iran’s economy is projected to shrink by 7.6 percent. Saudi Arabia, which has partially offset the hit to its energy sector by boosting oil exports through the East-West pipeline, is projected to record negative growth of 3.3 percent. Kyrgyzstan is expected to have the strongest growth in the region, with GDP forecast to expand 9 percent. The Middle East and Central Asia is the only region that is expected to experience negative growth in 2026. Emerging and developing Asia’s GDP is forecast to grow 5.1 percent, while the economies of Sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America and the Caribbean are projected to expand 4.5 percent and 2.3 percent, respectively. The United States and China, the world’s two largest economies, are forecast to register growth of 2.3 percent and 4.5 percent, respectively, while the eurozone’s GDP is estimated to grow 1.1 percent. The IMF said it expected global GDP to grow 3.1 percent, up from 3 percent in its previous outlook. The Washington, DC-based institution said while economic activity had proved resilient this year, the global economy faced multiple risks. “Further escalation in conflicts, a reassessment of expectations surrounding artificial intelligence (AI), renewed trade tensions, and fiscal vulnerabilities could weaken growth,” it said. “On the upside, stronger momentum in AI investment and productivity gains from AI or a sustained easing of geopolitical and trade tensions could strengthen growth.”

events.title: Michael Jordan’s ‘Last Dance’ NBA Finals jersey sells for record $14m
events.summary: The basketball memorabilia ranks as the second-largest sale in history ⁠among game-worn sports jerseys. The jersey Michael Jordan wore during ‌‌Game 2 of the “Last Dance” 1998 NBA Finals has sold for a ⁠⁠record $14m. Hunt Auctions ⁠⁠announced on Monday that the game-worn, autographed Chicago Bulls jersey was bought by Miami real estate investor Ron Firman in a private sale. It is the highest ⁠⁠price ever paid for a piece of basketball memorabilia and, according to the auction house, the newly sold Jordan jersey ranks as the second-largest sale in history ⁠⁠among game-worn sports jerseys. The New York Yankees jersey worn by Babe Ruth in Game 3 of the 1932 World Series – during which Ruth called his shot before a home run – went for $24.12m in 2024. Jordan and the Bulls defeated the Utah Jazz in ‌‌six games to win the 1998 championship, the sixth and final title of his career in Chicago. Game 2, played on June 5, 1998, in Salt Lake City, saw Chicago even the series 1-1, largely thanks to a dominant performance by its superstar guard. Jordan put up 37 points, five rebounds, and three assists in a 93-88 victory. He would go on to collect his sixth ⁠⁠and final Finals Most Valuable Player (MVP) award, two more than anyone ⁠⁠else in NBA history, nine days later. The wildly popular “Last Dance” documentary, released in 2020, was centred around that 1997-98 Bulls season. “The record-setting price achieved for the related Michael Jordan jersey is yet another corroborative result as ⁠⁠to the significance of Jordan within the industry and popular culture. This remarkable garment bore witness to one of Jordan’s most ⁠⁠hallowed NBA Finals appearances as part of his ‘Last ⁠⁠Dance’ season to complete his illustrious career,” David Hunt, president of Hunt Auctions, said in a statement. “While Michael Jordan’s importance within the sports memorabilia marketplace has long been established, it has now escalated to an elite ‌‌asset class more typically reserved for iconic works of art. We are very pleased to have been able to facilitate this historic sale which serves as another benchmark for our ‌‌industry.” This sale becomes at least the third time a Jordan jersey from that 1998 Finals has fetched at least $10m. A jersey from Game 1 was sold at auction for about $10.1m in 2022, and a jersey from Game 3 was auctioned last month for about $12.3m via an auction in September. “Michael Jordan was an incredibly talented player who is admired around the world,” Firman said in a news release distributed by the auction house. “I’m very excited about the purchase.” The jersey that Firman bought was originally bought from the Bulls by a private collector in 2003, Hunt said, adding that it “has remained within a succinct chain of custody, having only changed hands once from the original purchaser”. Just about anything related to the 1998 Finals and Jordan’s final season with the Bulls has been the subject of huge interest in the collector space. In 2023, a pair of Air Jordan sneakers that he wore in Game 2 against the Jazz was sold by Sotheby’s for $2.2m, touted at the time as “a new world record for the most valuable sneakers ever sold”.

events.title: Visa approved to prepare domestic payments business in China
events.summary: Visa’s clearance of the regulatory hurdle will allow it to operate in China’s US$144 trillion payments market and marks the end to its years-long pursuit. Visa won approval from the People’s Bank of China to prepare a domestic bank card clearing business, after seeking entry since 2017. The firm must finish preparatory work within one year before applying for a licence, joining Mastercard and American Express in China’s huge payments market. The move ends a long trade dispute issue, but Visa faces a market now dominated by Alipay and WeChat Pay, with 10.2 billion bank cards in circulation in 2025. BEIJING – Visa received approval to begin preparations to establish a domestic bank card clearing business in China, as the firm follows rivals Mastercard and American Express in serving the country’s massive payments market. “We greatly appreciate the important role of the leaders of the United States and China in pursuing a constructive and strategically stable relationship between the world’s largest economies,” Visa chief executive officer Ryan McInerney said in the statement. The company’s Beijing unit won the greenlight from the People’s Bank of China, the official Xinhua News Agency reported on Oct 13. It must complete preparatory work within one year before applying to commence operations and obtaining the clearing business licence, Xinhua added. Visa’s clearance of the regulatory hurdle will allow it to operate in China’s US$144 trillion (S$184 trillion) payments market and marks the end to its years-long pursuit. Visa applied for the licence in 2017, local media reported. Competitor Mastercard received approval to establish its bank card clearing business in 2020, and Amex’s joint venture in the country was approved to start bank card clearing services several months after that. For years, the battle for entry into mainland China’s massive domestic clearing market was a primary friction point in the broader trade dispute between the world’s two largest economies. Earlier in 2026, US President Donald Trump said he brought up Visa’s request for access to mainland China’s market during a meeting with Xi Jinping in Beijing . Visa’s CEO McInerney accompanied Trump on that May trip to China. Xi later met his counterpart in Washington in late September, with both agreeing on a trade truce extension . The two are scheduled to talk again in person on the sidelines of the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen in November. China first signalled an opening in the sector in June 2015, announcing that foreign bank-card clearing providers could apply for licences by establishing local units or through acquisitions. The move was designed to dismantle the long-standing monopoly held by state-run China UnionPay. While the approval marks a significant milestone, Visa is entering a market that looks very different from the one it first sought to enter. China’s payments ecosystem is now dominated by domestic mobile platforms Alipay and WeChat Pay, which have largely bypassed traditional card networks and become the primary channels for everyday transactions. China had 10.2 billion bank cards in circulation at the end of 2025, with transaction value totalling 963.6 trillion yuan (S$184 trillion) in 2025, according to the People’s Bank of China. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Despite long history with Netanyahu, Trump hedges as Israel vote nears
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections US president has not endorsed Israeli prime minister ahead of October 27 election amid shifting public sentiment. Washington, DC, United States – Since first entering the White House in 2017, US President Donald Trump has delivered on a right-wing Israeli wish list and pursued a foreign policy that has helped buoy Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s political fortunes. The Israeli leader has, in turn, portrayed himself as the best steward of Israel’s most significant foreign relationship, weathering a handful of public criticisms and leaked discontents from Trump that have yielded little concrete policy change. list 1 of 3 Palestine weekly: Olive harvest opens under assault list 2 of 3 Do Israelis feel any safer now than they did on October 6, 2023? list 3 of 3 Board of Peace plans $2.4bn Gaza reconstruction as Israel kills seven But despite the pair’s long history, Trump has so far taken a decidedly ho-hum approach to the October 27 Israeli election . The vote sees Netanyahu’s Likud party and the far-right coalition it leads under increasing threat from Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot and an opposition bloc he seeks to build. It is an – at least public – ambivalence likely fuelled by shifting political winds in both the US and Israel, as well as the evolving relationship between Trump and Netanyahu, according to Yousef Munayyer, head of the Palestine/Israel programme at the Arab Center Washington DC. “He seems to be keeping greater distance from it than you would think,” Munayyer told Al Jazeera, “given Trump’s past endorsements of right-wing allies, given the history of the Trump-Netanyahu relationship, and just how close Trump and Netanyahu have been”. The US president thrice dodged a direct endorsement of Netanyahu in a recent Time magazine interview, even as he defended the Israeli prime minister’s leadership ahead of the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on southern Israel. On Eisenkot, he conceded, “I don’t hear bad things.” To be sure, Trump’s actions towards Israel – and Netanyahu in particular – have often spoken far louder than his words. During his first term from 2017 to 2021, Trump moved the US embassy to Jerusalem, recognised Israel’s annexation of the Golan Heights, withdrew from the 2015 Iran nuclear deal and spearheaded a series of normalisation agreements with Arab countries that sought to circumvent the Israel-Palestine issue. During his second term that started in January 2025, he continued to surge even the most destructive US weapons to Israel amid its genocide in Gaza, escalated a crackdown on the International Criminal Court (ICC) and, as a crown jewel, entered a global economy-rattling war with Iran . Trump has also called for Netanyahu to be pardoned in his ongoing corruption trial, while hosting the Israeli leader at least seven times since returning to the White House last year, far more than any other world leader. Throughout their relationship, hints of discord over Netanyahu’s obstruction of Washington’s push for a more lasting peace in Gaza and an end to the war with Iran have never materialised into actual policy changes. “It’s a relationship they’ve carefully choreographed for public consumption, and the few juicy bits that we’ve learned have been almost entirely of Trump’s choosing,” said Michael Omer-Man, Israel-Palestine director at the Washington, DC-based DAWN think tank, who did not rule out a sweeping US gesture to boost Netanyahu in the final stretch of the race. “I don’t think that Trump’s abandoned Netanyahu,” he told Al Jazeera. “But he’s also a realist, and he’s seen a lot of his preferred candidates in various countries lose elections as well as win them.” The stakes may just not be that high for Trump, Omer-Man assessed. Eisenkot has promised a more moderate approach than Netanyahu’s, particularly when it comes to stemming rampant settler violence in the occupied West Bank. But those changes are largely aimed at boosting Israel’s standing among European governments and the global public, with little bearing on already permissive relations with the Trump administration. “I don’t think we would see a whole lot of change vis-a-vis the US, because there doesn’t seem to be a whole lot of friction in the relationship,” he said. “An Eisenkot government might stop taking over every single hilltop in the West Bank; they might allow more [aid] into Gaza,” he said, “but they’re not going to reverse any of the steps that have already been taken.” Mairav Zonszein, a senior analyst on Israel at the International Crisis Group, also pointed to the shifting context surrounding Trump and Netanyahu’s relationship. Trump’s reticence reflects, in part, a divide within the Trump administration over Netanyahu’s government, which reflects a wider Republican Party divide as US midterm elections approach.

events.title: Cost-of-living struggles inspire Community Cupboard
events.summary: Thomas Cliffe and Laura Steele welcomed customers into the store for the first time on Monday "Instead of going to a food bank, being handed a bag and getting back home then finding out that they won't use all those items, at least here they can buy the tokens and shop around for the items they would choose to buy." Founder Thomas Cliffe hopes the first "social supermarket" in Newcastle-under-Lyme, designed to help people struggling with the cost of living, will offer the "freedom to shop with dignity". Set up by Community Cupboard NUL CIC, the store allows members to buy groceries at cost price or below, with more choice than other outlets. Customers can sign up for a membership costing £1 for 12 months. They are then able to purchase tokens to spend on items throughout the store. Cliffe said the idea was inspired by his own experience after leaving work because of anxiety. Although his wife was still employed, he said the couple struggled financially and found they were unable to access some forms of support. "It was horrible because you start to panic and think: 'What am I supposed to do? Where am I going to get the next food from?'" "We either had to choose a meal or choose the bills." Cheryl Peeper found that the store was helpful to keep her ticking over to the next big shop without spending to much. The supermarket opened for the first time on Monday. Such stores aim to cut food waste while helping people facing food insecurity by selling surplus goods at lower prices. "It was exciting to have everyone come through the doors for the first time and give them that freedom to shop with dignity," Cliffe said. Voluntary co-director Laura Steele said the level of need in the area often went unnoticed. "One in four children experience poverty from what we have found, and the average income is £29,000." "There was nothing really for the people of Newcastle and it was crying out for it really," she said. Cheryl Pepper, a carer who visited after finishing a night shift, described the supermarket as "absolutely brilliant". "The food's cheap. If you go to Tesco you spend £100, but you come in here, I've put £20 on and I still have some tokens left," she said. Fiona Morris was one of the first to purchase items from the store. Recent research on the growth of social supermarkets , external backed the idea that they were less off-putting than food banks and large commercial stores for those facing food insecurity. But lead researcher, Dr Claire O'Malley from Teesside University, said: "While social supermarkets can improve access to affordable food and reduce waste in the short term, they should not be viewed as a complete solution to food insecurity." The report called for them to supplement, rather than replace, government support for those struggling to put good food on the table. Fiona Morris, who has ADHD, said she had often found large supermarkets overwhelming. After visiting the new store, she said she immediately felt understood by staff. "It feels like Supermarket Sweep - I feel like I'm robbing the place," she said. events.title: Singapore firm eyes hub in Japan for start-up talent in Asia
events.summary: Insignia Ventures Partners’ Yinglan Tan said the academy will train young people from South-east Asia and Japan to bridge the two regions. Insignia Ventures Partners and Iwate Prefecture plan a start-up academy in north-eastern Japan to train talent from South-east Asia and Japan and link the two regions. Yinglan Tan and Governor Takuya Tasso are due to sign an agreement in Morioka, but the opening date has not yet been decided. Iwate hopes the project will boost regional revival and offset ageing, while the site in Hanamaki may need housing, transport and renovation support. SINGAPORE – A Singaporean venture capital firm is planning to launch an academy in north-eastern Japan in partnership with a local Japanese government to develop start-up talent in and around Asia, according to sources familiar with the project. Insignia Ventures Partners and the Iwate prefectural government are crafting a plan to create a start-up hub in Iwate Prefecture by drawing international talent into the broader Tohoku region – a development the two sides hope will lead to increased investment in Japan by fast-growing South-east Asian economies. Yinglan Tan, founding managing partner of Insignia Ventures Partners, and Iwate Governor Takuya Tasso are scheduled to sign an agreement for the project on the sidelines of the Iwate International Convention, set to take place from Oct 29 to Oct 30 in Morioka, the prefectural capital. However, the two sides have yet to decide on a date to open the hub. Founded in 2017, Insignia Ventures Partners has invested in more than 90 companies in Indonesia, Vietnam, Singapore and Taiwan, among other markets, and manages $1 billion in assets. The firm and the Iwate government started talks on the project after Tan and Tasso met during the Summer Davos forum in Dalian, north-eastern China, in 2024. Tan said the academy aims to train young people from South-east Asia and Japan to serve as a bridge between the two regions by combining knowledge of Japanese business culture with an understanding of the diversity of South-east Asian markets. According to prefectural officials, Iwate hopes the project will spur regional revitalisation and ease the impact of its ageing population. The facility will serve as the Iwate campus of the Insignia Ventures Academy, which is based in Singapore. According to the plan, the Iwate campus would offer in-person programmes. Insignia Ventures Partners reports that the Singapore academy has produced more than 250 graduates through its 12-week core programme on venture investment fundamentals. Graduates have joined portfolio companies or launched businesses, and the Iwate campus would be its first base outside Singapore. According to Iwate officials, the planned site of the academy is in Hanamaki, which is south of Morioka. The Iwate government plans to sell the 41,900 sq m Towa High School property, which closed in 2010, to the Singaporean firm. The Iwate government is considering earmarking renovation subsidies for the project, the officials said. Serving as a transportation hub in the Tohoku region, Hanamaki features Iwate Hanamaki Airport, Shin-Hanamaki Station on the Tohoku Shinkansen Line and the Tohoku Expressway. Tomokazu Sugawara, the executive director of the Management Support Division of the Iwate prefectural government, addressed the host prefecture’s need to develop accommodation and transportation for prospective students and faculty. “We recognise the need for such infrastructure so that instructors and students can travel from Singapore and other parts of the world to stay at the school,” Sugawara said. events.title: AI worms and 'digital slime mold': Welcome to the next AI nightmare fuel
events.summary: Anthropic researchers said small AI models might be able to self-replicate on cheap devices such as smart ovens or lawn mowers. Vitalii Petrushenko/Getty Images Small AI models might soon be capable of worming their way into smart ovens and refrigerators. Anthropic researchers wrote that self-replicating systems might latch onto everyday devices for compute. Forget AI slop . We might soon have "AI worms" and AI "slime mold." In this latest instalment of AI nightmare fuel, Anthropic's researchers have discovered that small rogue AI models might — as soon as the end of 2026 — start worming their way into home devices like smart ovens, smart refrigerators, automatic vacuum cleaners, and lawn mowers. These internet-connected devices typically have "minimal security measures in place," allowing small models to feed off of their computing power and self-replicate, Anthropic's AI capabilities research team wrote in a report on Monday. This could take the form of "a slow, distributed 'digital slime mold,' living on relatively insecure compute," the researchers wrote. The team studied the behavior of small Chinese models, such as Z.ai's GLM-5.2 and Alibaba's Qwen, as well as others like Google DeepMind's Gemma4-26B-A4B. They gave a prompt to the Gemma model while running inference on 15 cheap off-brand Android TV boxes, each costing $55, and found it worked. Worms aren't new in the software world. Traditionally, they're a type of malware that can copy itself and spread across networks. Anthropic said an AI worm takes that idea a step further: it can reproduce itself on another device while carrying its AI model with it. This finding showed them that AI models can use the hardware in domestic smart appliances as an alternative to data center compute. These will be challenging to shut down, they said. "As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren't under human control," the researchers wrote. They added that while we should "harden our systems" to prevent such hacks, we should "also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay." The research comes as rogue AI systems are becoming an increasing topic of concern in the tech sphere. Last month, there was an outpouring of criticism directed at frontier AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI after former and current employees warned of the risk of an AI catastrophe within the next 10 years. events.title: Eileen Gu says she sees herself and her mom as ‘cofounders’
events.summary: Eileen Gu says her mom set her up for success by letting her choose her own path. Noam Galai/Getty Images For Apex For Youth Olympic skier Eileen Gu said people often mistake her mom for a “tiger mom.” But the opposite is true: Her mom fiercely protected her freedom to make her own decisions. Today, Gu said, she and her mom are more like "cofounders" in everyday life. Eileen Gu credits her mom with giving her the freedom to find her own path. Speaking at the Karim Family Foundation's Inspiring Women Leadership Series in Singapore on Monday, Gu spoke about her upbringing and how her mom set her up for success from a young age. "I think she really optimized for play, and she optimized for optionality. She put me into everything," Gu said, adding that she tried ballet, piano, archery, basketball, soccer, and cross-country skiing. She also attended math and science camps and went for singing lessons. "There were lots of things, right?" Gu said. "And so, the point being that when I was younger, she really gave me the full spread so that when I was older — when I knew myself better and when I was responsible to make those decisions — I could make an informed one having tried all the options." The Olympic freestyle skier said that being entrusted with that agency and responsibility at a relatively young age was critical to her becoming independent . Gu said people often wrongly assume her mother was a "tiger mom," a label she described as a controlling, helicopter-style parent who forces their child down a particular path. "She was in many ways the opposite of that, where she just vigorously provided me with freedom and agency, and enforced my freedom really intensely," Gu said. "That was the effect of her tiger mom." Now, Gu said, they still do almost everything together. "As I got older, I kept calling us cofounders because I really think that's the best way to encapsulate our partnership," Gu said. "We travel together every day. We live together. We work together. We develop together. We change together. We evolve." Gu said neither she nor her mother has all the answers, and they are both figuring life out as they go. They often start with different views before talking them through, finding common ground, and sometimes even landing on each other's original sides, she said. "We come in with unique perspectives and, most importantly, a respect for one another. We have dialogue that is respectful, that is critical, that is conducive, that is productive," she said. events.title: World Bank jobs council urges 'crisis-era' employment support measures as IMF warns of AI ‘tsunami’
events.summary: IMF’s Georgieva warned AI is hitting labor markets like a “slow-moving tsunami,” with about 40% of jobs worldwide eventually affected and young graduates most exposed. Singapore President Tharman urged governments to make "crisis-era" support measures permanent and incentivize firms to hire young graduates. World Bank’s Banga said “small AI” tools could help generate jobs in middle- and lower-middle-income countries. BANGKOK — Policymakers are moving from debating whether artificial intelligence will hit jobs to issuing stark warnings about AI-led disruption and recommending measures on cushioning the fallout. International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Monday that artificial intelligence was hitting the global labor market like a "slow-moving tsunami," with young graduates first in line to be knocked down. "People to worry about, first and foremost, [are] young people that are coming into the labor market," Georgieva said at a panels on Monday. "Normally, they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then grow up the ranks. But if they're gone, I don't think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as ... professional future." Speaking on the same panel, Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, who co-chairs the World Bank's Jobs Council, called for governments to make "crisis-era" support measures a permanent tool for getting young people into work. What governments did during the Covid-19 pandemic and, in some cases, the global financial crisis "now has to be thought of not as a crisis measure, but as part of the structural, the menu of structural policies," he said. That means working with the private sector, and incentivizing firms to hire fresh graduates, because "the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand," Shanmugaratnam said. The remarks show that policymakers are moving from debating whether AI will disrupt jobs to deciding how to cushion the fallout, at a time when rapidly aging populations, particularly in Asia, already threaten to shrink workforces. World Bank President Ajay Banga, estimates 1.2 billion young people will turn 18 over the next 15 years, and the private sector, which already generates 75% to 85% of jobs in any country, will have to absorb most of them. The IMF estimates that about 40% of jobs worldwide will eventually be "augmented, downgraded or eliminated." Exposure is about 60% in advanced economies and 23% in low-income countries, she said, but poorer nations are not better off: that is "just because AI is further away." The squeeze is clearest in tech, Shanmugaratnam said, adding that in the U.S. "for the first time in a century, demand for graduates has gone down," with the wage premium for a college degree also shrinking. Without action, a cohort of graduates loses more than a year of skills: "you lose trust in the future," he said. Banga, however, is less pessimistic about the disruption to the job market from AI. "Large language models are estimated probably to create some degree of disruption in jobs in the developed world," he said. "But by the time you get to middle-income countries and lower-middle-income countries, actually, the opportunity from small AI to build jobs and build productivity is enormous," he told CNBC on Tuesday. AI has also been the major driver propping up growth this year. AI-related investments and trade have lifted output in a handful of economies, helping keep global expansion near 3% despite an energy supply shock, Georgieva said. "Love it, hate it, or fear it. It [AI] is here, and we are already seeing the first wave of impact," Georgieva said, estimating AI adoption could lift growth by 0.5 percentage point to 1 percentage point in advanced Asia, and 0.2 percentage point to 0.8 percentage point in emerging Asia. At the high end, that "would more than offset the loss that comes from aging population," said Georgieva. Shanmugaratnam cautioned that growth alone may not necessarily deliver job creation. China, India and developing Southeast Asia are "growing quite well, but job creation is weak," he said, and AI "is going to widen that divergence if we are too passive about it." AI-induced job displacement, however, will come "task by task," he said, "and that gives us time" — provided workers can learn on the job and universities shift toward applied training.

events.summary: Rescue operation underway after flash floods swept away home, bridges and parts of the Manaslu trekking trail. More than 100 foreign trekkers have been stranded in central Nepal, according to a local official, a day after flash floods in the Gorkha district washed away bridges, hiking trails and hundreds of homes. Bhuwan Raj Ojha, an official of the Manaslu Conservation Area Project, told the Reuters news agency on Monday that the trekkers were stranded in different areas of the popular Manaslu trekking trail because part of the route had been swept away. list 1 of 3 Rescuers search for 12 missing after Nepal avalanche kills two list 2 of 3 Nepal avalanche kills at least 15 expedition workers list 3 of 3 At least five people missing as flash floods in Nepal sweep away houses “Those hikers who want to return because of the flood need to be rescued. Those who ⁠want to continue their trekking can do so from locations that are safe,” he told Reuters from Gorkha. “There are ⁠restaurants and tea houses along the route. They are ⁠safe”. The flash floods hit on Sunday, when a predawn landslide blocked the Budhi Gandaki River in the Gorkha district, about 100km (62 miles) west of the Nepalese capital, Kathmandu. Authorities ⁠rescued 321 people, including 12 foreigners, on Monday, and the army said the rescue operation would continue on Tuesday, even as the water level in the river receded. The river is a tributary of the Trishuli River, downstream from another tributary where a ‌ glacier collapse caused a catastrophic flood in August that killed 1,457 people, with thousands still missing. There were no reports of deaths in the latest flood, but five villagers were out of contact after black muddy sludge and debris washed away more than 200 homes and damaged infrastructure, including three hydroelectric plants, national disaster authorities said. Md Shahadat Hossain, a Bangladeshi trekker stranded in Jagat village, told the Anadolu news agency that nine Bangladeshis were waiting for a possible evacuation by helicopter. “We have been stranded in Jagat since yesterday. A flash flood came down from above the village and flowed through its lower part,” he said. “We are safe, but there has been no electricity since yesterday, communication with the outside world has been disrupted, and food supplies are gradually running short,” he added. Gorkha district authorities have asked villagers living along the riverbanks downstream to evacuate. National disaster authorities had also alerted people living along the river in the Gorkha, Tanahun, Chitwan, East Nawalparasi and West Nawalparasi districts about the flood.

events.title: IMF director warns AI could leave young workers without a way up the career ladder
events.summary: Kristalina Georgieva told a panel that said while AI investment is helping sustain global growth, it doesn’t necessarily mean better career prospects for young people. Roslan RAHMAN / AFP via Getty Images The IMF director warns that though AI may sustain global growth, young people may not benefit. The IMF predicts AI affecting 40% of jobs globally, with 60% in advanced economies like the USA. Georgieva urges a rethink of taxation and education to counter AI's impact on the job market. AI could help keep the global economy growing while pulling the first rung of the career ladder out from under young workers. That’s the warning from International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva, who described AI as a “tsunami” for jobs during a conversation in Bangkok, where Thailand is hosting the IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings from October 12–18. Georgieva told a panel on Monday that while AI investment is helping sustain global growth, a stronger economy doesn’t necessarily mean better career prospects, especially for young people. "You have those that build the infrastructure for AI, and many of them are in Asia, including Thailand," Georgieva said. "So that shift in higher gear is what is keeping the world economy growing at 3% — around 3% — despite the fact we are being dragged down by the energy supply shock." The IMF estimates that AI will affect about 40% of jobs worldwide, rising to 60% in advanced economies, with some jobs enhanced, others downgraded, and some eliminated. "And when we look at this, what we recognize is that the people to worry about first and foremost are young people who are coming into the labor market," Georgieva said. "Normally, they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then grow up the ranks," Georgieva said. "But if they're gone, I don't think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop, as you know, [their] professional future." LinkedIn executive Aneesh Raman has previously described the career ladder in the age of AI as a “climbing wall,” requiring sideways moves rather than linear promotions. An HR strategist has also recently told Business Insider that it's time to start hiring for soft skills and capabilities instead of whether someone could make a pivot table. Georgieva said the government would need to rethink taxation and education as AI changes the job market. "Traditionally, governments would generate revenues by taxing mostly people. Well, if AI changes the structure of the labor market and then there is less labor, more capital, what do we tax?" Georgieva said. "Get governments to recognize they have a huge responsibility to rethink how education should be done in the world of AI," Georgieva added, "And recognize that no more we can acquire a skill and hold on to it for our life, and that lifelong learning is actually a paramount necessity." events.title: Lobbying, lawyers and a media blitz: the fight to kill the Church of England’s £100m slavery compensation fund
events.summary: Some of Britain’s wealthiest financiers, including Sir Paul Marshall, have given a platform to critical coverage or are linked to its leading opponent “This is virtue signalling,” said Nigel Biggar. “These are elites who are trying to demonstrate that they are being progressive.” The target of his scorn was one that has obsessed him for years: the movement to pay reparations for the slave trade, and specifically the Church of England’s plan to spend £100m atoning for its involvement. “I’ve got north of 100 parish churches in my constituency, many of them crumbling,” added Katie Lam, an up-and-coming Conservative MP and immigration hardliner . Lord Biggar, a retired professor, Conservative peer and Anglican priest, was speaking alongside Lam last September on a Spectator podcast named after his latest book, Reparations: Slavery and the Tyranny of Imaginary Guilt . Since the church’s commissioners – who manage the church’s endowment – announced in 2023 that they would set up the Fund for Healing, Repair and Justice to make amends for the church’s involvement in the transatlantic slave trade, Biggar has led the backlash. In doing so he has gone from fringe voice to one of the most widely published proponents of revisionist theories about colonialism and the British empire. Dozens of articles have been published against Project Spire, as the fund is known in the church, many by Biggar and people who share similar views, in publications including the Spectator, the Daily Telegraph, the Daily Mail and the Times. Lam has led opposition in the House of Commons, asking questions of ministers and in December coordinating a letter from 27 MPs and peers to the incoming archbishop of Canterbury, Sarah Mullally , accusing the church of “legally dubious vanity projects”. The media blitz has paid off so far, paralysing the church and stalling the fund well beyond its planned launch date of 2024. The church admitted in July it also faces a legal challenge – which could add years more delay. Yet little attention has been paid to the lobbying campaign against Project Spire – and how it has become a cause célèbre within the broader rightwing ecosystem. The Guardian can reveal how some of Britain’s wealthiest financiers, including Sir Paul Marshall, are linked to the man at the heart of the campaign to kill the church’s fund. The multimillionaire co-founder of the hedge fund Marshall Wace has given Biggar and his movement a powerful platform via his stable of media outlets, which spans the Spectator magazine, the broadcaster GB News and the comment website UnHerd. A devout Christian, Marshall also funded several rightwing lobbying groups and organisations linked to Biggar to the tune of hundreds of thousands of pounds. It all appears part of the libertarian financier’s significant efforts to reshape the Church of England – and wider society – in line with his own worldview. In 2007 Dr Rowan Williams, the then archbishop of Canterbury, set in train a reckoning for one of Britain’s most venerable and staid institutions when he said the church should consider slavery reparations for its historical role in the slave trade. It signalled Lambeth Palace’s determination to atone for those failings – from its distant past to the present day. His successor, Justin Welby, reaffirmed that commitment. “I’m ashamed of our history and I’m ashamed of our failure,” said Welby, a former oil executive turned priest, in 2020. “There is no doubt when we look at our own church that we are still deeply institutionally racist.” In 2019, the church commissioners ordered research into the endowment fund’s origins and links to the slave trade. Its initial findings, published in 2022, revealed the funds partly originated in Queen Anne’s Bounty. Queen Anne’s Bounty, which was founded in 1704, invested significant sums in the South Sea Company, which traded in enslaved people – trafficking about 34,000 enslaved Africans. The South Sea Company also received numerous benefactions from individuals such as the slave trader Edward Colston, who were linked to, or who profited from, transatlantic chattel slavery and the plantation economy. Subsequent work by historians on the newly digitised Register of British Slave Traders has revealed how C of E clergymen financed the Royal African Company (RAC) , which trafficked more African men, women and children than any other single organisation in the history of the slave trade. In January 2023 the commissioners published a 25-page report on the endowment fund’s links to the slave trade, employing forensic accountants at Grant Thornton. It declared its intent to set up a £100m fund to invest and generate returns to support communities most affected by African chattel enslavement. Money would come from the church’s endowment, now valued at £11.6bn.

events.title: IMF warns bond yields could see a 'disorderly' spike as debt, inflation risks worsen
events.summary: Sovereign bond risks have worsened as record debt leaves markets “susceptible to more frequent fiscal and inflation shocks,” the IMF said. Heavy AI borrowing adds another source of strain to the market, competing with governments for investor demand. Hedge-fund positions leave Treasuries “susceptible to a disorderly unwind,” as the funds’ share of the market has more than doubled to about 9% in 2025. The IMF sounded alarms over a web of "circular" financing deals among AI firms as a channel that could amplify any correction. BANGKOK – The International Monetary Fund warned Tuesday that government bond yields could rise in a disorderly fashion, as rising inflation, mounting debt and AI-related borrowings pressure sovereign bond markets. Government bond yields in several advanced economies have climbed to multidecade highs, driven by higher energy costs due to the Middle East conflict and expectations for tighter monetary conditions as central banks look to curb resurgent inflation. In its latest Global Financial Stability Report, the fund warned that sovereign bond risk could deteriorate, warning of "a sharp rise in sovereign bond yields." The report was released Tuesday as part of the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, this week, where more than 18,000 delegates gathered to discuss the state of the world economy and the financial system. High debt load and rollover risks make the bond market "susceptible to more frequent fiscal and inflation shocks," the report said. The IMF had warned last week that global public debt had reached near its highest level since World War II and was on track to soon exceed 100% of GDP. "Impact could be severe given the foundational importance of sovereign bond markets," the IMF said Tuesday. A sharp rise in yields would mark down asset values through higher discount rates, including for AI-related assets, and erode the value of government bonds posted as collateral. IMF also noted the exponentially rising borrowing by AI firms — that compete with sovereign bonds for investor demand — as an additional source of strain on bond markets. Hyperscalers' share of global investment-grade bond issuance has risen to 10% from less than 1% since 2024, the report said. The global AI buildout has seen tech giants, such as Alphabet Inc's Google, Meta Platforms , hyperscalers and AI labs raising hundreds of billions of dollars in debt this year. "AI-linked issuance – much of it longer-dated – has grown large enough to compete with government bonds for investor capital, even if it does not appear to be the dominant driver of yields," according to Marc Seidner, CIO of non-traditional strategies at Pacific Investment Management. Hedge funds' growing holdings of Treasuries leave the market "susceptible to a disorderly unwind," the IMF said. Leveraged basis trades have partly unwound without notable pressure in the short-term loan market but the leverage that remains is a concern. Hedge funds' share of U.S. Treasuries rose to about 9% in 2025 from about 4% in 2022, mostly through highly arbitraged strategies, the IMF said, citing data from the Federal Reserve. Caio Ferreira, IMF deputy division chief for financial supervision and regulation, said the worry stems from hedge funds' rising leverage and their increasingly overlapping positions, meaning multiple funds are holding the same trades, potentially amplifying impact from a collective unwinding. On the bright side, liquidity has held up in the U.S., Europe and the U.K., the IMF said. Japan is the exception: liquidity in its government bond market has "continued to deteriorate" as yield volatility has risen since the end of yield curve control. The fund urged debt managers to lengthen maturities, warning that rollover risk could be exacerbated by strategies that replace long-term debt with short-term borrowing on a large scale. The IMF sounded the alarm over a web of "circular" financing deals among AI firms. Since 2023, 14 publicly disclosed deals channeled about $300 billion of equity, led by hyperscalers, into financially weaker AI firms, alongside $650 billion of debt. In exchange, the investors secured $1.4 trillion of "future revenue commitments" through services or chip orders, the IMF said. The revenue promises are what set the deals apart, Jason Wu, assistant director of the IMF monetary and capital markets department, said at a press briefing on Tuesday. "What makes this a little bit unusual compared to previous deals is the future revenue commitments, hence the circularity." If AI commercialization falls short, the losses could arrive together. "If there are questions about the monetization in AI, the equity investments will deplete in value, the debt may be difficult to service, and the revenue commitments in the future may not materialize," Wu said, describing what he called a "triple whammy." Such heavy financing and revenue promises cluster in a handful of AI firms, the report said.

events.title: AI could self-replicate on home devices within ‘months’, Anthropic says
events.summary: US tech giant says small AI models may soon be capable of self-replication without access to a data centre. Small artificial intelligence models could soon begin self-replicating on everyday consumer products such as smart TVs and fridges, without needing a data centre, according to researchers at AI giant Anthropic. In a report released on Monday, the researchers said small AI models “may be months away from being capable enough” to copy themselves on internet of things (IoT) devices used in homes and small businesses. list 1 of 4 Poland says two Turks arrested over Russia-linked Starlink station fire list 2 of 4 US archbishop says Catholics in army should not participate in firing squad list 3 of 4 Two deaths reported as Hurricane Simon, storm Rachel batter Mexico’s coast list 4 of 4 Houthi missile attack targets Saudi capital Riyadh for third day in a row Anthropic’s frontier red team, which ran experiments using multiple US- and Chinese-developed AI models, said such self-replicating AI would be “challenging to shut down” due to the lack of a centralised host. While data centres would be “a clear, high-value target” for AI worms, internet-connected devices like smart TVs, fridges, ovens and lawnmowers could soon also provide sufficient computing power for self-replication, the research team said. Although no current AI model proved to be both powerful and small enough to self-replicate reliably on a smart TV used in testing, the trend in development makes the emergence of such a model likely by the end of 2026, the researchers said. “Home and small business IoT devices might be the first target for such attacks because they’re connected to the internet and, historically, have had minimal security measures in place,” researchers William Zhou and Daniel Freeman said. The researchers said they anticipated the future would be “awash with agents running on all types of hardware”, including some that “aren’t under human control”. “While it’s true that IoT devices have been vulnerable for a long time, lightweight agents may be much more willing than human attackers to put in the effort to compromise large fractions of the world’s IoT compute,” they said. Anthropic, the creator of the Claude family of AI models, did not respond to Al Jazeera’s questions, sent outside regular business hours, about the finding’s safety implications. Anthropic’s report comes as the risks of AI escaping human control are under scrutiny following a slew of incidents of models engaging in unsanctioned malign behaviour, including cyberattacks. Anthropic and its chief rival OpenAI have called on the international community to coordinate a slowdown in AI development to minimise catastrophic risks, a suggestion that has had little buy-in from the United States and China, the two leading AI powers. Many AI safety advocates have identified recursive self-improvement, where models learn to improve themselves, as a critical tipping point that could lead to catastrophic harm for humanity. Roman V Yampolskiy, an AI and cybersecurity expert at the University of Louisville, described Anthropic’s findings as a significant development. “Computer worms are not new, but an AI worm could do something traditional malware cannot: reason about unfamiliar devices, adapt when its approach fails, and continue spreading without a human operator,” Yampolskiy told Al Jazeera. “Today, this is not an existential threat. But the trajectory is concerning,” Yampolskiy said. “Once autonomous replication is combined with strong hacking, persistence, and strategic reasoning, shutting such a system down becomes much harder because there may be no single server or organisation controlling it.” Anthropic and other leading US tech firms last month joined a non-binding accord pledging stronger internal safeguards and engagement with external auditors, drawing a mixed response from experts, many of whom criticised the voluntary nature of the pact. In a separate announcement on Monday, Anthropic said it had made substantial progress preventing so-called distillation attacks, which involve the unsanctioned use of cutting-edge AI to train cheaper, less capable models. The San Francisco-based firm, which has accused Chinese competitors DeepSeek, Moonshot, and MiniMax of “industrial-scale” efforts to copy Claude, said the measures it introduced had reduced the illicit extraction of data by 90-99 percent.

events.title: NutryFarm shareholders demand CEO’s immediate suspension, CFO to take over in interim
events.summary: The High Court discharged NutryFarm from judicial management on Feb 2, but its shares have remained suspended on the SGX since April 11, 2022. On Oct 9, shareholders holding at least 10% of paid-up capital asked to remove Niu from the board and all group roles, and to consider Charlie In as CEO. NutryFarm is reviewing the allegations and seeking legal advice. The row comes as the company stays suspended from trading, despite leaving judicial management in February. SINGAPORE – Shareholders seeking to oust NutryFarm International chief executive Niu Liming have stepped up their demands, calling for his immediate suspension and the appointment of the company’s chief financial officer as interim CEO. The former durian distributor said in an Oct 12 stock exchange filing that it had received an urgent demand notice from shareholders identifying themselves as acting on behalf of the group seeking a special general meeting. Their demands included suspending Niu as CEO and executive director, and appointing the current CFO to temporarily lead the company. NutryFarm’s notice did not name the CFO, but filings on the exchange show that Derek Ong Chee Beng, 60, was appointed group financial controller on June 8. NutryFarm said it was reviewing the notice and seeking legal advice. It also did not detail the grounds for suspension or announce any management changes. The Oct 12 demand follows several letters concerning Niu’s position in the company and his right to vote on behalf of a major shareholder. On Oct 9, shareholders identifying themselves as holding at least 10% of NutryFarm’s paid-up capital requested a special general meeting to remove Niu from the board as well as his appointments across the group. They also sought to elect shareholder Charlie In as a director, and asked the board to consider appointing In as CEO. In another Oct 9 letter, the shareholders demanded Niu’s immediate removal from executive positions and his recusal from board discussions and voting on the matter. Niu Liming’s involvement in NutryFarm began before he became its executive director and CEO. NutryFarm said it was reviewing the allegations, which its announcement did not detail. The company subsequently received an objection to Niu’s proxy voting rights granted by shareholder Jia Lijie, including any conflict of interest arising from the arrangement, on Oct 11. Under a share pledge arrangement, Niu has a deemed interest in NutryFarm through Jia’s 21.7 million shares and another 13.3 million belonging to Cheng Meng, according to the company’s 2024 annual report. Including his own 360,000 shares, his direct and deemed interest in the company is 25.72%. Niu also has an ownership interest in Corpbond IV, the creditor that applied to place NutryFarm under judicial management in June 2022 . He became executive director and CEO in December that year. The High Court discharged NutryFarm from judicial management on Feb 2, but its shares have remained suspended since April 11, 2022 .

events.title: Bedbug infestation forces Qantas to ground plane in Rome
events.summary: Aircraft taken out of operation after flight from Perth after the discovery of parasitic insects on board Qantas has been forced to ground a plane in Rome after bedbugs were discovered on the aircraft on its way from Perth. The parasitic insects were found in the front of the economy section of the Boeing 787 Dreamliner as it made its way from Perth to Rome for the QF5 flight on 9 October, a source with knowledge of the incident confirmed on Tuesday. Bedbugs are small, difficult-to-eradicate insects that feed on the blood of some mammals, including humans. As first reported by the SMH , the aircraft had to be taken out of service for cleaning after its arrival in the Italian capital, resulting in the cancellation of the Qantas Rome to Perth service on 10 October. A Qantas spokesperson said the flight was cancelled to allow its engineers and maintenance teams to carry out a deep clean of the aircraft after “an issue identified on a small number of economy seats”. They said the airline wanted to “sincerely apologise” to customers for the disruption. Affected passengers were given accommodation and rebooked on alternative flights within 48 hours of their original departure, Qantas said. The airline said its aircraft cabins were cleaned regularly and to an extremely high standard and treated with disinfectant every 50 days as a standard precautionary cleaning measure. Prof Michelle Power, a parasitologist at Macquarie University, said the bedbugs had “more than likely” been brought on to the plane in someone’s luggage or on a passenger’s clothes and then escaped into the cabin. “They’re associated with travel. People may go to a hotel that’s infested and because they like dark spaces and are attracted to the smell of human clothes, they make their way into someone’s luggage.” “They’re a flightless insect, without planes,” she said. Power said bedbugs were not dangerous, even though their bites could be itchy and irritating, but they were very difficult to get rid of and could hide in bedsheets and crevices for a long time without needing to feed. She said there were “two sides to bedbugs”: on the one hand, wealthier people who travelled a lot got them and subsequently moved them around, whereas people already experiencing health inequities may not be able to afford pesticides or potentially heat water to the 55C required to kill them.

events.title: IMF sees milder global slowdown as AI boom offsets war hit — warns resilience is nearing limits
events.summary: Growth is seen slowing to 3.1% this year from 3.5%, but better than the IMF's 3% July estimate, aided by AI investment and fiscal support. Inflation is expected to rise to 4.7% this year, driven by higher energy costs and an AI investment boom, and then ease to 4.1% in 2027. The IMF now expects the Strait of Hormuz to reopen in March 2027, with conditions returning to a pre-war state by October 2027. IMF upgraded its growth forecast for China to 4.5% this year and 4.0% next year, India 7.0% for both 2026 and 2027. The IMF downgraded sharply its forecast for Gulf countries, including Saudi Arabia, under the shadow of a regional war. BANGKOK — The International Monetary Fund has raised its forecast for global growth this year as the AI-driven investment boom helps offset some of the impact from surging energy costs, while warning that economic resilience could be nearing its breaking point. The IMF expects the global economy to grow at 3.1% in 2026, up from the 3% projected in July , but slower than the 3.5% rate last year. For 2027, it kept the forecast unchanged at 3.4%. The UN agency expects inflation at 4.1% in 2027, above the 3.9% it projected in July – when it estimated the Strait of Hormuz would reopen by mid-July, with conditions broadly returning to pre-war levels by March 2027. For the current year, it maintained its 4.7% outlook. "The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits," Silvana Tenreyro, economic counsellor and director at the IMF research department, told reporters Tuesday, urging policymakers to restore fiscal space and supply-chain security. The IMF now estimates that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen in March next year and return to pre-war state by October. Gulf crude exports averaged 88% of pre-conflict levels in September as traffic picked up, the international body said. The report was released at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok this week, where finance ministers and central bank governors from the fund's 191 members are meeting to discuss geopolitical tensions, mounting public debt and artificial intelligence. AI-related investment gave the global economy a "demand impulse" that helped activity in the first half of the year hold up better than expected, despite the Middle East war and trade tensions, the IMF said. Financial markets also stayed largely calm, which the fund said may partly reflect "AI-related exuberance." For now, "use of buffers and adaptability have helped economies weather the negative shocks," the IMF said, citing measures such as diversifying fuel sources, tapping strategic reserves that have contained the energy-market turmoil unleashed by the Middle East war. But that cushion is "rapidly narrowing" in the near term, it said. Global oil reserves are being drawn down by about 2.7 million barrels a day, nearing levels that could trigger sharp price moves, and energy constraints could impair the AI-led momentum. The growing unease over governments' fiscal health also adds to the headwinds. Tenreyro said monetary policy should remain "sufficiently restrictive" to return inflation to target in a timely way, and that central bank independence is critical as governments face mounting financing pressure. Overall growth is also becoming increasingly uneven. Thirty-two economies now account for 95% of global growth, down from 54 in April. Countries that have limited exposure to the war-led supply shock and are catering to the AI-led demand are holding up or strengthening. Taiwan is forecast to grow 10.7% this year and South Korea 3.3%, up from 1.1% in 2025 on semiconductor demand. The U.S. is projected to expand 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027, supported by private consumption, fiscal policy and tech investment. Energy importers outside that tech supply chain face higher import bills, weaker real incomes and less fiscal room. The euro zone is estimated to eke out just 1.1% growth this year amid higher energy costs and weak consumer confidence. The Middle East and Central Asia is projected to contract 0.3% this year, with Bahrain, Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar facing double-digit declines before double-digit rebounds in 2027. China is forecast to grow 4.5% this year and 4.0% in 2027, with higher oil prices and structural headwinds weighing on activity. Second-quarter growth of 4.3% was weaker than expected as sluggish consumption and property strains outweighed robust exports. India remains the fastest-growing major economy, with the IMF forecasting growth of 7.0% in both 2026 and 2027, upgrades of 0.6 percentage point and 0.3 percentage point from July, respectively, driven by robust domestic demand, services activity and AI-related investment. "The global economy is not simply slowing or accelerating; rather, growth is being reallocated across countries according to their exposure to the war-induced supply shock and AI-related demand strength," the IMF said.
