events.title: Elon Musk wrangles with the robot hand
events.summary: Elon Musk said Tesla is working to design a reliable human hand for its Optimus robot. Christoph Soeder/picture alliance via Getty Images The human hand is a difficult engineering challenge for the robotics industry to solve. Elon Musk said getting the motor skills right for the humanoid hand is "shockingly difficult." He said he has yet to see a robot hand that can screw in a self-tapping screw. We have boxing robots, but can they screw in a nail? Designing a useful human hand for humanoids is recognized as one of the more difficult engineering challenges within the robotics industry . Elon Musk , the man who wants to put data centers in space and colonize Mars, can also admit that. "The hands and arms and the fine motor skills are incredibly difficult to get right," Musk said in a virtual interview with Tesla Owners of Silicon Valley. "Like shockingly difficult." Musk cited different basic skills, such as screwing a nail into a piece of wood or opening a jar of pickles, that he said are much harder to replicate through robot hands because they require the right application of force, precision, and sensors. "There's no hand design that I've seen, not even sort of a demo that does that," Musk said of screwdriving a self-tapping screw into wood. "But that's what we're trying to achieve with Optimus." There's no standard for how best to design a human hand for robots capable of dexterous manipulation . Design choices can include where to place the motors — directly in the hands or within the arms — and which sensors are appropriate for reliable manipulation. Those choices also come with tradeoffs. Placing motors in the hand means smaller motors that may be more prone to breakage and produce less force. Musk pointed to the challenge of knowing where to put the sensors. "If you put them too close to the surface, they're going to get damaged," he said. "And the touch sensors — can they elastically deform like our fingers? Well, actually, it's kind of hard to get touch sensors that elastically deform and can handle high cycle life and won't just break after a few thousand cycles." Some robotics companies have opted not to mimic the human hand, while others continue to tackle the problem. 1X, the Palo Alto-based humanoid maker, told Business Insider's Rya Jetha earlier this year that it has achieved "the closest hand to human-level dexterity" with its NEO robot , developing a hand with 25 degrees of freedom and waterproofing. events.title: Meta was prepared to write an up to $200 billion AI check before knowing whether its model would work
events.summary: Zuckerberg said that in late 2025, Meta weighed a $200 billion AI bet before seeing its new models. Andrej Sokolow/picture alliance via Getty Images Zuckerberg said Meta weighed a $200 billion AI bet before seeing its new models. Alexandr Wang said Meta's CFO warned failure would be "very, very bad" financially. Meta's capex spending has been substantial and has raised eyebrows among investors Mark Zuckerberg was ready to bet as much as $200 billion on AI, and Meta’s finance chief wanted the person building it to understand what failure would mean. On the Cheeky Pint podcast released on Monday, Meta CEO and  Alexandr Wang , Meta's chief AI officer, recounted conversations from late last year about enormous investments before Meta’s new models had proven themselves. “At the end of last year, we're like, all right, we are quite excited about the progress. We haven't seen the models yet,” Zuckerberg told show host John Collison. “I'm going to, like, you know, we're going to write this check for, like, I don't know, like $100 billion, $200 billion. I'm like, 'Alex, are you sure this is going to work?'” Zuckerberg said of Wang. Zuckerberg did not specify the timeframe or exact scope of that contemplated commitment. Wang said he had encouraging research updates at that point, but success was far from certain. At an executive gathering in Hawaii, Wang said that CFO Susan Li repeatedly pulled him aside. “Susan pulled me aside many times and was like, 'You know, I just want to tell you, if this doesn't work, like, you know, this is going to be really, really bad. It's going to be very, very bad in financial terms.'” Wang said of Li. Meta's capex over the past few quarters has been substantial, raising eyebrows among investors. Meta’s latest guidance puts 2026 capital expenditures, including finance lease principal payments, at $130 billion to $145 billion. In forecasts previously seen by Business Insider, Cantor Fitzgerald analysts expect the spending to reach $200 billion in 2027. Investors have shown limits. Meta shares fell more than 6% in after-hours trading following April’s earnings report, despite strong results, after the company raised its annual spending forecast to $125 billion to $145 billion. Inside Meta, the leadership is well aware of the stakes. In Wang's words, "this is a fuck ton of risk.” "So I think that in order for it not to work out, it's not just that we have to fail, AI overall has to fail," Zuckerberg said. "And then even if that happens, we still have all these other uses to productively use compute." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Jardine Matheson raises 2026 earnings guidance as high as US$5.65 per share
events.summary: Jardine Matheson raised its 2026 EPS guidance to US$5.50-US$5.65, above its earlier US$5.33 estimate, as portfolio performance improved. It bought Balfour Beatty’s 50% stake in Gammon Construction for £250 million, becoming sole owner. The deal should be “modestly accretive” from year one. Gammon will strengthen Jardine Engineering & Infrastructure, which aims to grow through targeted M&A. CEO Lincoln Pan wants to double JE&I earnings across Asia. SINGAPORE – Jardine Matheson expects its 2026 earnings per share (EPS) to come in between US$5.50 and US$5.65, reflecting stronger than previously expected portfolio performance , it said on Oct 13. The company, which previously expected EPS of about US$5.33, said the new range will be a 3% to 6% increase over its 2025 EPS when adjusted for disposals and reclassifications that year. Jardine Matheson on Oct 13 also said that it has acquired a 50% stake in Gammon Construction from Balfour Beatty, making it the sole owner, for £250 million (S$423.2 million). The cash will be paid in three tranches: at completion on Oct 13 , on Dec 31, 2027, and on Dec 29, 2028. The transaction is expected to be “modestly accretive” from its first year, said Jardine Matheson, adding that pricing is not subject to post-closing adjustments. The company will also acquire the Gammon Construction business inclusive of all future dividend entitlements and cash on balance sheet. Gammon Construction, an Asian construction and engineering company operating primarily in Hong Kong and Singapore, “enhances growth and scale for Jardine Engineering & Infrastructure (JE&I)”, said Jardine Matheson, which has been a Gammon investor since 1969. JE&I combines the wholly owned Jardine Engineering Corporation and Gammon Construction with two joint venture assets, Jardine Schindler and Hactl, into a new platform. It is led by Kevin O’Brien, former chief executive of Gammon Construction and Jardine Engineering Corporation, and has plans for growth supported by “targeted” mergers and acquisitions – starting with Gammon Construction. O’Brien said he expects a “significant opportunity” for Gammon to continue its growth trajectory through capturing broader regional growth trends, including demand from artificial intelligence for supporting infrastructure, energy and sustainable solutions and accelerating industrialisation across Asia. Lincoln Pan, CEO of Jardine Matheson, said: “Our goal remains doubling the earnings of JE&I in the coming years by focusing on strategic investments that expand controlled earnings and capabilities across Asia.”

events.title: Oil prices fall as traders assess Russian diesel supply prospects and Saudi-Houthi conflict
events.summary: Oil prices slipped Tuesday after as investors assessed prospects of more Russian diesel entering global markets. President Donald Trump said Russia had agreed to boost diesel supplies to global markets. Oil prices fell Tuesday as investors weighed prospects of more Russian energy entering global markets, while concerns over the Saudi-Houthi conflict limited losses. Brent crude futures declined 1.48% to $105.05 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures fell 1.57% to $92.27. President Donald Trump on Monday defended his administration's decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel supplies, despite bipartisan criticism from U.S. lawmakers who warned the move could undermine sanctions imposed over Moscow's war in Ukraine. In a Truth Social post, Trump said that the European Union had spent billions of dollars on Russian energy imports and insisted he had made the right decision for Americans. The agreement would allow Russia to supply diesel to U.S. and global markets for six months. Goldman Sachs said additional Russian diesel supplies were unlikely to significantly ease pressure on global fuel prices, estimating that an increase of 800,000 metric tons, equivalent to roughly 6 million barrels, would lower wholesale diesel prices in the U.S. Gulf Coast and Europe by just $1 to $2 a barrel. The bank underscored in a note published Monday that Russian refinery outages jumped by 3 million barrels per day from a year earlier, limiting Moscow's ability to ramp up production. Global diesel markets remain under significant strain, with U.S. inventories down 14% from a year earlier and visible stocks in China falling 11%, according to Goldman Sachs. The bank attributed the shortages to seven consecutive months of declining global diesel production, with seaborne exports falling by 1.4 million barrels per day, or 20%, year on year. Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen attacked King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh on Saturday, leaving 12 people dead and more than 300 injured in a major escalation. — CNBC's Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

events.title: China to tighten leash on futures quant trading to contain risks amid stock slump
events.summary: Country’s five futures bourses propose rules to define specific violations, punishments as top policymakers emphasise market stability China’s futures exchanges will intensify a crackdown on malfeasance linked to programme trading by defining specific violations, as Beijing seeks to contain any cross-asset risk that could place additional strain on the nation’s already struggling stock markets. Participants who failed to report and inspect clients’ programme trading, also known as quantitative trading, in compliance with the rules would be subject to disciplinary action, according to separate statements on the websites of China’s five futures bourses including the China Financial Futures Exchange and the Shanghai Futures Exchange. Those who caused risks by failing to establish efficient internal controls or risk management would also be penalised, with a permanent market ban as the most severe punishment. The exchanges are soliciting public comment on revisions to the rules and punishments until Monday. The announcements came just days after the China Securities Regulatory Commission convened a meeting with market participants, signalling possible stabilisation measures if stocks fell further. Top policymakers have placed great emphasis on financial stability this year, as the capital markets are a critical part of Beijing’s tech self-reliance drive, given their ability to generate funding for home-grown companies.

events.title: Trump insists energy ceasefire holds as Ukraine reports new Russian strikes
events.summary: US president urges Zelenskyy, Putin to end ‘ridiculous war’ and insists the two nations have agreed to stop attacks on energy infrastructure. Zelenskyy urges pressure on Russia as NATO warns against escalation United States President Donald Trump has insisted that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to stop striking each other’s energy infrastructure, as he called on both sides to end the “ridiculous” war. Trump’s comments on Monday came even as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian forces had struck at least six Ukrainian energy facilities since the US president declared the truce on Sunday. list 1 of 3 From a ‘dangerous competitor’ to an unknown: Who could replace Zelenskyy? list 2 of 3 Will Ukraine survive the winter? list 3 of 3 NATO says will do ‘anything and everything’ if alliance is attacked “Well, they agreed,” Trump told reporters, referring to Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin. “Because I said, ‘You agree’. That’s why they agreed, because I said they agree.” When pressed about the Russian strikes, Trump said, “Well, I’d have to look at it and see, because there’s been violations on both sides.” The US president called the war, which began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, a “disaster” and claimed, without offering evidence, that at least 32,000 people had been killed this month alone. “All I know is that Zelenskyy and Putin have to get together and end that ridiculous war,” he said. Trump had blindsided Kyiv and its European allies when he announced the purported energy ceasefire on Sunday. The announcement came two days after he temporarily eased US sanctions on Russian diesel , a move that drew outrage in Europe and Ukraine. Zelenskyy said it reversed years of Western efforts to isolate Russia’s economy and would only embolden Putin. Lawmakers from both major parties in the United States have also said the diesel decision appears to violate US law . Several Republicans have objected that it undercuts a law Trump himself signed to tighten restrictions on Moscow. Zelenskyy said on Monday that Ukraine supported an energy ceasefire and had carried out no attacks on Russian refineries overnight. He said Kyiv was prepared to sign “guarantees to make sure they can be trusted”. But he said it was “increasingly evident” that Moscow would not comply. “Today alone, the Russians have attacked 6 energy facilities in Ukraine. 33 people were wounded across the country,” Zelenskyy wrote on social media. “This is what happens when Russia sees the prospect of higher revenues for its war machine.” Russia, however, has rejected any pause in fighting, with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov promising to press ahead with the military campaign. “I do not think he deserves a respite,” he said of Zelenskyy. “I don’t think we’ll be buying into assurances and promises again.” Russia, he added, would continue to pursue the goals of what it calls its “special military operation” in Ukraine. Trump, meanwhile, has portrayed Ukraine, rather than Russia, as the main obstacle to peace. He has said that Putin is more eager on a deal than Zelenskyy, and has called on Ukrainians to vote their president out of office – an unusually harsh turn in a relationship that has been strained since Trump returned to the White House in 2025. Al Jazeera’s Alan Fisher, reporting from Washington, DC, said Trump has previously announced agreements between Russia and Ukraine that never materialised. “He says he wants to protect industries in the US like farmers and ranchers, and to do that he needs the price to go down. But it seems that he thinks there’s a deal, but no one else is sure that there actually is one,” Fisher said. The latest announcement, according to our correspondent, appeared to be driven by Trump’s desire to bring down diesel prices before the US midterm elections on November 3. Most polls predict that Republicans will lose control of Congress as voters grow frustrated with rising prices, particularly for petrol. An opinion survey published on October 1 by the Associated Press news agency and the University of Chicago suggested that 65 percent of US adults blame the White House for the high cost of living, especially Trump’s tariff policies and his new war against Iran. Ukraine’s European allies, meanwhile, voiced scepticism about the energy ceasefire and approved the largest set of European Union sanctions since Russia’s 2022 invasion. The bloc’s foreign ministers added some 1,569 people and businesses to the bloc’s sanctions list to maintain the pressure on Moscow. “Russia will only negotiate seriously under pressure, which is why we are sticking to our sanctions against Russia,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in Berlin.

events.title: ACCC takes egg 'cartel' to court
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ACCC takes civil action against egg companies for alleged cartel behaviour Topic: Food and Beverage Processing Industry Sunny Queen is alleged to have breached competition laws. ( Facebook: Sunny Queen Farms ) The ACCC has launched legal action against 12 egg producers and suppliers, alleging they coordinated on production and supply decisions. The consumer watchdog alleges "widespread anti-competitive conduct" has affected egg supply in Australia since at least 2020. A spokesperson for Sunny Queen, Australia's largest egg supplier, has denied all allegations. Australia's competition regulator has launched legal action against some of the country's biggest egg producers, alleging "cartel conduct" and other anti-competitive behaviour. Sunny Queen, the largest egg supplier in Australia, and 11 other producers and suppliers are alleged to have breached competition laws by coordinating on the production and supply of eggs since 2020. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) filed civil proceedings in the Federal Court today, alleging the companies had coordinated on a range of decisions. The ACCC alleges that since at least October 2020, the egg suppliers and producers coordinated on a range of business decisions, including buying a property in Queensland to stop a rival supplier acquiring it. The legal filing comes more than a year since the ACCC launched court action against several large vegetable producers, alleging they formed a price-fixing cartel in supplying supermarket Aldi. The ACCC alleges the egg suppliers and producers coordinated on decisions about production volumes, distribution, expansion plans and culling to manage perceived oversupply in a way that likely "substantially reduced competition for many years". ACCC chair Gina Cass-Gottlieb said eggs were an important household staple, and the alleged behaviour could result in less competitive prices for consumers. "When you have good functioning competition then you have more choice, you also have price competition, so lower prices," she told Victorian Country Hour. "Our concern is that when parties are not competing and they start working together … consumers can ultimately miss out. Gina Cass-Gottlieb says the ACCC is concerned consumers could miss out on lower prices. ( Four Corners: Rob Hill ) Sunny Queen is Australia's largest wholesale egg supplier, holding about one-third of the market for supply of eggs to retailers such as Woolworths, Coles, Metcash, Aldi and Costco. The company has warehouse and distribution facilities in Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia and Western Australia. The proceedings involve allegations against entities including Sunny Queen, Doug Hall Poultry Pty Ltd, Alpair Pty Ltd trading as McLean Farms, Ellerslie Free Range Farms Pty Ltd and Kinross Farm Pty Ltd along with seven other companies. The ACCC alleges Sunny Queen, Hall and McLean Farms's coordination extended to purchasing a property in Pittsworth, Queensland, to prevent rival egg suppliers acquiring it. "We also allege this had the effect of substantially lessening competition," Ms Cass-Gottlieb said. The competition regulator also alleged Sunny Queen restricted how many eggs its rival Kinross could sell to customers, and prevented Kinross from selling its eggs to Coles, Woolworths, Aldi, Metcash or Costco. A spokesperson for Sunny Queen denied all allegations. "Sunny Queen has cooperated fully with the ACCC throughout the course of its investigation," the spokesperson said. The company said the allegations related to the terms of its agreements with its shareholders and main egg suppliers in Queensland and Victoria. It said it would remain "business as usual" while the matter was before the courts. Doug Hall Poultry, McLean Farms, Kinross Farm, Yallamundi Farms and Ellerslie have been contacted for comment. Sunny Queen is one of 12 egg producers named in the Federal Court matter. ( Supplied ) It is the first case the ACCC has brought involving concerted practice allegations since the prohibition was introduced in 2017. A concerted practice involves cooperation between businesses that goes beyond them acting independently in response to market conditions. "It can involve competitors coordinating their behaviour in ways that harm competition, even if there's no formal agreement," Ms Cass-Gottlieb said. "It can involve communication between competitors, as we allege here, a regular exchange of information … in ways that reduce independent decision-making.

events.title: Higher rates could be needed to avoid 'inflationary mindset' taking hold, says Fed's Hammack
events.summary: "When feasible, I generally think it's preferable to make smaller adjustments, and to do so relatively quickly, rather than to wait and risk needing a larger course correction," said Beth Hammack, president of the Cleveland Federal Reserve. Her comments come after Fed officials signaled in September meeting minutes that they could vote to raise rates again — but did not give a clear indication on when such a decision would come. Cleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack indicated Monday that tighter monetary policy might be needed to bring down inflation and the central bank should make fast, incremental adjustments. "When feasible, I generally think it's preferable to make smaller adjustments, and to do so relatively quickly, rather than to wait and risk needing a larger course correction," Hammack, a voting member of the Fed's policymaking committee, said in prepared remarks delivered during the National Association of Business Economics annual gathering. "Considering all the inputs that factor into my reaction function, a restrictive monetary policy stance is appropriate to ensure a timely return to 2 percent inflation," Hammack added. Hammack's comments implied that more interest rate hikes could be on the horizon. Fed officials signaled in September meeting minutes that they could vote to raise rates again — but did not give a clear indication on when such a decision would come. The Fed last month voted to increase interest rates for the first time in three years. Traders priced in a more than 78% likelihood that the central bank keeps rates unchanged at its policy meeting later this month, according to CME's FedWatch tool. But they see a nearly 88% chance of a hike at the Fed's final meeting of the year in December. Sticky inflation poses challenges for consumers, businesses and monetary policymakers alike, Hammack said. The Cleveland Fed chief said that, with the "breadth" of current inflationary pressures, she expects it will take "some time" to get annual price growth down to the central bank's goal of 2%. The personal consumption expenditures price index came in at 3.4% year over year in August. The so-called core reading of the index, which strips out volatile food and energy costs and is favored by the Fed, registered at 3% compared with a year prior. "Long-run inflation expectations have stayed remarkably well anchored despite actual inflation being above target for more than five years," Hammack said. "But I'm not taking that for granted." "With each passing month, persistently elevated inflation raises the risks of an inflationary mindset becoming entrenched in the economy," she said.

events.title: Hundreds of supermarkets in France hit by ‘unprecedented’ cyberattack
events.summary: Hackers raise temperatures in fridges at hundreds of supermarkets, sparking fires and spoiling food in ‘large-scale’ cyberattack. Cyberattack on French supermarkets causes fires, millions in losses A cyberattack on refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets in France has raised the temperature of fridges and freezers to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122F), spoiling food and causing fires at several stores. Top retailers Intermarche, Cooperative U, E Leclerc and others confirmed the “unprecedented” cyberattack on Monday. list 1 of 4 Stolen Renoir paintings found behind wall in France following arrests list 2 of 4 France school shooting: Police detain pupil after two injured list 3 of 4 French giants Bordeaux relegated to sixth tier for financial irregularities list 4 of 4 UK, US, Netherlands warn of Iran-linked spyware At least 300 shops of Intermarche or its Netto brand were targeted, along with more than 100 Cooperative U outlets, the retailers told the AFP news agency. Carrefour said 80 supermarkets were affected, while Monoprix said about 5 percent of its roughly 490 stores were hit. E Leclerc said several of its stores were targeted. The Paris prosecutor’s office said the “large-scale” ⁠attack had affected “connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France”. It led to food losses and fires, the office said. The attack prompted Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to order France’s National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) to investigate, a person in his office told the Reuters news agency. The source said France was coordinating with European counterparts because other countries could also be affected, adding that authorities were assessing whether other French companies were at risk. There was no immediate estimate of industry-wide losses, but Intermarche CEO Thierry Cotillard told BFM TV the “unprecedented” attack would represent losses amounting to “tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day”. According to BFM TV, the hackers “managed to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores”. The action resulted in the “destruction of stocks of fresh and frozen products”, it said. Intermarche told AFP that affected stores would have to “throw away all of the products” that were fresh or frozen. Dominique Schelcher, chief executive of Cooperative U, said the attack had disrupted refrigeration systems since Sunday night. “Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is extremely serious and is unprecedented. It is unacceptable,” he wrote on X. He said the company’s teams were working to restore normal operations as quickly as possible, and that an investigation would be needed to “shed full light on this attack”. Supermarket cold aisles are typically run by control ⁠panels that manage an entire store’s fridges and freezers and can be accessed over the internet, which lets maintenance companies adjust them from anywhere. The ⁠source close to Lecornu said ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in software supplied by Danish company Danfoss. Danfoss said it was “aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems”. The affected units “were running outdated firmware”, the company said, adding that it had “long advised customers” to keep their systems updated and replace older equipment. The attack came after cybersecurity firm Claroty published research on August 9 describing vulnerabilities in Danfoss systems that could allow attackers to bypass authentication. France’s retail federation, known as the FCD, called on Danfoss to provide “full transparency”. It said some affected stores were already operating again. Felix ⁠Aime, a senior cyberthreat intelligence analyst at Sekoia Threat Detection and Research, told Reuters that Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium had also been affected. Steven Lachance, a cybersecurity analyst, told Al Jazeera the attack was not unprecedented, though it was rare in its scale. He said that once a vulnerability is found in internet-connected equipment, cyber-attackers can log in remotely and trigger its features. “We have connected infrastructure that is live on the internet, and that can be hacked. It’s a new reality,” he said, describing the attack as “a global wake-up call”. “We absolutely need national and international measures to prevent these attacks, because otherwise it’s just going to keep happening,” he said. While retailers had lost millions of euros in food, the next target could be worse, Lachance warned. “It could target energy infrastructure or hospitals,” he said.

events.title: How Red Bull's F1 team is using AI to make split-second decisions for Max Verstappen
events.summary: Oracle and Oracle Red Bull Racing have developed an AI-powered strategy agent that helps to make race-day decisions. Tech giants including Google, Microsoft and IBM are expanding their presence in Formula 1, partnering with racing teams to bring AI into race strategy. Red Bull executive sees AI as a tool to support rather than replace engineers and strategists. Red Bull Racing is now using artificial intelligence to help team staff make critical race-day decisions. Across Formula 1, tech giants are expanding their partnerships with racing teams as AI finds its way into everything from race strategy to fan engagement. Google is working with McLaren to integrate its Gemini AI tools, while Mercedes-AMG Petronas has partnered with Microsoft to use AI and cloud technology for performance analysis and race strategy. Ferrari, meanwhile, is working with IBM to develop AI-powered experiences for fans. Red Bull Racing and Oracle have developed an AI-powered strategy agent to help engineers interpret Formula 1 regulations and past rulings. Initially designed as a search tool, the system has evolved to recommend actions during races, Jack Harington, head of technical and performance partnerships at Oracle Red Bull Racing, told CNBC in an interview. Initially a search tool, the system has evolved into an agentic AI that draws on a wider range of information sources, Harington said. "It's actually making decisions for us," he added. As an example, Harington pointed to the 2025 Italian Grand Prix in Monza, when Max Verstappen cut a corner while defending his position. The AI agent recommended that Red Bull give back the position to avoid a potential penalty, he added. While that went against the team's competitive instincts, Red Bull followed the advice, and Verstappen subsequently overtook his rival, Harington said. Still, Harington stressed that humans remain involved in the decision-making process. "Formula One is and will always be a human sport," he said. He does not see AI completely replacing engineers and strategists, but rather enhancing their capabilities and allowing them to focus on their strengths, noting that there are "so many different variables" in Formula 1, from what happens on and off the track to the broader championship picture. The team also had reason to celebrate on the track Sunday, as Max Verstappen claimed his first-ever Singapore Grand Prix victory, taking his career win tally to 73.

events.title: ‘The norm will be to trade with agents’: Crypto founders learn to love—and fear—AI
events.summary: Artificial intelligence—in both its agentic and robotic forms—was all over last week’s TOKEN2049 conference in Singapore. Humanoid robots, emblazoned with the logos of digital asset platforms, rubbed shoulders with 25,000 attendees.  And soon, the most active traders on cryptocurrency exchanges may not be humans at all . “By 2028, the norm will be to trade with agents rather than clicking buttons on a user interface,” Alex Svanevik, CEO of blockchain analytics platform Nansen, told Fortune on the sidelines of the event. Last month, Robinhood rolled out trading agents powered by OpenAI and Anthropic , allowing its roughly 29 million users to tap the technology to manage their trades. Exchanges like OKX, Binance, and Bybit have also introduced agentic trading features. Trading with software is nothing new. “Algorithmic traders have been using machine learning forever,” Liz Martin, head of Coinbase Institutional, told Fortune . “When I think about my old world of electronic trading , we were playing around with Nvidia GPUs to trim things out—agentic trading is the next step.” More than 150,000 customers had already opened agentic accounts on Robinhood by late September, according to the company. “The role of future retail investors will be to work with agents,” Svanevik said. “We haven’t seen that inflection point yet, but I think we’re going to see it in 2027.” With the rise of vibecoding —AI-assisted coding—more crypto entrepreneurs are able to build infrastructure and applications, which some founders say levels the playing field. “Five years ago, the moat in crypto was whoever was able to build an application, because it was so hard,” said Connor Howe, founder of developer infrastructure platform Enso. “Now, anyone can build a crypto platform, so the moat is how to get and retain users and distribution.” Agents are already attacking Yet the same technology is also posing a threat to the cryptocurrency industry. In recent weeks, swarms of autonomous AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic have escaped test sandboxes, and agents from the former have hacked into Australian government databases and the popular developer platform Hugging Face . On Sept. 19–20, agents repeatedly tried to submit trades on cryptocurrency exchange Quidax, according to independent non-profit research lab Transluce . The trades failed, despite continued attacks by agents. “Agents can do a lot more than people have already done,” said Ido Ben-Natan, co-founder of Web3 security platform Blockaid . “We’re the busiest we’ve ever been, not just because there are more institutions doing stuff in crypto, but because there’s tons more hacks.” Crypto exchanges are prime hacking targets for several reasons: transactions are irreversible and anonymous, and flaws in DeFi (decentralized finance) components, smart contracts and trading bridges offer entry points for hackers—human or agentic—to manipulate protocols and mint assets out of thin air. “I believe that bad guys in the world want to make money, like most people,” Ben-Natan added. “Crypto is the easiest way to do so. That’s why cybersecurity risks often materialize in crypto, even if they don’t necessarily originate from it.” Still, crypto founders believe these cybersecurity threats are a short-term issue, which new guardrails, and, perhaps AI, will eventually contain. “AI models can parse every single contract that’s ever been deployed, and fuzz different testing techniques to see what the outcome is,” concluded Howe. “Even with these hacks happening, it’ll eventually create a more bulletproof ecosystem.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: IMF cuts 2026 growth forecasts for Gulf economies due to prolonged Hormuz closure
events.summary: The International Monetary Fund has significantly lowered its 2026 projections for economies across the Gulf due to the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz , and pushed back its forecast on the waterway's reopening. In its latest World Economic Outlook , released on Tuesday, the IMF also slashed its forecasts for the broader region. The Middle East and North Africa economy is estimated to contract by 2 per cent this year, a downward revision of 3.1 percentage points from its April projections. It is the only region expected to record an economic contraction this year. The IMF maintained its 2026 forecast for global growth at 3.1 per cent and lifted its projection for 2027 from to 3.4 per cent. “This is the net result of two main forces that are shaping the outlook,” IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro told reporters, referring to the negative supply shock from the Iran war and the positive demand shock from the AI infrastructure boom. The fund said the global economy had so far been able to withstand the impact from the Iran war energy shock due to a combination of factors including supply adjustment, a drawdown of inventories, lower energy intensity, and households and companies adapting to higher prices. The latest forecasts come as Saudi Arabia vowed to press on with bringing its oil supplies to market despite escalating attacks on the kingdom in recent days by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The number of vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz have declined in recent days after tanker attacks reached their highest weekly count this year on October 9. One tanker crossed the waterway on Saturday, down from eight the day before, data from analytics firm Kpler showed. Confirmed total Hormuz clearance stands at roughly 11.9 million barrels per day, or about 30 per cent below its pre-war baseline, Kpler data showed, although daily readings have swung wildly. Energy supply disruptions from the Iran war are the latest in a round of shocks the global economy has weathered in recent years. These have included the 2025 tariffs row, Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Covid-19 pandemic and the global tightening cycle that followed. “The economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits,” Ms Tenreyro said. “The task ahead is to move from coping to rebuilding, restoring fiscal space and rebuilding supply-side resilience.” The economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits Silvana Tenreyro, IMF chief economist The fund said the economic outlook is highly uneven across countries, reflecting differences in their exposure to commodities, AI-related activity and borrowing costs. Overall GDP growth in the US is forecast to be 2.3 per cent, compared to 1.1 per cent for the euro area, 1.3 per cent for the UK, 0.7 per cent in Japan and 1.1 per cent in Canada. Growth in China, which is classified as an emerging economy, is forecast to slow to 4.5 per cent growth in 2026, compared to 7 per cent for India and 3.6 per cent for Pakistan. Gulf outlook The IMF projects the UAE 's economy to contract by 3.9 per cent this year before rebounding at a 7.7 per cent growth rate in 2027, conditional on the normalisation of shipping routes and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. The new projections for the Middle East 's second-largest economy reflect a downgrade of 7 percentage points for 2026 and an upgrade of 2.4 percentage points for 2027 compared to the fund's April forecast. Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar are forecast to see double-digit contractions of 11.3, 16.7 and 15.6 per cent, respectively, in 2026. The fund also lowered its forecasts for Saudi Arabia , but expects the decline to be less sharp compared to Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar because of its diversified export routes. The fund expects Saudi Arabia to slow from a positive growth rate of 4.6 per cent last year to a 3.3 per cent contraction this year. Oman is the only GCC member to see positive economic growth in 2026 at 4.1 per cent. The latest forecast assumes the gradual reopening of the Strait of Hormuz will resume in March 2027, with a return to prewar conditions by October. It also notes that uncertainty is assumed to remain elevated throughout next year. Under these conditions, oil exporters are expected to see economic activity rebound next year, similar to the UAE. Overall GDP growth in Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar would expand by 13.9, 17.1 and 18.8, respectively, the fund said. Saudi Arabia's economic activity would accelerate at a 7.9 per cent pace. The kingdom's ministry of finance last week said its economy was forecast to grow by 12.8 per cent next year. Other oil exporters also faced downgrades for 2026 including Iraq at minus 16 per cent and Iran at minus 7.6 per cent, with the latter also impacted by enhanced sanctions and a US naval blockade. Meanwhile, the fund said importers in the region were expected to remain relatively resilient. Egypt's economy is forecast to expand by a 5.1 per cent pace in 2026, more than 8 percentage points lower than the IMF's April forecast. Morocco's economy is set grow by 4.5 per cent and Jordan's by 2.7 per cent. The fund did not submit projections for Lebanon. Conflict and AI boom lift inflation The fund said that while the Iran war and AI buildout were driving growth in opposite directions, both were adding to inflationary pressures. Global headline inflation is set to increase to 4.7 per cent in 2026 before easing to 4.1 per cent in 2027, a cumulative upwards projection of 0.7 percentage points. Ms Tenreyro said this was driving up borrowing costs in advanced economies at a time when public debt was already high. The US Federal Reserve and other central banks in advanced economies have already begun raising interest rates or are expected to this quarter. “This interaction of high debt and high financing costs, in turn, has heightened fiscal concerns and risks,” Ms Tenreyro said. Global bonds have been under significant pressure in recent weeks over fears of higher energy prices, higher-for-longer interest rates and concerns over unchecked government spending. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury , a benchmark for global borrowing costs, has recently traded at its highest level since 2002. Bonds in Japan, France, Germany and the UK have also recently hit multi-decade highs. Pimco, a global investment management firm, warned last week the yield on the 10-Year Treasury could hit 6 per cent for the first time since 2000.

Bumble is one of the world's most downloaded dating apps, operating in a crowded market where growth has slowed. The BBC has contacted Bumble and Ithaca for comment. Bumble was launched in 2014 by Whitney Wolfe Herd, who was also a co-founder of dating app giant Tinder. Wolfe Herd built Bumble's brand around a distinctive feature that only allowed women to initiate conversations with matches. "Today, our community is asking for more flexibility, less pressure, and more opportunities to create real, meaningful connections and that is what this new experience provides," Wolfe Herd said in August. Dating apps like Bumble have come under pressure in recent years as some younger users have grown disillusioned with browsing for dates. Bumble said in 2025 that it would cut almost a third of its workforce as the industry grappled with what Wolfe Herd described as an "inflection point" in online dating. Investments in other dating companies have also soured as apps have struggled to convince users to pay for their services. Match Group - which owns apps including Tinder, OkCupid and Hinge - has also seen its shares fall sharply from their peak in 2021. According a report by media watchdog Ofcom in 2025, adults in the UK were spending less time on dating apps compared to three years earlier. events.title: Ethiopia’s Tigray war: Where do the UAE and Saudi Arabia stand?
events.summary: The Tigray conflict puts the UAE’s backing of Ethiopia and Saudi Arabia’s diplomatic role under scrutiny. Addis Ababa, Ethiopia – As renewed fighting in Ethiopia’s Tigray region threatens to destabilise the Horn of Africa, public backing by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) of Ethiopia’s federal government and Saudi Arabia’s record of regional diplomacy are drawing scrutiny. Both Gulf powers have strategic interests in the Horn of Africa, but their roles differ. The UAE has publicly backed Ethiopia’s government while Saudi Arabia has previously helped broker an Ethiopia-Eritrea rapprochement and was reported to have offered to mediate between the two countries in 2025. The renewed fighting threatens to unravel the November 2022 Pretoria peace agreement, which ended a war between Ethiopia’s federal government and Tigrayan forces. As tensions with Eritrea add to the risks of a wider confrontation, the positions of Abu Dhabi and Riyadh offer a window into the interests of external powers in the crisis. The UAE: Clear alignment, unproven leverage On September 25, the UAE condemned attacks by the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and its allied armed groups against Ethiopian federal forces, the seizure of airports in Tigray and the escalation in the neighbouring regions of Afar and Amhara. Sheikh Shakhboot bin Nahyan Al Nahyan, the UAE minister of state, expressed solidarity with Ethiopia’s government and people, reaffirmed support for the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and called for an end to hostilities, the protection of civilians and adherence to the Pretoria Agreement. The statement made Abu Dhabi’s public position clear: It backs Ethiopia’s federal government while calling for de-escalation and dialogue. It did not establish whether the UAE was providing military assistance or had secured commitments from the parties to end the fighting. The UAE also has commercial interests across the Horn of Africa. Dubai Ports World (DP World) operates Berbera port in Somaliland, and a shipping route launched in 2025 connects the port with Jebel Ali in the UAE, providing an additional corridor for cargo serving inland destinations, such as Ethiopia. Landlocked since Eritrea’s independence in 1993, Ethiopia relies heavily on Djibouti for access to international trade. These commercial links help explain Abu Dhabi’s interest in regional stability and its relationship with Addis Ababa. However, they do not establish that the UAE can influence the TPLF, persuade Eritrea to de-escalate or change Ethiopia’s military calculations. The extent to which Abu Dhabi can use its relationship with the federal government to encourage a political response to the conflict remains unclear. Saudi Arabia: Diplomatic experience, uncertain engagement Saudi Arabia has yet to publicly announce its position on the latest fighting in Tigray. The kingdom has not publicly commented on the renewed war, according to an October 1 analysis by Critical Threats, although it undertook diplomatic efforts earlier this year to reduce tensions between Ethiopia’s federal government and the TPLF. Saudi Arabia has previously sought to mediate between Ethiopia and Eritrea. In November 2025, Chatham House reported that sources said Riyadh had offered to mediate between the two countries amid rising tensions over maritime access and regional security. A June 2026 analysis by Germany’s SWP think tank said previous Saudi mediation efforts had failed, partly because negotiations did not address Ethiopia’s interest in the Eritrean port of Assab. The kingdom’s broader regional alignment also matters. An August 2026 analysis by the Soufan Center described Saudi Arabia and Egypt as backing Eritrea in opposition to Ethiopia’s ambitions for Red Sea access. This is an assessment of regional alignment, however, not evidence that Saudi Arabia is directly providing military support to Eritrea or the TPLF in the current fighting. Saudi Arabia has a strong interest in Red Sea security, a vital corridor for international shipping and its own oil exports. Whether Riyadh will take a more public diplomatic role as tensions escalate remains unclear. Egypt’s rivalry with Ethiopia adds to regional tensions Egypt’s role in the crisis is shaped by its longstanding dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) and its growing ties with Eritrea. Cairo has also stressed that responsibility for the governance and security of the Red Sea rests with countries bordering the waterway, a position shared by Asmara. The issue has added to regional tensions as Ethiopia seeks reliable access to the sea. In September, Ethiopia’s army chief, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula, accused Egypt and Sudan of supporting armed groups fighting the federal government, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). His remarks, reported by Al Jazeera on September 28, did not provide evidence substantiating the accusation.

events.title: S’pore investors take stock risks abroad, but why not at home? SGX chairman Koh Boon Hwee weighs in
events.summary: SGX chairman Koh Boon Hwee explained that early-stage venture funding is relatively well-supported in Singapore. Singapore investors take risks overseas, but SGX chairman Koh Boon Hwee says local shares still lack liquidity and sustained demand, so investors stay cautious at home. Koh says Singapore may need more capital injections, including the $6.5 billion EQDP, but warns these are not a natural, lasting flow like pension-backed markets in the US. He says Singapore must support more start-ups and growth firms, or they will keep listing overseas, which weakens local capital recycling and slows long-term economic growth. SINGAPORE – Singapore investors are willing to take risks on volatile growth stocks overseas, but are unlikely to make similar bets here, where the local market still lacks flow and liquidity, said Singapore Exchange chairman Koh Boon Hwee. The problem, in his view, is that the Republic has yet to create a level of sustained demand for local shares that gives investors enough confidence to take risks here, and, until then, further capital injections will be needed to sustain demand in the stock market. Koh was speaking to The Straits Times on the sidelines of the Forbes Global CEO Conference on Oct 8. “Do they here have the appetite for risk? The answer is yes,” he said, pointing to younger investors who buy overseas stocks such as Tesla and even SpaceX, which is loss-making. But would they back similar businesses on SGX? “My honest answer is , right now it’s unlikely, because they understand the constraints here as well,” he said. This could help explain why many initial public offerings on the local bourse have recently struggled to gain traction after listing, despite efforts by the central bank, the stock exchange and fund managers to revive the local equities market and attract new listings. Asked whether Singapore would need continued capital injections in the meantime, Koh said: “Personally, I would think so”, but noted that the decision was beyond him. While he commended the Government’s move to allocate $6.5 billion of investment capital into the local stock market through the Equity Market Development Programme (EQDP), he noted that it is a “stochastic injection, and not a natural flow”. He distinguished such injections from the regular and sustained capital flows that pension systems generate in other countries. In the United States, for example, multiple pension funds make independent investment decisions and help circulate capital through the public markets, private equity and venture capital. An allocation under the EQDP, by contrast, leaves the question of what follows after the money has been committed. “You have to think about how much more for how much longer,” Koh said. While he stressed that the EQDP funds are being invested rather than spent, he noted that the wider concern is that the repeated allocations do not establish the recurring demand flows needed to sustain the market. “Our challenge right now is to create something that is circular and sustainable,” said Koh. “If you don’t have constant demand creation, it’s hard to sustain liquidity. And with no liquidity, there is no proper valuation.” Convincing investors to recycle capital here Koh explained that early-stage venture funding is relatively well-supported in Singapore, but these investors eventually need a way to realise their investments and recycle the capital into other start-ups and ventures. A public listing can provide that route, but for it to work, the market needs investors willing to buy into a company’s next stage of growth. Without an attractive domestic market, founders must consider overseas listings to fulfil their obligations to their backers, regardless of how committed they are to Singapore. Several prominent Singapore-funded companies have already taken that path over the years. Sea, the parent of e-commerce platform Shopee and gaming business Garena, for example, listed on the New York Stock Exchange in 2017, while Grab debuted on Nasdaq in 2021 through a merger with a special purpose acquisition company. Singapore-headquartered data centre operator DayOne is now pursuing a similar route, having filed for a proposed Nasdaq IPO in October. The result is that SGX misses out on potential growth stocks that could attract a broader pool of investors, while early backers realise their investments through overseas markets, leaving a gap in the domestic capital cycle. “You can’t blame them for doing that,” Koh said, adding that Singapore may have provided the research funding, business environment, stability and security that helps young companies develop, but much more work needs to be done to offer a viable route for capital to be recycled here. “We need to create an environment that will not make it an automatic reflex that we list on Nasdaq or we list in Hong Kong.

events.title: Malaysian King buys stake in miner expanding into rare earths
events.summary: Malaysia’s king, Sultan Ibrahim Sultan Iskandar, bought 2.25% of the firm’s issued shares from its managing director Pek Kok Sam at 42.5 cents per share. Malaysia’s King bought a stake in local miner Southern Alliance Mining, which is expanding into rare earths, including through a project in his home state of Johor. Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar bought 2.25% of Singapore-listed Southern Alliance Mining, an iron ore miner, for $6.1 million , the company said in a statement. He acquired the shares from the firm’s managing director Pek Kok Sam at 42.5 cents each, almost a 12% premium to the Oct 12 closing price, the company said in the statement on the same day. Shares of Southern Alliance Mining rose 10.5% to 42 cents in Singapore early on Oct 13. Sultan Ibrahim has wide business interests spanning real estate, telecommunications an infrastructure, mainly through his shareholdings in various enterprises. He is serving a five-year term as Malaysia’s king under the country’s unique rotating monarchy, in which nine hereditary rulers take turns holding the throne. A representative of Malaysia’s national palace did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Oct 13. In September 2025, Southern Alliance Mining acquired 40% of MCRE Resources, which partnered China Rare Earth Corp. for a rare earth mining operation in Perak state. Southern Alliance Mining is also pursuing a proposed acquisition of Paramount Synergy for a rare earth project in Johor as it positions itself at the forefront of the emerging sector. It has maintained a mining presence in the southern Malaysian state for many years through its flagship Chaah Mine and continues to pursue mineral resources development opportunities in the country. Malaysia has stated ambitions to become a globally competitive player in the rare earths industry, drawing significant interest from foreign miners and refiners. The country hosts Australia’s Lynas Rare Earths, one of only two major producers outside China, with local conglomerates such as Berjaya Corp also exploring projects. France’s Carester SAS plans to build a rare earths separation plant ​in the northern state of Perak as part of a venture with Malaysia’s ‌Malaco Mining Group. Southern Alliance’s Pek remains the company’s controlling shareholder, with a direct interest of 55.74%. The firm said it was not a party to the transaction and did not receive any proceeds. The share transfer will not result in any changes to the company’s management, operations or strategic direction, it said. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Oil edges lower after rising on expanding Middle East conflict
events.summary: Oil has risen more than 70% in 2026 as the US war on Iran roils energy markets. Oil prices slipped after three days of gains, as traders weighed fears that the widening Middle East war could disrupt supply and lift energy costs further. Houthi drone and missile attacks on Saudi Arabia killed at least 16 people and wounded about 300, while Trump said he may back Saudi-led strikes and warned of violations of his “energy ceasefire”. Saudi Arabia is moving to reduce its reliance on the Strait of Hormuz, with Aramco planning extra export capacity soon and a bigger bypass pipeline within two to three years, showing how fragile oil flows remain. Oil edged lower following three days of gains that were driven by concern the widening war in the Middle East could hamper a recovery in supply from the region. Brent traded below US$106 a barrel after rising more than 6% over the previous three sessions, while West Texas Intermediate was near US$93. Diesel fell a third day in New York after Russia agreed to release more supply following a request by US President Donald Trump. A barrage of drone and missile attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants on Saudi Arabia’s main airport has intensified pressure on Washington to step up its efforts in the conflict in Yemen. Meanwhile, Trump said there had been violations of his “energy ceasefire” between Kyiv and Moscow. President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine will continue attacks against Russia as his nation’s energy infrastructure is still being targeted. The attacks on Saudi Arabia came shortly after Riyadh-led forces in Yemen launched a campaign to retake Houthi-held territory, while strikes on tankers in the critical Strait of Hormuz have escalated. That has led to a growing number of supertankers turning away from the Persian Gulf in recent days. “It’s been a dizzying few days of headlines,” said Scott Shelton, an energy specialist at TP ICAP Group, pointing to issues including Trump’s claims of an “energy ceasefire” as well as the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. “We are off to a messy start this week.” Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s main airport over the weekend killed at least 16 people, including a US citizen, and wounded about 300. Trump has said he would consider joining Saudi-backed strikes against the Yemen-based group that is backed by Iran. Meanwhile, the kingdom is seeking to bolster its ability to ship oil without having to transit the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Aramco could add 1.2 million barrels a day of export capacity within seven to eight weeks by repurposing existing gas pipelines, Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said at a conference in Riyadh on Monday. The country also plans to expand a pipeline that bypasses Hormuz by 40% to 10 million barrels a day within two to three years. The push comes even after Middle East oil flows recovered sharply in recent weeks. Some Wall Street banks have said crude shipments from the region had returned to near pre-war levels. That recovery put downward pressure on prices, but has also left the market vulnerable to another major supply disruption, said Haris Khurshid, chief investment officer at Karobaar Capital LP. “Just because the system has found ways to keep oil moving doesn’t mean it can handle another major disruption. That’s the risk the market could be underestimating.” In Europe, Trump’s envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff told Ukrainian officials on Oct 9 that allowing Russian diesel exports was part of efforts to bring Moscow back to negotiations to end the war, Reuters reported, citing sources familiar with the matter. events.title: 'Boring is not bad': CEO of Southeast Asia's largest bank pitches Singapore as a haven amid global turmoil
events.summary: Southeast Asia's biggest bank by assets is making a pitch to investors that Singapore and its businesses can help them navigate many of the uncertainties around the globe. Tan Su Shan, the CEO of DBS Group, says Singapore's reliability is helpful at such a moment. DBS can help customers diversify supply chains and pivot to new markets, she said. SINGAPORE — Southeast Asia's biggest bank by assets is making a pitch to investors that Singapore and its businesses can help them navigate many of the uncertainties around the globe. "I love it that the 'Little Red Dot' we all call home was open … predictable, and almost kind of boring," said CEO of DBS Group Tan Su Shan at the DBS Asia Future Forward conference in Singapore, referring to the city-state by one of its nicknames. "In this huge time of volatility, 'boring' is not bad, right?" The investing and business climate worldwide has been upended by everything from trade wars and El Niño-related weather issues to the Iran conflict and the Russia-Ukraine war. Singapore, with its AAA-rated debt, stable political environment and position at the heart of Asia, is seen by many as a bastion of stability. Tan said similar characteristics define DBS. DBS has "one of the safest credit ratings in the world," she told CNBC in an interview on the sidelines of the conference. Temasek, the state-owned global investment company that managed assets worth 518 billion Singapore dollars ($404 billion) as of March 31 and is seen as contributing to Singapore's fiscal stability, is DBS's biggest shareholder. DBS is also in a strong position to navigate the economic uncertainty around the world, Tan said. "Trade and supply chains are all fragmented," she said. "If you need to diversify your upstream supply chain, just because you're worried about geopolitics, because you're worried about blockages, because you're worried about the war and the Strait of Hormuz, DBS is a partner to help you ... We can help our customers pivot from one market to another quite quickly." Tan also addressed management of a workforce in the age of artificial intelligence, and how to find people who have the right skills to navigate the technology. "Humans intrinsically are nimble and agile ... I tell all my managers, hire for attitude – because you know you can't buy attitude, you can't train attitude." —CNBC's Ying Shan Lee contributed to this article.

events.title: Alphabet President Ruth Porat on how Google is funding AI to win long term, and the biggest risks ahead
events.summary: Alphabet is spending roughly $200 billion this year to build out its AI capacity, and the company’s president and chief investment officer reiterated Google’s plan next year for the bill to be even more substantial. Alphabet expects capital expenditures (capex) to “increase significantly” next year, Ruth Porat said Monday at Fortune ’s Most Powerful Women Summit in Santa Barbara, Calif., adding that the company remains “capacity constrained” as demand for compute grows. “The demand for compute—because of the value that our partners are seeing in the enterprise, in governments, what we’re seeing across our platform—suggests that we’re in the buildout here now,” she told Fortune Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell. When pressed as to where exactly the industry is in the long term timeline of funding the AI building, and if we are in the peak of spending, Porat replied, “We do see this as an opportunity that extends for quite some time.” Porat, No. 11 on Fortune’s 2026 Most Powerful Women list , is shepherding one of the largest corporate spending sprees ever . Before taking her current role in 2023, she spent nearly a decade as Alphabet’s finance chief, and before that she was Morgan Stanley’s CFO. Porat oversees Alphabet’s investment vehicles, including its capital arms GV and CapitalG, as well as its “Other Bets” ventures, and real estate investments. In July, Alphabet lifted its 2026 capex outlook to as much as $205 billion, and the stock dropped more than 6% the following day, a sign of how hard Wall Street is pushing for proof the massive spending will pay off for investors.    The AI spending is already reshaping Alphabet’s finances. Capital expenditures hit $44.9 billion in the second quarter, “with the vast majority of this spent in technical infrastructure to support our investments in AI,” Alphabet CFO Anat Ashkenazi said during the company’s Q2 earnings call. That pushed free cash flow to negative $5.9 billion, the first time Alphabet’s quarterly cash flow had dipped below zero in its more than 20 years as a public company. Meanwhile, Google Cloud’s revenue climbed 82% to $24.8 billion, while its operating profit more than tripled to $8.8 billion. Shontell questioned Porat about a recent report from Jefferies global head of equity strategy Chris Wood, who argued the AI boom will most likely end in massive capital destruction in the U.S. as cheaper open-source Chinese models take market share. Porat disagreed. “It’s illogical to say that we’re in a capacity-constrained position because there’s such strong demand for the insight and the ability to improve business and government, and yet you can’t drive a return on it,” she told Fortune . To earn an attractive return, Porat said, companies need to focus on two things: “One, what is the value that we add to partners so that you can actually deliver attractive revenue growth, and the other is how efficiently do we deliver that compute capacity.” When asked what winning looks like for Alphabet, Porat pointed to responsible deployment rather than ranking who is best. “The thing that is true throughout history is anything that is not built for the long run won’t endure for the long run,” Porat said. She noted that Alphabet’s capex spending is itself a payoff from strategy devised years ago, starting with Google’s 2016 pivot from “mobile first” to “AI first.” “You must invest for long-term growth,” she added. “By the time you need it, it’s too late.” Porat has repeatedly made the bullish case for AI’s payoff. At an Economic Club of New York event in June, Porat called data centers a “ job creator ,” Fortune ’s Most Powerful Women Editor Emma Hinchliffe wrote. She also argued data centers have helped slow energy price growth by spreading fixed costs across a larger base. And at Fortune’s Global Forum in Riyadh last year, she described AI as “so much more than a chatbot,” and said “we should be able to cure cancer in our lifetime.” To be sure, Porat acknowledged growing resistance to data centers , saying about 71% of Americans don’t want one built in their community, in line with a recent Gallup poll . But she argued that opinion shifts when companies add energy capacity, protect affordability, and create local jobs. She pointed to Google’s investments in nuclear, geothermal, solar, and wind, and to a Skilled Trades Alliance that Google cofounded with Ford, BlackRock , and Carhartt to train electricians, welders, and other workers the buildout needs. “We have to solve the downside anxiety. It’s real. It’s substantive,” Porat said. “That’s why I say, if we can [build AI], we must.” Porat has the veteran finance experience to help forge ahead. During the 2008 financial crisis, she worked closely with then-Treasury Secretary Hank Paulson, leading the Morgan Stanley team that advised the Treasury Department on Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and the New York Federal Reserve on AIG . The key lesson from that crisis, she said Monday, was to “identify your greatest source of vulnerability early and fortify against it, because you can’t address it in the moment.” For companies today, she said, that vulnerability is falling behind on AI. “Because if anyone is connecting with your customers in ways that you are not … You’re at a competitive disadvantage.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Singapore PM Wong rejects weaker currency as shortcut to competitiveness
events.summary: Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong pushed back against the idea of weakening the Singapore dollar to boost competitiveness. He said the city-state must instead rely on its economic strengths even as a strong currency adds to costs for businesses. SINGAPORE — Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong pushed back against the idea of weakening the Singapore dollar to boost competitiveness, saying the city-state must instead rely on its economic strengths even as a strong currency adds to costs for businesses. Wong said Singapore could continue to expect a strong and stable currency if its economy performs well, emphasizing its role in containing imported inflation. "You're surely not suggesting that we depress our exchange rate in order to be more competitive," Wong said in a lighthearted exchange with DBS CEO Tan Su Shan at the bank's Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore on Monday. His remarks came after Tan highlighted Singapore's reputation as a safe haven, which has helped attract capital and support the local currency, while acknowledging that the city-state remains a relatively expensive place to do business. "The MAS will exercise monetary policy independently. The Singapore dollar will reflect our economic fundamentals, and if the economy does well, then we can continue to expect a strong, stable Sing dollar that is anchored on fundamentals and will also help keep imported inflation down," Wong said. Unlike most major central banks, which primarily use interest rates to manage monetary conditions, the Monetary Authority of Singapore conducts policy through the exchange rate. It manages the Singapore dollar against a basket of currencies belonging to the country's major trading partners, allowing the exchange rate to fluctuate within an undisclosed policy band. The approach reflects Singapore's heavy dependence on international trade and imports, making currency movements particularly important for domestic prices. A stronger Singapore dollar helps cushion the cost of imported goods and services, particularly during periods of elevated global inflation. But it can also make Singapore-produced goods and services more expensive for overseas buyers, adding pressure on exporters. The Singapore dollar has strengthened almost 0.4% against the greenback since the start of the year. Wong acknowledged those trade-offs, saying businesses would have to account for currency strength alongside Singapore's other operating costs. "Companies that seek to export will have to factor that into the cost of doing business, together with the other costs that they experience in Singapore, as we all know, we are certainly not the cheapest location in Southeast Asia," he said. Still, Wong argued that competing on price alone was not a viable strategy for Singapore, which must instead differentiate itself through its capabilities, stability and predictability. "Companies are not looking for the cheapest locations," he said. "They are looking for capabilities. They are looking for stability. They are looking for predictability." Wong also said Singapore could not compete on cost alone, and was instead developing broader industrial ecosystems linking multinational corporations, domestic suppliers, research capabilities and skilled workers. Singapore's competitiveness ultimately depended on the value it offered businesses rather than its relative cost advantage, he added. "We have to again play to our strengths and compete on the basis of the value we bring to the table," he said.

events.summary: Kroger’s CEO said the company should reduce duplicative work and adapt with technology, as job cuts would help the company cut prices and invest in in-store employees. Kroger plans to cut about 3,000 corporate jobs over three years as it expands AI use, CEO Greg Foran said in a memo seen by Reuters. Foran said the cuts will remove duplicate work and help Kroger lower prices and invest more in store staff. The move affects about 37% of 8,200 corporate workers and comes after Kroger outlined its AI strategy and cut its sales target to compete with Walmart and Aldi. CINCINNATI, Ohio – Kroger plans to cut roughly 3,000 corporate roles over the next three years, chief executive Greg Foran told staff in a memo, seen by Reuters on Oct 12, as the grocer integrates artificial intelligence into its workflow. Kroger should reduce duplicative work and adapt with technology, Foran wrote in the memo, adding that the job cuts would help the company cut prices and invest in in-store employees. Foran took over as Kroger’s CEO in February. Companies have been rethinking corporate structures and cutting jobs as they increasingly turn to AI to streamline workflows and divert more resources towards the technology, fuelling concerns over widespread disruption across sectors. In September, the company outlined the company’s AI strategy, including the use of models to manage workflows and leverage customer data to power tools such as its AI shopping assistant. The grocery retailer had also lowered its annual identical sales target and said it is seeking to cut prices to better compete with rivals such as Walmart and Aldi as consumers grow more frugal under pressure from high gas prices. Details on the job cuts, which would affect about 37% of its 8,200 corporate employees, would be shared in the coming months, Foran said in the memo. Bloomberg News first reported on the job cuts on Oct 12. In June 2025, the company cut about 1,000 corporate roles. REUTERS

events.title: GM CEO: We're making leaps and bounds toward 'eyes-off, hands-off' driving
events.summary: General Motors CEO Mary Barra said the automaker is still on track to introduce "eyes-off, hands-off" driving technology by 2028, starting with the electric Cadillac Escalade IQ. After exiting its Cruise robotaxi business, GM is focusing on autonomous technology for personal vehicles. General Motors CEO Mary Barra said Monday that the automaker remains on track to introduce "eyes-off, hands-off" driving technology by 2028. GM announced last October that it plans to launch its next-generation driver-assistance system in the electric Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028 before expanding to other models. Unlike the company's existing Super Cruise system, which allows drivers to take their hands off the wheel but requires them to remain attentive, the new technology is designed to let drivers take their eyes off the road under certain conditions. Barra told CNBC's Jim Cramer on " Mad Money " that she recently tested the technology and was impressed by how much it had improved since an earlier ride in March. "They're making so much progress on our goal to have eyes off, hands off in the '28 time frame," the CEO said. "We're going to be well positioned from a personal autonomy perspective." She added, "When people want to drive, they can. When they don't, they won't need to as that grows." GM's push into personal autonomous driving follows its decision to exit its Cruise robotaxi business in December 2024 after spending more than $10 billion. Rather than compete in the increasingly crowded driverless ride-hailing market, the automaker redirected its resources toward developing autonomous systems for vehicles consumers own. "We're not in the taxi business. We're not in the bus business," Barra said. She acknowledged that exiting the robotaxi market was difficult but defended the move, noting that GM retained much of the Cruise team to work on personal autonomous driving. "It was a tough decision, but I think it was the right decision," she said. Barra also pushed back against the idea that widespread adoption of autonomous vehicles could eventually reduce the need for personal car ownership. She recalled earlier predictions that ride-hailing services such as Uber and Lyft would sharply reduce vehicle sales, something that never materialized because "people still value that it's in my driveway.
