events.title: Top execs say the $124 trillion Great Wealth Transfer, women entrepreneurs, and veterans are poised to remake the financial landscape
events.summary: The landscape for money is shifting, and top executives say that the Great Wealth Transfer, the new generation of entrepreneurs, and veterans are paving the way. At Fortune ’s 26th annual Most Powerful Women conference in Santa Barbara, Deloitte U.S. federal health sector leader Beth Meagher said that women are poised to play a huge role in shaping how wealth is invested and deployed. It’s estimated that around $124 trillion in wealth will be passed down by 2048, according to Cerulli Associates, with $54 trillion going to women, $52 trillion to children, and $18 trillion charity. On top of that, women entrepreneurs are on the come-up—Meagher said that they’re one of the fastest growing sources of wealth concentration, up over 125% over the past decade. And women who have served our country are also building momentum, reaching roughly 300% growth over the past couple of years, the Deloitte exec pointed out. “These trends are changing everything,” Meagher told Fortune executive editorial director Diane Brady onstage. “I think we spend a lot of time on frontier models, and we probably spend a lot of time on geopolitical [issues]. And this shift is something that I think we have a tremendous opportunity to lead from the front of.” Seema Hingorani, managing director and senior client advisor at Morgan Stanley , caught wind of this trend more than a decade ago. When she was working at the New York City Pension Fund in the early 2010s, she noticed something worrying. Every asset manager in the world was coming to meet with her, yet each had few to no women on their investment teams, Hingorani said. They wrote it off as a “pipeline issue”—but Hingorani didn’t buy it. So she started a nonprofit called Girls Who Invest to get more women into the industry, with 5,000 college women having gone through the program since 2011. Every year they receive around 4,000 applications, and support 700 women annually. Hingorani also pointed out that for the past seven years, Morgan Stanley has run an incubator helping to invest in more women starting tech businesses. And when they scale billion-dollar companies and take their successes to the bank, they’ll be looking for women to help guide their decisions. “[Women are] going to have all the wealth,” Hingorani said. “[For] those women—you guys—do you want to have a male financial advisor? If you had a choice, would you want to have a woman financial advisor? A lot of firms out there are hiring all my women, because they get it.” Beyond how they manage their wealth, women are also setting new expectations about spending it. Carmen James Randolph, founding president and CEO of the Women’s Foundation of the South, is seeing a major shift in her own backyard. Randolph said that the South is one of the fastest-growing regions in the country, and with 41.5% of America’s women of color as the area’s constituents, there’s a new frontier for wealth creation and investment. She’s already seeing that the old-school models of philanthropy are being rewritten to prioritize tangible impact. “I’ve worked in philanthropy now for about 28 years, and I understand that at its best, philanthropy can be a catalyst for what’s possible. Old models see philanthropy as charity, and new wealth recipients do not see philanthropy as charity,” Randolph explained onstage. “They want to understand and see firsthand the impact that their dollars can have.” The Deloitte and Morgan Stanley execs agree that the way women want to invest is different from previous generations, by prioritizing social impact in tandem with financial returns. Meagher said that women poised to inherit substantial wealth are focused on three key areas of investment: health, education, and justice. She’s picked up on a trend where wealth advisors are also specifically offering health services; and Randolph says that her foundation is making a big bet on improving maternal healthcare in southern states with difficult access to emergency and routine medical care. Hingorani also noted that every trustee has an interest in affordable housing—even if it means a smaller return than what they could earn at a venture fund. “Women are looking to pull their investments so that they can have an outsized impact,” Meagher said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.summary: The BIS supports central banks' pursuit of monetary and financial stability through international cooperation. Cyber Resilience Coordination Centre BIS research focuses on policy issues of core interest to the central bank and financial supervisory community. Our authors publish economic analysis and research on monetary and financial stability issues. The BIS hosts committees engaged in standard setting & the pursuit of financial stability through the Basel Process. Access our statistics in the BIS Data Portal Ethics & conduct, risk management & internal audit Consultative Council for the Americas Historical monetary & financial statistics Regulatory Consistency Assessment Programme (RCAP) Countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) Global systemically important banks (G-SIB) The Basel Committee has published assessment reports on the implementation of its leverage ratio framework (LEV) in Australia, Canada, Japan, Korea, Switzerland and the United Kingdom. Australia, Japan, Korea and Switzerland are assessed as compliant; Canada and the United Kingdom are assessed as largely compliant. This publication concludes the first round of multi-jurisdictional assessments of the leverage ratio. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision today published assessment reports on Australia, Canada, Japan, Korea, Switzerland and the United Kingdom’s implementation of the Committee’s leverage ratio framework (LEV). Australia, Japan, Korea and Switzerland were assessed as compliant with the Committee’s global standards, the highest overall grade. Canada and the United Kingdom were assessed as largely compliant, which is one notch below the highest overall grade. These assessments form part of the Committee’s Regulatory Consistency Assessment Programme (RCAP), which evaluates the consistency and completeness of Basel standards’ implementation across member jurisdictions. With the publication of these reports, the Committee has concluded the first round of multi-jurisdictional assessments of the leverage ratio. In line with its work programme, the Committee initiated in H1 2026 jurisdictional assessments of the Basel III revisions to risk-weighted assets and continues to assess the implementation of the leverage ratio.

events.title: ‘If you take your foot off the pedal at all, you will start to stall’: Women in C-suite roles have stagnated, and the reasons go beyond the pipeline
events.summary: The rate of women being promoted into senior executive roles is slowing down, and experts warn a shaky labor climate and dearth of professional infrastructure are further exacerbating an already obstruction-filled pipeline for women to become CEOs. At the Fortune Most Powerful Women Summit in Santa Barbara, Calif., on Monday, Kelly Baker, executive vice president and chief human resource officer at financial services firm Thrivent, explained that there has been less of a focus on developing and recruiting women to join executive leadership. The slowdown is a byproduct of a frenetic environment that has deprioritized cultivating these leaders. “I don’t think we can ignore the fact that there is a climate where organizations aren’t quite as focused,” Baker told Fortune Leadership Editor Claire Zillman. “If you take your foot off the pedal at all, you will start to stall.” The Fortune 500 has 56 companies led by women, or about 11.2% of the list, up from 7.4% six years ago. However, women’s share of roles in both the C-suite and at the board level has stalled at about 30%, marking the first decline in women’s board representation in more than a decade. Toni Townes-Whitley, a former Fortune 500 CEO and Nasdaq corporate board member, suggested fewer discussions about workplace diversity has led to less of a spotlight on promoting and developing women leaders, and in an attitude shift toward women’s capabilities. “We can’t take away an environment where there is a question, almost a recalibration of women in the world, where unfortunately negative rhetoric from lots of different dimensions have women being challenged externally, internally, by the boards,” Townes-Whitley said at the summit. “That’s a concern, underlined, that’s just not talked about.” To be sure, problems in getting across the last mile before taking the helm of companies are persistent, and are also, in part, a result of women not viewing themselves as leaders. That’s despite having skillsets and experience that would qualify them for these roles. Only 36% of women in the workplace have considered becoming a CEO or said they wanted to be a CEO, according to Jenna Fisher, managing director of global leadership advisory firm Russell Reynolds Associates: “We can’t 3D print our candidates.” Hayden Brown, president and CEO of freelance marketplace platform Upwork, was one of those women who didn’t consider taking on the role of top brass, despite her mother running the women’s empowerment program at her workplace.   “I grew up in like the most pro-women household, and yet it took our board chair,, probably 10 years ago, to say to me, ‘You should be a CEO,’” Brown told Zillman. “And I was like, ‘Really?’” Brown has worked to change how women view themselves in relation to leadership roles in her own home, editing the books she reads with her children to be more gender inclusive, or to switch out adjectives like “smart” to “hard-working” to guide them toward the traits she wants them to embody. But making larger changes in the workplace will also require the awareness and backing of men, Baker said. Those in influential senior positions in the office, particularly men, will have to serve as both mentors, who support women through their careers, as well as sponsors, who advocate for  high-potential women leaders in front of coworkers and other leaders. While creating systems to reinforce women’s leadership pipelines are perhaps not being discussed or strengthened as much today, there’s some good news, according to Fisher: AI has created pressure to have leaders who are adaptable and fluent in emerging technologies. Russell Reynolds Associates research indicates women are ahead of men in AI adoption and implementation, perhaps because of a willingness to adapt. “Even though DEI is not being talked about as much as it used to be,” Fisher said, “there is still so much demand for women in executive roles and board roles.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Houthi missile attack targets Saudi capital Riyadh for third day in a row
events.summary: Saudi Arabia says it intercepted a ballistic missile fired towards Riyadh, as Houthis say they targeted the King Khalid airport. Houthi missile attack on Riyadh airport: Saudi Arabia vows resilience The Saudi Arabia-led coalition fighting in Yemen has said its forces intercepted another ballistic missile launched by the Houthis towards the Saudi capital, Riyadh, as the city reels from attacks that have killed at least 14 people in recent days. In a statement on X, Turki Al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the coalition, said the Houthis fired one ballistic missile at Riyadh and two towards Khamis Mushait, a city in the southwest. list 1 of 4 Iran sets crosshairs on ‘US-UAE’ oil shuttle out of Strait of Hormuz list 2 of 4 Why are the Houthis striking Saudi airports? list 3 of 4 Giants Brigades lead southern Yemen fightback against the Houthis list 4 of 4 ‘Energy ceasefire’: What’s behind Trump’s love-hate ties to Russian oil? All three were “intercepted and destroyed”, he said. Residents of Riyadh reported several powerful explosions on Monday night, moments after a text message to their phones warned of an aerial threat. The Houthis, who control Yemen’s most populous areas, including the capital, Sanaa, said their target in Riyadh had been King Khalid International airport. Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesman, said the group had also sent a drone towards a military airbase at Khamis Mushait, near the Yemeni border. He again warned international airlines and travellers “against operating flights to airports” in Saudi Arabia, except in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, saying the facilities were “unsafe”. The renewed attacks came as King Khalid International airport in Riyadh remains closed after a Houthi attack on Saturday that killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300 others. Another strike on Sunday killed one person and wounded 11. Saudi authorities said the airport would remain closed until this Saturday, and airlines have canceled flights. The Houthis have also struck Saudi oil facilities. The attacks come as the Houthis fight forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government for control of the country. The Saudi-led coalition has carried out an air campaign against the Houthis and backed the government’s ground forces. The fighting erupted amid regional tensions set off by the United States and Israel’s war on Iran. Speaking at an energy conference in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia’s Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud said the attacks on airports over the last week have tested the kingdom’s resilience. “The events of recent weeks are serious,” the minister said. “Our response must be equally serious.” He added that Vision 2030, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s plan to diversify the Saudi economy, “must continue. Investment must continue”. Saudi authorities have meanwhile opened an investigation into why the country’s air defences failed to stop the barrage, according to two regional officials who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity. An initial inquiry found that the Houthis first launched several drones to clear a path for a mix of cruise and ballistic missiles, which then reached the airport, the officials said. The Houthis possess ballistic missiles with warheads that can change direction in flight, posing a challenge to the Patriot interceptors and other systems the Saudis rely on. One official told AP that investigators also wanted to know why the defences had not given earlier warning of an attack in which missiles and drones flew more than 1,000km, or 620 miles, to reach Riyadh. US President Donald Trump separately criticised the Houthis but gave no indication that Washington would intervene. “Well, the Houthis are misbehaving very badly. No good,” he told reporters when asked what he planned to do about the group. A Houthi official warned that US involvement would bring retaliation. “If the US becomes involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond; rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the US and all its interests in the region,” Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthis’ political bureau, told the AFP news agency. Al-Bukhaiti also warned “all employees and workers at Saudi oil facilities and airports to stay away from these sites, as they have become legitimate targets”. The attacks have put events scheduled in Riyadh this month under pressure, including the kingdom’s flagship investment conference and the WPC Energy Congress, where several top oil executives were dropped from the programme. The United Arab Emirates’s national carrier Etihad Airways announced on Monday that it was cancelling all flights to and from Riyadh until next week. It also suspended flights to Dammam and Jeddah. Bahrain’s national carrier Gulf Air said it, too, was cancelling all Riyadh flights until Saturday.

events.title: Scoop: Top Trump operative enlisted to rescue Kansas senator's campaign
events.summary: A top Trump political operative has been tapped to help boost Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall 's campaign in the weeks before the Nov. 3 election, the latest sign of how Republicans are scrambling to defend the red-state seat. Why it matters: The hiring of veteran strategist Chris Grant reflects the GOP's growing anxiety over Kansas' Senate race. Marshall is running neck and neck with Democrat Adam Hamilton in a state President Trump won by 16 points in 2024. Republicans fear losing Kansas could be a domino in costing them their Senate majority. Driving the news: GOP operatives have become increasingly frustrated with Marshall's reelection campaign, which they believe hasn't been aggressive enough at a time when soaring fuel prices have particularly hurt farmers in Kansas and elsewhere in the Midwest. Grant, who helped lead the main pro-Trump super PAC in 2024 and has remained involved in Trump's political operation, will be a senior adviser to Marshall and help guide strategy in the final three weeks. Grant also worked on Marshall's 2020 Senate campaign. What they're saying: "Chris is an absolute pro who has been a longtime friend to Team Marshall. Having him help land the plane these last three weeks is a no brainer," Brent Robertson, Marshall's chief of staff, told Axios. Zoom in: Two GOP outside groups — the Senate Leadership Fund and Club for Growth — are pouring millions into the Kansas race. SLF, the principal super PAC aligned with Senate GOP leadership, is spending $14 million in Kansas after shifting resources from the Senate race in North Carolina, where Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper has a significant polling lead over former Republican National Committee chair Michael Whatley. Trump said in a social media post Monday that he would campaign for Marshall "very soon." A Democrat-aligned super PAC has announced plans to spend $5 million to help Hamilton. Between the lines: Marshall has faced damaging headlines recently, including a New York Times r eport that his medical practice sued more than 700 former patients over unpaid medical bills, and that 81 were later arrested for missing court appearances. The other side: Hamilton, a Methodist pastor, has won endorsements from two former Republican governors in Kansas, Mike Hayden and Bill Graves.

events.title: Publicly owned rail is popular. But is it making the trains run on time?
events.summary: The early afternoon of Wednesday 6 August was an unremarkable one on the rail network. Then suddenly, shortly before 14:00, a power failure brought trains across the north-west of England to a halt. Chaos ensued: passengers told the BBC they were stranded on platforms for hours, with some having to book hotels for the night. This incident, stemming from a short power cut that affected Network Rail's operating centre in Manchester, was, in itself, unusual. But it added to a difficult summer for train passengers. Repeated heatwaves required risk control measures like speed reductions to avoid tracks being damaged in the heat, leading to delays and cancellations. There was a serious derailment near Lewes, East Sussex, and another smaller-scale incident near Wickford in Essex soon after. Against a backdrop of relatively high cancellation rates and steep fares compared with previous decades, rail users could be forgiven for forming the impression that things are not working. Something is changing, though: Labour is steadily bringing nearly all passenger rail services into public hands. Nationalisation is a popular idea - a YouGov tracker poll suggests almost two thirds of the public support public ownership. August's 90-second power outage sparked chaos for rail commuters But in reality, plans are still in their early stages. Big structural changes have yet to be introduced. And experts caution that it's too early to say how successful these will be. So can rail nationalisation meet the public's expectations? Or are the ongoing delays and cancellations that we're currently seeing under a part-nationalised network a sign that it might struggle to deliver real improvement? South Western Railway (SWR) was nationalised in May 2025, the first of six services to be brought into public ownership under Labour so far. At Woking station, which is served by SWR, regular commuter Leo tells me he had been optimistic about public ownership, but hasn't noticed it making any difference so far: "I think the phrase 'emperor's new clothes' comes to mind… it's still unreliable." SWR saw a clear increase in cancellations during its first year in public hands. But how much of this was due to nationalisation? The Conservatives have cited SWR as an example of how public control does not necessarily mean improvements or fix key problems. But the government argues SWR's early period in public hands was affected by high summer temperatures, signal failures and trespass incidents. Lord Hendy, the rail minister, says work to turn the operator around has included introducing long-delayed new trains on suburban routes and recruiting more drivers, resulting in a drop in those cancellations that are due to staff shortages. TransPennine Express was nationalised in May 2023, under the Conservative government. Many passengers had been at their wits' end as the operator struggled to fulfil its timetable and suffered from poor industrial relations. A plan to improve reliability was put in place, which included cutting some services and even removing one type of train as a way of sorting out staffing problems. A new deal with the drivers' union also helped - something an insider at the former private sector operator claimed to me their company had not been permitted to do. So has it worked? Cancellations have fallen noticeably. But they were still above the Great Britain average in the year to August. It's really important to say the data can only tell us so much. There are so many different factors that might affect the performance of each service: for example, the state of the infrastructure it relies on, weather events or simply how well it was working before the government took over. Plus, of the operators nationalised since Labour came to power, only SWR and c2c have completed a whole year in public hands. Even for those nationalised years earlier, the picture is clouded by the impact of the pandemic, when passenger numbers fell off a cliff. But according to Alex Hynes, chief executive of DfT Operator Limited (DfTO), the government company that currently owns publicly-run operators, it has been possible to make some short-term changes. Notably, these include making one team jointly responsible for managing infrastructure and passenger train services in some areas including the south-west of England. "The railway is a system: track, train, people," he says. "So by putting one person in charge, they can fix all elements of the system to deliver a better service to customers." Hynes also gives examples of changes on the recently nationalised Thameslink; investment in better cleaning, improving toilets and replacing unpopular upright "ironing-board" seats. But when it comes to the pure performance data of operators nationalised in the past few years - delays, cancellations - can we really draw any conclusions yet to tell us whether the policy is working?

events.title: What we know about Lady Violet Bridgerton ahead of Netflix spin-off
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Netflix has announced a Bridgerton spin-off focusing on Lady Violet. ( Supplied: Netflix/Liam Daniel ) This article contains spoilers from seasons one to four of Bridgerton. In previous seasons of the Netflix and Shondaland series Bridgerton, Lady Violet has expressed a great affection for her late husband Viscount Edmund Bridgerton. She experienced intense heartbreak and sorrow when he died. Now, fans of the television show will get to see their love story. In the same way Queen Charlotte: A Bridgerton Story delved into the early life of Queen Charlotte, a yet untitled series will chronicle the early life of a young Lady Violet. It promises to tell the story of Violet's romance with Edmund (Rupert Evans). There have been two actors so far who have taken on the role of Lady Violet. Ruth Gemmell plays her in the main series and appeared in the Queen Charlotte spin-off, in which Connie Jenkins-Greig played a younger version in flashbacks as a then Violet Ledger. Lady Violet is depicted in Bridgerton as a kind, warm and wise matriarch with the interests of her family at heart. As we gear up for the spin-off, here's a trip down memory lane exploring some of what we already know about Lady Violet and her relationship with Lord Bridgerton. Violet Bridgerton (née Ledger) holds the title the Dowager Viscountess Bridgerton. Lady Violet is the family's matriarch and has eight children. ( Supplied: Netflix/Liam Daniel ) A Dowager Viscountess is the widowed wife of a viscount who retains her aristocratic rank after her husband's death. Violet was pregnant with Lord Bridgerton's eighth child Hyacinth when he died from anaphylaxis. He'd suffered a severe allergic reaction after being stung by a bee. He was in his late 30s at the time. He'd been out hunting with eldest son Anthony and was picking hyacinths for his wife when it happened. In a conversation with Anthony in season two, episode eight of Bridgerton, titled The Viscount Who Loved Me, Violet tells her son she would go through the pain of losing her husband again because the beauty of love overpowers the risk of grief. "Losing Edmund was the most difficult time of my life," Violet said. "And the pain that I felt … beyond description. "But there is one thing that has given me at least some modicum of solace. "It's knowing that I would still choose the life I led with him, each and every time. "And I would undoubtedly feel the same pain I felt all over again if I had to because real, true love is worth it no matter what." Lady Violet is close friends with Lady Danbury (right). ( Supplied: Netflix/Liam Daniel ) Violet is keen to see each of her eight children marry, but she wants them, too, to experience true love, rather than marry for the sake of it. While no marriage is perfect, the union between Violet and Edmund is so idealised that each of her children aspire to live a similar fairytale. In season one, episode eight called After the Rain, Violet points out to her daughter Daphne that marriage is hard, and the reason why hers worked was because they chose to love each other through each obstacle. "It is a rarity, I have come to realise," Violet said. "That is not to say it was without its trials. "Your father and I faced many difficulties, indeed, but we overcame them. "We made a decision early on to do so. "We chose to love each other every single day. "It is a choice, dearest, one that is never too late to make." Lady Violet remains devoted to her late husband throughout the first few seasons of the television series. Lady Violet develops feelings for Lord Marcus Anderson, but not enough to marry him. ( Supplied: Netflix/Liam Daniel ) That is, until Lord Marcus Anderson (Daniel Francis) catches her eye. He is Lady Agatha Danbury's (Adjoa Andoh) younger brother, and they meet in season three of Bridgerton. In season four, they kick it up a notch into a steamy, passionate, but secret dalliance. Finally, Violet is exploring her own desires after mostly focusing her efforts on matchmaking her children. Lord Marcus wants to marry her, but the "not yet" response to his offer of engagement turns into a "not ever" in his eyes. With Queen Charlotte being as juicy as it was stunningly heartbreaking, this author cannot wait for the Lady Violet spin-off, dearest gentle reader. The spin-off will be written by showrunners and executive producers Shonda Rhimes and Nicholas Nardini. Bridgerton is based on the popular historical romance novels written by Julia Quinn. The TV show debuted on Netflix in 2020 and captivated global audiences. Season five is currently in production.

events.title: Elon Musk takes a dig at Waymo's pet collision history and says Tesla Robotaxi has a solution
events.summary: Elon Musk said Waymo's robotaxis are "pet destroyers." PATRICK PLEUL/POOL/AFP via Getty Images Waymo has previously caught flak for its robotaxis colliding with stray animals. Elon Musk took jabs at Waymo, calling the robotaxis "pet destroyers." Musk said Tesla gave itself challenges to solve the problem of robotaxis running over animals. Elon Musk took a dig at his robotaxi rival, Waymo , calling the vehicles "pet destroyers," and said Tesla Robotaxi has solved the issue of avoiding stray pets. During a livestreamed interview at an event hosted by Tesla Owners of Silicon Valley on Saturday, Musk called out Waymo for its reported collisions with animals. "What a lot of people don't know is that Waymos are like pet destroyers," Musk said, laughing. "Well, maybe Waymo's made some improvements on that front, but they do run over a lot of pets, and we don't want to run over pets." Waymo has gotten flak over animal collisions before, most notably after its run-in with a beloved bodega cat in a San Francisco neighborhood back in October 2025. The feline, named KitKat, died after it was run over by Waymo's rear right tire, video obtained by The New York Times showed. That is not Waymo's first collision with an animal. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration's Standing General Order requires autonomous vehicle companies like Waymo to report qualifying crashes. NHTSA data showed that between July 2025 and July 2026, Waymo reported at least 9 crashes involving animals, 6 of which Waymo described as domestic animals. A Waymo spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment. Tesla's robotaxi service also reported a collision involving an animal during the same time period, but the incident involved a supervised robotaxi. Tesla also operated a smaller fleet, and most of its unsupervised operations were concentrated in one city: Austin. Musk said during the virtual interview that Tesla Robotaxi will be able to detect roaming pets at night. "We have these challenges of literally like: gray kittens on a gray tarmac with tar seams at night in low visibility. And it's like, 'Can we not run over the kittens,' type of thing," he said. Musk added that Tesla will deploy the update, though he did not specify when. Have a tip on Tesla or Waymo? Contact this reporter via email at lloydlee@businessinsider.com or Signal at lloydlee.71. events.title: Two deaths reported as Hurricane Simon, storm Rachel batter Mexico’s coast
events.summary: Simon caps a Pacific season of record-breaking intensity, as deadly storms wreak havoc from Hawaii to Mexico. At least two people have died in Mexico after Hurricane Simon and former tropical storm Rachel brought torrential rain and catastrophic flooding to Pacific coast communities. At a Monday news briefing, Guerrero Governor Evelyn Salgado confirmed that a 71-year-old man had died during Hurricane Simon after a retaining wall collapsed under the weight of intense precipitation. list 1 of 3 Hurricane Isaias: Four dead and thousands without power in US Southeast list 2 of 3 Isaias weakens after making landfall in US Gulf Coast as hurricane list 3 of 3 Hurricane Isaias leaves trail of destruction across the US Gulf Coast According to the Guerrero-based news agency IRZA, the man, identified by his family as Albino Moreno Jimenez, had been feeding his animals on the western outskirts of Chilpancingo when a wall came crashing down on him. A second death was announced later in the day in the state of Baja California along Mexico’s western coast. There, Governor Marina del Pilar said that a young girl had died from the effects of what was once Hurricane Rachel, which peaked in early October as a Category 3 storm. At least 10 more people remain missing in Baja California, according to the governor. Eight were reported missing in the city of Ensenada, on the Pacific coast, and two in the fishing town of San Felipe on the Gulf of California. The figures remain preliminary, with local newspaper La Jornada reporting a higher death toll of two in Baja California and 11 missing. Rachel made landfall in the Mexican state as a post-tropical cyclone, and its remnants have travelled north through southern California in the southwestern United States. Hurricane Simon, meanwhile, has churned off the coast of Mexico since the weekend. By late Monday morning, it had weakened from a powerful Category 4 storm to a Category 2. Its maximum sustained winds had slowed slightly to around 155km/h (100mph), according to the US National Hurricane Center. Its centre was about 115km west-southwest of Cabo Corrientes, a cape in the state of Jalisco, drifting west at 3km/h. Forecasters predict Simon could make landfall on Thursday or Friday. Hurricane warnings remain in effect for western Mexico, which is vulnerable to landslides and deadly surf conditions as a result of the storm. Experts warn the death toll from both storms could rise, and officials have called on residents to exercise caution amid the devastation wrought by downed trees, high winds and floodwaters. The Spanish newspaper El Pais reported the death of a cliff diver, Juan Patines, who was killed in Mazatlan, the northwestern state of Sinaloa, after jumping into the sea on Saturday night. According to Mexican media, the heavy surf hampered his efforts to return to shore amid dangerous coastal conditions associated with Hurricane Simon. Local authorities later halted cliff-diving at the site due to hazardous sea conditions. Officials have yet to confirm whether his death was directly linked to Hurricane Simon. Rachel and Simon have battered Mexico’s western coast as part of an extraordinary stretch of hurricane activity across the Pacific. The northeastern and central Pacific Ocean has experienced a record storm season this year, fuelled in part by the El Nino weather phenomenon, which results in warming waters in parts of the region. Twenty-one named storms have been recorded in the Pacific so far. On Sunday, Simon tipped the region to a historic high for accumulated cyclone energy (ACE), a metric of the combined strength and longevity of tropical storms. This year has already surpassed the previous high set in 2018. The US island chain of Hawaii has been among the hardest-hit places. In August, Hurricane Lala unleashed ruinous flooding on Hawaii’s Big Island as a Category 1 storm, killing a 93-year-old woman and destroying some 100 homes, according to state officials. A few weeks later, Hurricane Lowell , a Category 4 hurricane at its peak, struck the Hawaiian islands of Kauai and Niihau, where powerful winds, storm surge and flooding overwhelmed towns and roads. Roughly 90 percent of Kauai’s power customers were plunged into darkness as a result of electricity outages. At least two deaths were linked to Lowell. In late September, Hurricane Nolo brought another round of flooding and landslides to the Hawaiian islands, though it did not make landfall.

events.title: Heating oil customers face tough winter despite shake-up promise
events.summary: Heating oil customers facing soaring bills have been promised better regulation of the sector by the government. Ministers say they will tighten up rules, promote competition and give customers clearer compensation routes if things go wrong. Minimum order levels, set for some customers, will be reviewed. With prices close to having doubled in the past year, some campaigners have called for heating oil customers to benefit from the same cap as regular, variable gas and electricity tariffs in England, Scotland and Wales. But there is no sign of the government proposing such a change, nor when the stricter rules will take effect. Ministers said they would work with industry to "develop a regulatory regime for the heating oil market, protecting consumers and promoting competition". In the meantime, oil users have been offered discounts on heat pumps, a code of practice is in place, and industry practices setting minimum order volumes at 500 litres for some consumers will be reviewed. Domestic tanks typically hold between 1,000 and 2,000 litres. The government said this had left some people having to pay for more heating oil than they might need. Buy now or wait and hope? Families face gamble on heating oil Published 10 September Prices have soared since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran. In March, the government announced a support package worth £53m for low-income families who use heating oil. The funding is distributed by local authorities, which set their own criteria for eligibility. A subsequent inquiry by the UK's competition watchdog, the Competition and Markets Authority, found that 1,700 households were forced to "re-order at significantly higher prices or go without fuel" after the war broke out, costing them up to £350. But those whose orders were cancelled and prices raised were told they were entitled to compensation. The government has now announced it will accept the CMA's recommendation to strengthen regulation in the sector. Energy minister Polly Billington said: "Thousands of heating oil customers felt they had nowhere to turn when they paid the price of rising oil and gas costs earlier this year. "We won't accept that. Energy is an essential good and people should not have to think twice about whether they're protected in the market. That's why we will reform the sector." Nick says heating his home now feels more like an investment than a regular household bill Nick, a heating oil customer from West Suffolk, told the BBC's Your Voice that "off-grid households remain a major policy blind spot" for the government. "Any protection from UK government for domestic heating oil users will be very welcome, providing this is for all domestic heating oil users," the 28-year-old said. He rents a three-bedroom home with his partner. He said they had seen prices more than double in a year, to quotes of 111p per litre. "Heating my home is now no longer another household bill, but almost an investment," he said. He called on tax cuts for customers, or the extension of the price cap to heating oil - a demand also made by charity National Energy Action. Tim Buckman, chief executive of price comparison site Boiler Juice, told the BBC he wants stronger protections for consumers but the main problem was that heating oil is twice as expensive as it was before the war. "Just putting regulation in place is not going to reduce the price for customers. What we would like to see is the VAT off heating oil or targeting that specifically." Some 1.5 million households depend on heating oil, but they do not have the same consumer protections as electricity and gas customers. However, energy regulator Ofgem, which sets the cap for standard variable tariffs, only covers England, Wales and Scotland. Most heating oil customers are in Northern Ireland, where 60% of households rely on it, but where regulation is separate. It is likely Ofgem will regulate heating oil in England, Scotland and Wales, and the UK government said it would "engage with the Northern Ireland Executive as they consider these recommendations in parallel". events.title: I earn £120,000 a year making social media videos go viral
events.summary: Eknoor Singh's successful social media video clips include one of popstar Dua Lipa Eknoor Singh says he only needs his mobile phone and a decent internet connection to earn more than £120,000 a year. The 22-year-old Londoner is a professional "clipper". He is paid by clients to make short, vertical videos for social media, in the hope of them going viral. "The more views a clip gets, the more money I make," he says. The way it typically works is that the client - who could be anyone from a clothing brand to a record label, movie studio, podcaster or influencer - has a longer video that the clipper watches first. He or she then makes 30 to 60-second clips of what they consider to be the best bit or bits, and uploads them to Instagram, YouTube, TikTok or other platforms. The idea is that the clippers, who are typically aged from 16 to 25, will have a better understanding of what will connect with that demographic, and get the short videos as many views as possible. With clippers able to earn up to $3 (£2.30) per 1,000 views across platforms, it can be very lucrative if a particular clip does take off. Singh says he got hooked on clipping last year when he made $300 from posting a short video of popstar Dua Lipa on Instagram. "I was like, 'OK, this is a lot of money for simply posting a video.' I instantly knew how lucrative it could be." Now he says he is earning "at least £10,000 a month". He adds that he looks for clips that are funny, quick to watch and engaging, such as a short video he made in May of Sabrina Carpenter's reaction to having the tails of her dress stepped on at the Met Gala in New York. Singh did not reveal who the client was. Singh's clip of Sabrina Carpenter went viral For 24-year-old clipper Ethan Weems from Wichita, Kansas, it's a lucrative side hustle to his other video-making work. He says he makes "at least $1,000 a month" from clipping. He does this by making short videos for YouTuber and podcaster Caleb Hammer, who is best known for hosting a show called Financial Audit, which analyses the personal finances of his guests. Weems says clipping helps him make a living from home – giving him more time to spend with his wife and one-year-old son. "I don't want that typical nine-to-five job where I have to go into an office every day," he says. Yet while some clippers can make good money, social media consultant Lia Haberman cautions that there are very few of them. "It mirrors the creator economy more broadly. The vast majority make little to nothing," she says. Meanwhile, streaming industry analyst Devin Nash says it's easy to underestimate the time required to make clipping a success. He warns that successful clippers must "watch hours and hours of content, and they just live in that world". Ethan Weems says the income helps him continue to work from home Connecting clippers with their prospective clients are a number of intermediary websites, where available video jobs are listed. These range from pages on general online forums such as Reddit and Discord, to dedicated clipping sites such as Clipping Culture, Vyro, Whop and Kick. The latter websites take a fee from the companies wanting the work done. Clipping Culture lists clients including Capital Records, Universal Music Group and HBO Max. For firms such as these, hiring a teenager or 20-something working from his or her bedroom is far cheaper than paying for traditional adverts on social media, and likely to be more effective in terms of getting eyeballs. That's the experience of Boxabl, a Las Vegas-based firm that makes modular homes. "I think we've done probably a billion views [of clips] so far," says founder Galiano Tiramani, who features in many of the company's videos. In the UK, Jimmy McLoughlin, a former Downing Street adviser and now host of the Jimmy's Jobs of the Future podcast, has also embraced clips. "The clips are almost like trailers for the main events," he says. For instance, a recent podcast with Prime Minister Andy Burnham "had close to 50,000 long plays, but in terms of clips, it's done millions". Eknoor Singh says he can make clips anywhere with just his mobile and a good internet connection Evan Stanfield, the founder and boss of Clipping Culture, is himself just 21. He set up the business last year after dropping out of the University of Kansas. Stanfield says that the website connects brands to more than 340,000 clippers from all over the world. He has a simple theory for the popularity of short videos: "People's attention spans are getting shorter and shorter." He adds that making the clips is a young person's game because "they're most of the consumers of short-form videos". Back in London, Eknoor Singh says he is "kind of clipping non-stop", wherever he is. "I could be anywhere. I could go on holiday and make money." I paid £30,000 for an 'influencer' degree.

events.title: CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: How a gold-buying spree helps the yuan go global
events.summary: China has increased its gold purchases every month for nearly two years. The stockpiling comes as Hong Kong plans to become a global gold trading hub, with support for yuan-denominated transactions. It's the latest sign of diversification away from the U.S. dollar. Hi, this is Evelyn, writing to you from Beijing. Welcome to the latest edition of The China Connection — a snapshot of what I'm seeing and hearing from local businesses. Buying gold every month for nearly two years is just part of China's plan to narrow a gap with the U.S. on holdings of the precious metal. What does that do to the yuan? China's decades-long push for yuan internationalization is getting a lift from the buildout of Hong Kong as a gold trading center — denominated in the Chinese currency. "As those trading volumes grow, there would be a growing volume of the physical gold trade that is denominated in RMB and not linked in USD," said Charles Chang, managing director and Greater China country lead for corporate ratings at S&P Global Ratings. The Chinese yuan, also known as the renminbi, accounts for a fraction of international transactions in a global financial system dominated by the U.S. dollar. Analysts I spoke with don't expect major changes to that dynamic anytime soon, but Beijing's gold purchases and Hong Kong trading platform are just the latest steps toward supporting greater use of the yuan globally. "The challenge with internationalizing the RMB it's somewhat more challenging to find places where you can use the RMB," Chang said. "In terms of gold particularly, if the RMB that the buyer receives can be converted to gold, then it gives more channels for the spending to be done." Hong Kong, home to one of the world's largest stock exchanges, last month confirmed its efforts to develop a yuan-denominated gold market . In a major move last year, the special administrative region of China linked its gold vault with one in Shanghai , allowing physical gold delivery to international institutions in Hong Kong denominated in yuan. Over the next three years, Hong Kong plans to expand the capacity of its Shanghai-linked gold vault from 150 tonnes to over 2,000 tonnes , S&P's Chang pointed out. That's nearly as large as all the gold reserves in China , he added. "If Hong Kong is able to complete this transaction, then it would become of the largest gold trading centers in the world." The U.S. still has the largest gold reserves in the world at over 8,100 tonnes, according to World Gold Council figures for the second quarter. China held about one-third of that at over 2,300 tonnes. "China's 23-month gold buying streak reinforces the credibility of the renminbi's internationalization drive," said Hao Zhou, head of research and chief economist at Guotai Junan International in Hong Kong. "By steadily increasing gold reserves, Beijing is strengthening the long-term backing of its financial system and reducing reliance on dollar-denominated reserve assets," he said. "While gold alone will not determine the RMB's global role, it enhances confidence in the currency and supports broader efforts to expand its use in trade, investment and official reserves." Gold accumulation by China and other countries' central banks will help reduce global reliance on U.S. Treasurys and U.S. dollar reserves, said Xia Yingying, head of the precious metals and new energy research group, at Hangzhou-based Nanhua Futures. That's according to a CNBC translation of the Chinese. "This will suppress the U.S. dollar's premium from being a core reserve currency, and raise the risk premium associated with the dollar regarding credit, fiscal policy and sanctions," Xia said. "In the medium to-long-term it will gradually weaken the U.S. dollar's monopolistic position in the global reserve system." China's growing gold purchases, however, also come as U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday named gold-standard supporter Judy Shelton as a senior advisor focused on China . The Asian economy's rise as a manufacturing powerhouse benefited from the U.S. decision to abandon the gold standard more than 50 years ago. "With the delinking of the dollar and gold, and the consequent rise in the oil price, western manufacturing became less economic, and capital went to Asia in search of cheap labor and overall lower costs," wrote the central bank research group OMFIF in 2021. While China is the largest consumer and producer of gold, it is just one of many developing economies that has expanded its reserves since 2022, according to S&P. The World Gold Council showed Poland has increased its gold reserves by more tonnes than China. The trend goes beyond financial transactions. Like with rare earths, Beijing's gold ambitions start with control of some of the product. China has acquired major gold mines across Latin America, Africa and Asia, according to S&P Global Ratings. "China's plans for gold and its activities in gold are comprehensive and long lasting.

events.title: New report shows US chip industry's reliance on China
events.summary: More than 5% of equipment and materials supplied to US chipmakers originate in China, which also possesses some 90% of the rare earths required to manufacture semiconductors, a new report showed. The figures highlight the structural reliance of US tech on China, and the difficulties of erecting a materials and software firewall against Beijing. “We’re so deeply intertwined,” Brookings’ AI specialist Kyle Chan told The Washington Post: “ There’s a lot of actual dependency .” Beyond materials, the US tech startup ecosystem also relies on cheaper, open-source Chinese AI, so much that when the Trump administration considered banning it, nearly 300 US firms spoke out — marking “the moment open intelligence itself becomes a geopolitical dependency,” an analyst wrote. — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Airtable's new owner is laying off a 'large part' of its team
events.summary: Layoffs have hit Airtable. Illustration by Idrees Abbas/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images A "large part" of Airtable's workforce is being laid off, the company's new owner said. Bending Spoons' product leader said smaller teams and AI features are central to its new strategy. Cut employees will leave by the end of the week with "substantial separation packages," he said. Big layoffs are coming to Airtable. Airtable's new owner, Italian tech conglomerate Bending Spoons, said Monday it is laying off a "large part" of the software company as it reshapes the business around smaller teams and AI features. In an X post , Federico Simionato, Bending Spoons' product leader, said the cuts were not a reflection of employees' work but of the company's "deep belief that small teams ship more and better." "To everyone leaving: thank you. If you're hiring, these are excellent people and worth a call," Simionato said. Bending Spoons announced in August that it was acquiring Airtable , the spreadsheet and database app, for $1.28 billion. It was not immediately clear how many people would be affected by the layoffs. A Bending Spoons spokesperson said they were "not able to share additional details on the number of individuals impacted." Airtable product lead Alessandro Savarese said in a blog post on the company's website that the employees being cut will leave by the end of the week with "substantial separation packages." "At Bending Spoons, we've seen firsthand how smaller, faster-moving teams with streamlined responsibilities can have an outsized impact, and we have the same ambitions at Airtable," Savarese wrote. "We intend to make Airtable a better product while providing our customers with an exceptional level of reliability and support." Savarese said the company will focus on improving Airtable's core platform and investing in AI features. Laid-off Airtable employees may already have some job prospects: X product engineer Mridul Singhai responded to the job-cuts announcement in a post , saying X will "continue to hire & grow people who want to commit." events.summary: President Donald Trump said he is "not happy" with Kimberly Guilfoyle, and is considering whether to fire her as U.S. ambassador to Greece. Trump's comments came after a series of critical articles in The Wall Street Journal about Guilfoyle's conduct before and after she became ambassador. The former Fox News personality was at one time engaged to Donald Trump Jr., the president's eldest son. President Donald Trump said Monday that he is "not happy" with Kimberly Guilfoyle , and is considering whether to fire her as U.S. ambassador to Greece . Trump's comments at the White House after a series of critical articles in The Wall Street Journal about Guilfolye's conduct before and after she became ambassador. Asked by a reporter if he was weighing firing Guilfolye, Trump replied, "Well, we're looking at it." "Yeah, we're not happy," the president said. Guilfoyle previously was engaged to Trump's eldest son, Donald Trump Jr. After the couple broke up, the president appointed the former Fox News personality as ambassador. Russian lab worker dies amid plague reports — here's what we know Trump's nemesis in Europe: Why Spain's Sanchez is calling a snap election Trump tells South Korea to sign on to Alaska LNG deal or 'I'll just charge them more' CNBC has requested comment from Guilfoyle's attorney about Trump's remark. The Journal on Sept. 25 published an article under the headline, "The Mystery Man Shadowing Kimberly Guilfoyle as She Pushes Deals Across Europe." The story detailed Guilfoyle's push to get U.S. allies in Eastern Europe to buy billions of dollars of American natural gas. The article said that Guilfoyle told people who were the targets of her effort that "they should deal with a Greek construction firm called Aktor Group, a newcomer to the gas business that had teamed up with a Greek state-backed energy company to bring in liquefied natural gas from the U.S." The article detailed how Guilfoyle had traveled frequently with a top lobbyist for Aktor named Christos Marafatsos, who has been "joining her for meetings at her ambassadorial residence and with government officials in countries around the region—a highly unusual move for a private citizen." On Oct. 7, the Journal published an article detailing how Guilfoyle allegedly asked a Trump donor named Eric Deters in July 2025 to pay $100,000 for what she said was an American Express bill before her upcoming Senate confirmation hearing for the ambassadorship. A lawyer for Guilfoyle told the newspaper that Deters owed her a balance for "traveling to and supporting" events where she was hired to speak. On Saturday, the Journal published another article that said during the January 2026 World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, she had "boasted ... about her close ties to two Greek tycoons and said they were bankrolling her high-rolling trips around the world." In a statement on Sunday, Guilfoyle's lawyers "denied she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from the Trump donor was payment for services — public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination — that had not been paid," The Associated Press reported. The lawyers "also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle's travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she 'sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department's travel regulations,' " The AP reported, citing the statement.

events.title: Feds search Rep. Ilhan Omar's home in immigration probe
events.summary: Federal agents conducted a pre-dawn search Monday at the Washington home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) as part of an ongoing immigration probe, a DOJ spokesperson confirmed to Axios. Why it matters: Searching Omar's home marks a substantial escalation of the Trump administration's fight with the outspoken progressive, who has condemned the immigration crackdown in her state. It's also an unusual move against a candidate less than a month before an election, something the Justice Department has typically avoided . The latest: President Trump said authorities are looking at Omar "very carefully" when asked whether he knew about the search of her home in advance. "I've always found her to be totally crooked personally, but that has nothing to do with me," Trump said. "I think she's a terrible person. She comes from a country that is a non-country." What they're saying: "I'm ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement," Omar said in a Monday afternoon post to X. "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced." Driving the news: Fox News first reported that Homeland Security Investigations agents conducted the search, citing a Justice Department statement. A DOJ spokesperson confirmed to Axios that DHS agents "executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice" as part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation. DHS referred Axios to the DOJ. The other side: Omar's office blasted the search. "This raid by Trump's DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies," Omar spokesperson Jacklyn Rogers said in a statement. "The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong." House Democratic leaders separately issued a joint statement calling the search "deeply disturbing" and part of a "rogue abuse of power" by the administration. Zoom out: Last month, border czar Tom Homan confirmed an ongoing criminal probe into Omar, though he declined to offer details. Fox reported Monday that the search was tied to a fraud investigation into Omar's immigration paperwork. The Somali native came to the U.S. in 1995 as a 12-year-old refugee. Between the lines: Trump has for years demanded that Omar leave the country or be deported , citing, among other things, unsubstantiated claims that she married her brother to help him circumvent immigration laws. Omar has dismissed the claims about the marriage in question as "baseless rumors." Trump has made Minnesota's Somali community one of the most frequent targets of his anti-immigration rhetoric, and Omar the face of those attacks. Just last week, he called on Minnesotans to " fight back " against the state's Somali population. Editor's note: This story has been updated with comments from President Trump, as well as statements from Omar, her House office and House Democratic leaders, and with more context. Andrew Solender and Torey Van Oot contributed reporting.

events.title: Uber struggles to solve Broome's late-night transport issues
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Late-night transport issues remain in Broome despite arrival of Uber Travellers say they opt for e-scooters after failing to book an Uber. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) Residents and tourists in Broome have long raised concerns about the lack of transport options late at night. The arrival of Uber was touted as a potential solution, but those in Broome say they have struggled to book a ride through the app. Police say the issues people have getting a ride home are no excuse for drink driving. Global rideshare giant Uber has struggled to fill the void of late-night transport in Western Australia's far north. Like many remote locations across Australia, transport options in Broome, 2,000km north of Perth, are progressively limited as the evening wears on. Buses cease at 7pm during the peak tourist season, and many taxi operators stop their service from a similar time. While some drivers continue throughout the night, residents say they face long wait times with expensive fares. Limited taxis operate during the night in Broome. ( ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler ) Uber was touted as a potential solution during its July launch, but those in town said the app has had little impact. Jenny Antonipillai recently travelled to Broome from Perth, and attempted to find a ride home from the pub. "We tried to get a taxi or an Uber, but there's not much available out here. It's very hard," she said. "We went on the Beam [e-scooter] and my boyfriend fell, so not a good idea." Jenny Antonipillai says she was not able to order an Uber home from the pub, despite the app launching in Broome two months ago. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) Travellers Noah Clancy and Orlando Dixon said they had also had no luck with Uber and opted for e-scooters to get around. "There was nothing available at all in the area," Mr Clancy said. "We got taxis quite easily earlier in the day, but later at night it's a bit more trouble." Noah Clancy and Orlando Dixon opted for the e-scooters to get around in Broome. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) Resident Lili Walker said she was used to long waits and expensive fares costing up to $60 for a 10-minute ride. The state government increased the flexibility of taxi authorisation in 2020, resulting in a number of drivers offering a private service throughout the evening. But their contacts are not always readily available. Matty Arai says many people struggle to organise a taxi through automated answering services. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) Pub security guard Matty Arai said it was common to see patrons huddled out the front looking for a way home after close. "There are a couple of good guys around town that will be out all the time, but then trying to pick them up is also hard," he said. Partygoers said expensive fares, long wait times and limited options created a dangerous incentive for drink driving. Sergeant Tony Di Giuseppe says educating the community on safe e-scooter use is a priority. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) But Kimberley District traffic Sergeant Tony Di Giuseppe said inconvenience did not justify breaking the law. "I understand there are difficulties … transport, distance, everything else like that, but it's not acceptable," he said. Sergeant Di Giuseppe said police had been working to educate community members they were subject to the same road rules on an e-scooter as they were driving a vehicle. Broome and Karratha were the first off the rank for Uber's regional WA expansion in July. Broome Private Taxis owner Paul Rewell said he was not surprised the rideshare service has reportedly struggled to take-off. "If people like our group are struggling to find drivers, Uber won't be any different," he said. Paul Rewell says he is not surprised the app has struggled to attract drivers. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) Mr Rewell has been operating taxis in the town for the past six years, and said his business had trialled working throughout the evening. Repeated incidents of vandalism during the night led to the decision to close after 6 or 7pm. He said he welcomed Uber's arrival should they have enough drivers. Transport Minister Rita Saffioti said she recognised the challenges of catching taxi services at night in remote towns. She said the government was committed to "providing accessible and affordable" public transport for regional communities, pointing to an expansion of Broome's bus timetable put in place for this year's tourist season. events.title: Susan Collins’s allies spent $25,000 attacking her rival in the Oregon version of Portland: ‘They can’t even find it on a map’
events.summary: Since 1997, Susan Collins has served as one of Maine’s senators, and she may be the epitome of Maine. She, like her opponent Troy Jackson, grew up in the state’s northern tip. Her family ran a lumber business for generations in Caribou, and she’s well regarded by Mainers as someone from “the County,” not a politician. During the Barack Obama era, her bloc of crucial swing voters included Arlen Specter from Pennsylvania and fellow Mainer Olympia Snowe, but she’s the last of those Republican moderates standing, giving Maine an outsize national footprint. So when a political attack ad ran in Portland last week, it would be safe to assume the Portland in question was in Maine. So why did Defending Main Street, a super PAC backing Collins, run an ad in the wrong Portland? Defending Main Street spent nearly $25,000 on digital placements for “So Many Taxes,” a 30-second ad against Jackson, to run the ad in hundreds of zip codes across Oregon and Washington State from Oct. 8 to Oct. 11, according to Google’s Ads Transparency Center . It came to light when an Oregon X user reported seeing five anti-Jackson ads in one day. “I choose to believe they mixed up Portlands,” the user wrote. The same ad aired on broadcast TV in the intended market, Portland, Maine, reaching about 675,000 impressions over the same four days, according to AdImpact data cited by MS NOW . Defending Main Street told Newsweek that its media vendor mistakenly placed the digital ads in the Oregon market, and Newsweek reported the targeting was fixed by Monday afternoon. Sarah Chamberlain, president and CEO of the affiliated Republican Main Street Partnership, told NBC News she was furious at the ad buyer, Cross Screen Media, which she said refunded the money. “I would never run an ad in Portland, Oregon, for Susan Collins,” she said. The mix-up didn’t stop Jackson’s campaign team from commenting on the snafu. “Susan Collins’s allies are so out of touch with Maine, they can’t even find it on a map,” campaign spokesperson Dan Gottlieb told Fortune . “Good luck convincing Mainers you know what’s best for them when you don’t know which Portland they live in.” Defending Main Street and the Collins campaign did not respond to Fortune’ s requests for comment. A $26.8 billion mix-up The super PAC got its money back, but the mistake mirrors a problem that costs corporate advertisers billions. The Association of National Advertisers estimates that $26.8 billion in global ad spending is lost each year to middlemen’s fees, fake traffic, unseen ads, and low-quality sites, up from $20 billion in 2023. That’s more than double the $11.6 billion AdImpact projects will be spent on political ads in the entire 2026 election cycle. Much of that waste comes from ads running in places advertisers never chose. In the ANA’s 2023 study, the average campaign ran on 44,000 websites , even though a few hundred sites would have reached most of the intended audience, and even as participants hadn’t approved about 38,000 of those sites . In the group’s latest benchmark, more than a third of automated ad spending still went to ads that failed basic quality standards. AdImpact has projected $384 million in ad spending on the Maine Senate race, nearly double the roughly $200 million spent when Collins last ran in 2020. And in this race alone, Republicans are outspending Democrats but getting less for each dollar. From July 26 to mid-September, Republicans spent $82.1 million on TV ads in the race to Democrats’ $55.5 million, according to AdImpact data . Super PACs pay full price for TV ads , while candidates’ campaigns get discounted rates. Location targeting, the tool that sent DMS’s ad to Oregon, can backfire. A 2019 analysis by data firm Location Sciences of 500 million location-targeted ads found that 29% were delivered outside the area the advertiser paid to reach. In 2017 the New York Times showed JPMorgan Chase one of its ads on a site called Hillary 4 Prison. The bank found its ads had appeared on about 400,000 websites in a single month, but only 3% of them produced any activity beyond someone seeing the ad. Chase cut its list to about 5,000 preapproved sites and saw little change in the cost or visibility of its ads, its chief marketing officer said. That same year, after activists flagged Uber’s ads on Breitbart, the company began cutting its online ad spending. Kevin Frisch, Uber’s former head of performance marketing, later said the company turned off $100 million of its $150 million annual online ad budget for riders and saw no change in app installs. He blamed ad networks that took credit for sign-ups that would have happened anyway. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Kroger to cut 3,000 corporate employees over the next 3 years. Read the memo.
events.summary: Kroger's corporate workforce is going to get leaner. Brandon Bell/Getty Images Kroger is making big cuts to its corporate workforce. CEO Greg Foran said about 3,000 roles will go away in the next three years. Foran said the corporate-level reductions will allow Kroger to invest in frontline workers. Kroger plans to cut about 3,000 roles from its corporate workforce  over the next three years  to simplify operations. In a memo to staff that the company shared with Business Insider, CEO Greg Foran said the corporate-level reductions will allow Kroger to invest in frontline workers. "Our business is becoming leaner, more focused and more competitive," he said. The former Walmart US CEO took the helm of Kroger earlier this year and has set to work cutting prices and tightening operations over the past several months. Foran also cited the impact of technology on the century-old company, saying that it merits a close look at where work can be done. Read the memo from CEO Greg Foran FROM: Desk of Greg Foran inbox TO: All company RE: Changes to Our Organization We shared important information on our all-company call today, and we're following up to make sure everyone is aware of the changes ahead. As a company, we have made great progress on many fronts with our customers. We started reducing prices and improving our customer experience in stores and online, and we made investments in simplifying our associates' lives through technology. Our business is becoming leaner, more focused and more competitive. We are working to be more agile; more precise in our execution; and deliver benefits to our customers, associates and our shareholders. This transformation will also result in fewer roles across the company, which means we will reduce our corporate workforce across many functions, by approximately 3,000 roles over the next three years. These reductions will allow us to continue to invest in our frontline associates. These are difficult decisions, and we do not make them lightly. This is the right thing for the company's long-term future. Here's why: Simplifying our operations is critical . Simplifying means making faster decisions and deploying more resources where they matter most, so that we deliver lower prices and a better experience for our customers. Our company has more layers, more handoffs and more overhead than we need, so we are addressing this issue. Technology is reshaping what's possible. The way work gets done is changing across every industry; we must adapt and take advantage of technology. We need to adopt capabilities, reduce duplicative work and look closely at where work is best fit to be done. We have the opportunity to make changes that will create broader roles and faster decision making. This lets us move vital resources closer to the customer to lower prices, invest in our associates and create a better shopping experience. When and how this will happen These reductions will take place across multiple years. We will share updates when we can. We expect decisions about impacted roles to start being communicated in the coming months. Our values at work During these difficult moments, we will continue to be guided by Our Values. We will communicate directly with impacted associates as we make decisions, and we will not ask anyone to wait longer than necessary for clarity about their roles. We are grateful for each one of you. With the Kroger Leadership Team, we are committed to leading this company through this moment with transparency, integrity and respect. events.title: Phillip Island business operators prepare for MotoGP's final lap
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Topic: Tourism and Leisure Industry Phillip Island has relied on the MotoGP to bring in tourists and revenue. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) Phillip Island will host its final MotoGP race at the end of October before the race moves to Adelaide in 2027. The GP and World Superbikes inject about $80 million into the island's economy each year. Businesses, councillors and the island's tourism board are calling for government support. Every October, Phillip Island emerges from a sleepy winter season and roars to life with the sound of motorcycles travelling in convoy to the MotoGP. The weekend of racing turbocharges the island's summer tourism season, culminating in the World Superbikes event in February. But Cowes and the broader island community are preparing to host their final MotoGP later this month at the picturesque cliff-side track, before the race moves to its new home in Adelaide from 2027. The loss has hit businesses and residents hard, with many reeling emotionally and financially. During the 1990s, Bass Coast Shire Council Mayor Brett Tessari worked at a caravan park on the island. "The vibe of the motorbikes coming in and the people, it was awesome," he said. Brett Tessari says the region's tourism future will need to rely on new ideas. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) "I remember being stuck on the [Phillip Island] bridge, trying to get over back to Wonthaggi and people were starting up barbecues and cooking sausages on the side of the road because we were at a standstill," Cr Tessari said. "Things like that are just etched in your memory. "To be the mayor, unfortunately, at the last one, it's pretty surreal and quite sad." For the past decade, Samantha Hampstead has run a tattoo business in Cowes with her husband Jason. They are both members of the social motorcycle club Trust No One, and are key organisers of the annual community motorcycle convoy that heralds the start of the motoring weekend. "We do it because of the love of the ride," she said. "It's a full-blown rush when you have all these riders together. "You look in the mirror and you can see this full parade of bikes behind you and it just goes on forever." Samantha Hampstead organises a community motorcycle run in Cowes. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) Ms Hampstead said for many business operators the weekend was their busiest time of the year. "It's part of the island," she said. San Remo Fisherman's Co-Op chief executive Wolfgang Platzer said the GP brought thousands of visitors to the island who may not otherwise have visited the region. Wolfgang Platzer says the community needs develop fresh ideas to attract tourists. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) "There would be a large portion of people that come here for the GP and see that the island and the area is very beautiful and then might think about, oh, we'll come back because we liked it and it was so beautiful," he said. Phillip Island is the state's most tourism-reliant region. According to Destination Phillip Island (DPI), more than $80 million in annual economic activity is linked to the World Superbikes and the MotoGP. The accommodation sector is the island's largest employer, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, accounting for almost 4 per cent of jobs. Cafes and restaurants are the third-largest employer. San Remo is the gateway to Phillip Island. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) DPI chief executive Kim Storey said while the event's loss had accelerated the need to broaden the island's outlook beyond motoring events, the role the track had played could not be understated. Economic uncertainty, a lack of infrastructure such as a car ferry and the potential toll of the H5N1 virus on the island's wildlife were all cited by DPI as upcoming barriers to success. "The MotoGP has provided that platform of security and the resource for businesses," Ms Storey said. DPI and Bass Coast Shire Council have called for government funding to help develop new events, such as The Hills are Alive music festival, the Island Whale Festival, the island hot springs, and a new festival of motorsports to capitalise on the island's motoring history. One Nation candidate for Bass Nikole Schellekens, Liberal candidate Rochelle Halstead and Labor candidate Chris Buckingham were asked what commitments they would make to the island's economy if elected at the November state election. All three candidates stressed the importance of tourism for Phillip Island and support for ongoing development of the island's resources.
