events.title: Nasdaq falls ahead of earnings, economic data while oil rallies
events.summary: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange at the opening bell on Oct 5 in New York City. The technology-heavy Nasdaq composite closed lower on Oct 12 as oil prices jumped nearly US$2 (S$2.6) a barrel after attacks on a Saudi airport , and investors waited for banks to kick off the third-quarter earnings season and for economic data this week. The S&P 500 ended the session barely lower while the Dow advanced. Oil futures rallied after deadly strikes on Riyadh’s international airport over the weekend. The attacks overshadowed the prospect of increased supplies after US President Donald Trump hailed fresh Russian diesel exports and talked about a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire on energy targets. In coming days, US investors will focus on corporate earnings, with major US banks including Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and JPMorgan Chase reporting early on Oct 13. Analysts were expecting S&P 500 earnings to surge 30.6% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES data. Also due out this week are September readings for US consumer and producer inflation as well as retail sales data. While the US Treasury market was closed on Oct 12 for Columbus Day, stock investors have been wary of bond yields’ recent advance to 24-year highs as elevated energy prices have stoked inflation concerns. “Looking out further in the week, we have some big economic reports,” said Tim Ghriskey, senior portfolio strategist at Ingalls & Snyder in New York. He said investors were also cautious due to a lack of direction from bonds. “We’re also waiting on earnings and that’s significant. The four large banks reporting on Tuesday can have a big impact,” he said. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 195.60 points, or 0.38%, to 51,850.55, the S&P 500 lost 4.30 points, or 0.06%, to 7,807.24 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 120.27 points, or 0.44%, to 27,245.90. Trading volume was relatively light with 12.67 billion shares changing hands on US exchanges compared with the 20-day moving average of 17.62 billion. “There’s a lot to be wary of,” said Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth in Fairfield, Connecticut, pointing to upcoming data and earnings along with rising oil prices. “You’re walking down a train line and you don’t know, because it’s dark, if a train is coming and so, you know, you’re just being real careful,” he said. With oil prices rising, energy outperformed among the S&P 500’s 11 major industry sectors with a 1.5% advance. The defensive consumer staples sector rose more than 1% along with the S&P 500 communication services index, which was boosted by a more than 3% gain in heavyweight Meta. Technology, down 0.9%, and consumer discretionary, off 0.7%, were the biggest sector laggards. Technology’s weakness was most pronounced among chip stocks with the Philadelphia semiconductor index finishing down 2.7% after hitting a three-week low. In consumer discretionary, Chipotle Mexican Grill shares fell 3.8% after Starbucks said it was not buying the burrito chain. Starbucks shares closed up 1.7%. Microsoft finished up 1.1% with its market capitalisation climbing above US$4 trillion for the first time in a year after it announced plans for major deployment of its own AI chips. Salesforce shares added 2% after BofA Global Research upgraded the stock to “buy” from “underperform.” And eBay rose 2% after Morgan Stanley added the stock to its top-pick list. Meanwhile, Cleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack said the US central bank should move “relatively quickly” to a more restrictive monetary policy stance to fight inflation, which she feels has become more broad-based and is starting to influence firms’ price-setting plans. Traders were pricing in an almost 22% chance the US Federal Reserve will hike interest rates this month, according to CME’s FedWatch tool, up from 17.7% on Oct 9. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.09-to-1 ratio on the NYSE where there were 149 new highs and 272 new lows. On the Nasdaq, 1,888 stocks rose and 3,008 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.59-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 10 new 52-week highs and five new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 51 new highs and 318 new lows. REUTERS

events.title: Elon Musk gives $276 million to Republican groups, becomes biggest known 2026 midterm donor
events.summary: Elon Musk has poured more than $276 million into Republican groups since July, making him the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterm election. Musk gave $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund and more than $76 million to America PAC, in newly disclosed spending, bringing his known federal political giving this cycle to roughly $366 million. His 2025-26 giving has already surpassed the roughly $290 million he spent during the 2024 election, despite saying last year he planned to spend “a lot less” on politics. Elon Musk spent more than $276 million in newly disclosed donations to Republican groups since July, making him the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterm election as the party fights to hold its majorities in Washington this November. The largest share – $158 million – went to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing Republican Senate candidates, according to figures provided by Musk's representatives to The New York Times and confirmed Monday to CNBC by Lindsey Curnutte, a spokesperson for Musk's America PAC. The Tesla and SpaceX CEO also gave more than $76 million to America PAC , the group he founded during the 2024 election, which has built a large voter-turnout operation in competitive Senate and House races . The new contributions bring Musk's known federal political giving for the 2025-26 cycle to roughly $366 million, already surpassing the approximately $290 million he spent during the 2024 presidential election . The scale of the latest giving is historic: Musk's $158 million contribution to Senate Leadership Fund is among the largest known political donations by an individual in U.S. history. The new figures were disclosed days ahead of a Thursday Federal Election Commission filing deadline , when political committees are due to report their third-quarter finances. The Senate Leadership Fund has spent heavily this cycle to defend the Republican majority, including in Texas, where GOP Attorney General Ken Paxton is running against Democrat James Talarico . Talarico leads Paxton 48.4% to 45.0% in FiftyPlusOne's polling average as of Oct. 12. Musk separately gave $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC , which supports Paxton. He also contributed $20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund , the leading super PAC supporting House Republicans, $10 million to the Republican Governors Association and $2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association, the Times reported and Curnutte confirmed. The trillionaire's footprint in Texas has expanded rapidly in recent years, with Tesla, X and The Boring Company now headquartered in the state and SpaceX growing its manufacturing and launch operations there. The political spending is also a sharp reversal from Musk's public comments last year. "In terms of political spending, I'm going to do a lot less in the future," Musk said in May 2025. At the time, Musk was stepping back after a highly visible role in President Donald Trump's administration and a public falling-out with the president. The two have since repaired their relationship, appearing together at several recent events. Musk also retains deep ties to the federal government through SpaceX, a major NASA and Pentagon contractor . Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last month also named him co-director of Project Meridian , a Pentagon panel studying the future of warfare. — Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

events.title: Anthropic is making a $100 million bet on deployed AI engineers, and it seeks 5 key attributes
events.summary: Anthropic's developer conference in May. Don Feria/AP Content Services for Anthropic Anthropic is putting $100 million into a new training program for other companies' workers. The push is an effort to create more "deployed engineers," who can ramp up AI usage at companies. Executives explained the program and described the ideal forward-deployed engineer. Forward-deployed engineers are all the rage in AI, and Anthropic is going to other companies to train up top talent. The AI company announced a $100 million investment into an FDE training initiative earlier this month. It's a quasi-fellowship that engineers from other firms have already begun applying for. They'll attend four-day on-site intensives and then complete 12-week "residencies" working with Anthropic's Claude tools at their own companies. The company says it hopes to train 10,000 people through the program by the end of 2027. As Anthropic approaches its gigantic initial public offering , it's using the new training model to get more of the corporate world used to AI — and ramp up Claude spending. Job postings for FDEs have boomed over the last couple of years, as more companies buy software from AI firms and need help deploying it. Two Anthropic executives leading the push told Business Insider that their customers see AI's advances, notice competitors grabbing market share, and feel pressure to change their own work. "Everybody understands the model capability is expanding extremely fast," said Shambhavi Shambhavi, Anthropic's head of go-to-market strategy and operations for partnerships. "So, what can be done with the technology is greatly appreciated by the customers." Enter the FDE — which Anthropic calls "Frontier Deployed Engineers," rather than the standard " forward-deployed engineer " title that Palantir helped popularize . Both roles essentially mean someone with deep technical expertise in AI and the mandate to create new modes of work at a company. Shambhavi and Steve Corfield, Anthropic's head of global business development and partnerships, broke down the FDE role as they see it and how Anthropic hopes to set a "gold standard" with its new skills push. Anthropic execs say FDEs are curious Shambhavi said that the best FDEs have four main attributes. They are familiar with agentic AI systems. They're good problem-solvers. They're excellent communicators. And they're experienced, skilled engineers. Corfield tacked on a point he thinks helps Anthropic thrive: "You've got to be super, super curious. If you walk around this organization, everybody talks about curiosity." Communication is particularly important, Shambhavi said. She said that as companies try to overhaul entire workflows and approach agentic AI holistically, someone who can navigate the interpersonal dynamics goes a long way. "Our own Frontier Deployed Engineers work with these kinds of problems day in and day out," Shambhavi said. "And so we kind of applied the mindset of, we need to take this skill and bring it to our customers and partners and to the top engineers in those organizations, so that they can derive the benefits from Claude." Anthropic wants to set the 'gold standard' for AI skills Engineers who can expand their teams' use of AI have become a hot commodity in Silicon Valley. Salesforce, a major Anthropic partner , announced a plan in May to recruit 1,000 early-career workers into "AI builder" roles. Anthropic's program, in Corfield's view, goes a step above other industry attempts to recruit and train FDEs. Combined with other company initiatives to teach people AI, he hopes Anthropic will set "the gold standard for AI skilling." The first cohorts have begun in New York and San Francisco, including engineers from Accenture, Bain, Novo Nordisk, and other organizations. Companies nominate engineers for the training, and Anthropic interviews candidates. If they're accepted, they work for the four-day residency on a "simulated environment," an agentic system that they have to learn how to build and deploy. Then they take a practical test, before returning to their companies while staying in touch with Anthropic mentors for 12 more weeks. Anthropic is still building its assessments throughout the program. Shambhavi said they'll focus on "what does a great FDE look like" — articulation, problem solving, coding skills. Corfield said corporate customers wanted a program like this to help them figure out how to deploy Claude more effectively, and the holdup isn't motivation. "This is a skills gap problem, and that creates a market problem," he said. "What we're trying to do is fill that gap," he added. Have a tip? To help jump-start those plans, Lonely Planet in September released its annual "Best in Travel" guide for 2027, highlighting 25 destinations chosen by its global network of writers and contributors. The guide's destination picks span Argentina's mountains , Canada's red-rock beaches, a Caribbean island, and California's ancient redwood forests, among other places. Here are the 25 best travel destinations featured in Lonely Planet's annual list. The Tweed, Australia The Tweed is "best for Hinterland detours." James D. Morgan/Getty Images The Tweed region is in far northeastern New South Wales, between the Gold Coast and Byron Bay. Visitors can enjoy activities such as hiking and biking. The Veneto, Italy Morning mist on the Venetian Prealps, Veneto region, Italy. DeAgostini/Getty Images Veneto, the northeastern Italian region, is far more than just Venice . It stretches from the Prosecco Hill vineyards to the Dolomites and Lake Garda, offering visitors a bit of everything: historic cities, mountains, lakeside towns, and a top-class food and wine scene. New Mexico, US Carlsbad Caverns National Park - New Mexico. (Photo by: Edwin Remsberg/VW Pics/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) : Edwin Remsberg/VW Pics/Universal Images Group via Getty Images New Mexico offers a range of activities and sights : desert landscapes, mountain towns, ancient sites, and a mix of Native American, Hispanic, and Anglo cultures. Prince Edward Island, Canada Beach along the North Shore of Prince Edward Island, Canada. However, it packs in red sandstone cliffs, fishing villages, and a food scene centered on the sea. Fans of "Anne of Green Gables" can also visit the places that inspired author Lucy Maud Montgomery’s novel. events.title: 22 romance books to read while you wait for Emily Henry's next novel
events.summary: Emily Henry in September 2026. Cindy Ord/WireImage/Getty Images Emily Henry announced her next novel, "Modern Classic," will be published on April 6, 2027. Henry's novels are romantic and sexy, often leaving readers wanting more.  You can read similar romance novels to help pass the time while you wait for Henry's next book. Emily Henry fans are in luck. On September 22, Henry revealed her next romance novel will be released on April 6, 2027. She unveiled the title, "Modern Classic," by posting it on movie theater marquees across the US and UK. "Modern Classic" will be Henry's seventh romance novel to date. She smashed onto the romance scene in 2020 with " Beach Read " and has written five more books since then, each of which has made The New York Times' bestseller list.  Henry's summer romance books often approach love with a sense of honesty and fun that the genre needs to thrive. Her characters may be enemies who find themselves living next door to each other or best friends who are scared to risk it all for something more, as was the case in " People We Meet on Vacation ," which was turned into a Netflix film released in January 2026. Henry has yet to release a cover or description for "Modern Classic," but the marquee announcement and title have fans wondering whether the book will have anything to do with movies. It will be a while, though, before readers know for sure. Luckily, there are plenty of other romance books to pass the time with, including Henry's earlier works if you haven't read — or reread — them yet. "Beach Read" by Emily Henry Penguin Random House In Henry's 2020 novel "Beach Read," which is being adapted into a film , author January Andrews is in a writing rut. She can't seem to think of her next big idea for a romance novel, so she decides to retreat to the beach house she inherited from her father, hoping inspiration will strike. To her dismay, January discovers Augustus Everett, an acclaimed literary author who happens to be her college archnemesis, is living next door.  January plans to steer clear of Augustus for the duration of summer — until she finds out he's having writer's block, too. They decide the solution to their problem is for each of them to try their hand at each other's writing style. Augustus will have to show January the ropes of capital-L literature, and she'll have to make him fall in love with writing about love.  However, falling for Augustus was never part of the plan. As you dive into "Beach Read," it's easy to see how it turned Emily Henry into a household name. "People We Meet On Vacation" by Emily Henry "People We Meet on Vacation" by Emily Henry. Berkley No one expected Alex and Poppy to become best friends less than Alex and Poppy. After a fateful road trip in college, free-spirited Poppy and buttoned-up Alex become inseparable. To keep their friendship alive after graduation, the pair agreed to take a trip together every summer, exploring a new place side by side. The trip is Poppy's favorite week of the year, but when "People We Meet on Vacation" begins, they haven't been on a trip — or spoken — in two years, distance growing between them after one night changes everything. As Poppy feels more bogged down than ever by her life in New York, she knows reuniting with Alex would make everything better. So Poppy proposes one more trip, hoping a week together can get their friendship — and her life — back on track. Will Poppy or Alex be willing to face the feelings that sent them running from each other in the first place? "Book Lovers" by Emily Henry "Book Lovers" by Emily Henry. Penguin Random House "Book Lovers" is Henry's third summer romance book , and it's both an epic love story and an ode to books themselves.  Nora Stephens doesn't think anything is missing in her life. She loves her job as a literary agent, her apartment in New York, and living near her sister, Libby, and her nieces. When Libby asks Nora to escape to Sunshine Falls, North Carolina, for a month, Nora can't say no, especially since Libby is several months pregnant at the time. Libby has big dreams of small-town romance for Nora during their getaway, but instead of finding a local man to have a fling with, Nora keeps running into Charlie Lastra, a grumpy New York editor she's never gotten along with.  Despite their less-than-romantic history, Charlie and Nora keep crossing paths in Sunshine Falls, making the ever-growing list of things they have in common harder to ignore. And when Nora discovers her life as she knows it is about to change, Charlie might be the exact thing she needs. "Happy Place" by Emily Henry "Happy Place" by Emily Henry. Penguin Random House Henry is at her best in "Happy Place," a novel that ruminates on what it means to fight for love. Harriet has spent her entire adult life loving Wyn. Their relationship consumes her, and the fact that she met him through her best friends, Sabrina and Cleo, only makes her love him more. Between Wyn and her friends, Harriet found the family she had always wanted in college, and she plans to spend her entire life with them. When Wyn abruptly breaks up with her after she starts her medical school residency, Harriet is heartbroken and terrified she's going to lose everyone she loves. She manages to avoid telling Sabrina and Cleo what happened for five months, planning to burst their bubble on their annual group trip to Maine . Then Wyn shows up, telling her they'll have to pretend to be a couple for the duration of the trip, since it's the last vacation the group will ever spend in the house they've loved for years. Harriet doesn't want to cause her friends pain, so she's willing to torture herself for a week. All she has to do is stop herself from asking Wyn what went wrong for seven days, but as his displays of fake affection start to feel more and more real, Harriet might have to face her fear of rocking the boat if she wants a true chance at happiness. She was going to marry her doting fiancé, Peter, quietly thrive at her dream children's librarian job, and settle down in his hometown of Waning Bay, Michigan. Then, Peter leaves her for his childhood best friend , Petra, leaving Daphne at a crossroads. events.title: A PR pro says Kelly Clarkson made one big mistake in her feud with a Brooklyn toy shop
events.summary: Kelly Clarkson hosts "The Kelly Clarkson Show." Weiss Eubanks/NBCUniversal via Getty Images Kelly Clarkson publicly scolded a small business in Brooklyn after visiting the store. The store, Art of Play, responded with two public statements attempting to reframe the interaction. PR pro Evan Nierman says both parties attempted to position themselves as victims to gain sympathy. When a feud is brought into the court of public opinion, the winner isn't necessarily the one who's technically "right." It's the one who crafts the better narrative. That's the main thing that Kelly Clarkson is missing in her viral clash with a small business in Brooklyn , according to Evan Nierman, CEO of the global PR firm Red Banyan. "This is more about feelings than facts," Nierman said. The much-publicized kerfuffle started on Saturday, when Clarkson shared a post on X about her recent visit to Art of Play, a store that sells toys, puzzles, gifts, and other oddities. Clarkson said she was treated poorly at the store, comparing herself to Julia Roberts' " Pretty Woman " heroine — specifically, the memorable scene in which she is rejected and mocked in a fancy Beverly Hills boutique. Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad and had a few things in mind to buy and literally was looked at as if I couldn’t afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me. Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a huge sale. But y’all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts character in Pretty Woman. For sure, check it out 👎 — Kelly Clarkson (@kellyclarkson) October 10, 2026 Clarkson said she tried to buy something expensive at Art of Play but was treated as if she "couldn't afford it." However, the shop employee Clarkson dealt with remembers the interaction differently. Art of Play responded with a public statement , saying that Clarkson inquired about a one-of-a-kind mechanical bird puppet nicknamed "Molly," and she was told it wasn't for sale. When Clarkson doubled down , insisting that Molly came with a $15,000 price tag and calling the employee a "liar," Art of Play clarified its claim. In a follow-up statement on Instagram , the store said that Clarkson had been offered a nearly identical version of the bird, created by the same artist, for $15,000, as well as a comparable version by a different maker for $2,000. Who's right, and what really happened? We may never know, and it probably won't matter in the long run. But from a PR perspective, Nierman said this back-and-forth over trivial details is neither convincing nor productive. "Both Kelly Clarkson and the store are trying to play the victim card in this dispute," Nierman explained. "But the only people who really know what happened that fateful morning were the sales associate, Kelly Clarkson, and Molly, the bird, who will never sing." The 'victim card' can only get you so far Nierman pointed out that Clarkson doesn't have much to lose by airing her petty grievances on social media. She's a rich, famous singer with three Grammy Awards and nearly 9 million followers on X. "You'd be hard pressed to make the case that her life is going to be derailed in any significant way, even if she was mistreated by the store and its staff," Nierman said. But Clarkson doesn't have much to gain here, either. By playing the "victim card," she has ignored the etiquette of online power dynamics, siccing her loyal fans on a small business over a brief interaction. Even if everything she said was true and Clarkson really was mistreated by the store's staff, the fallout isn't flattering. "They both want to be right, whereas what they should be looking for is an off-ramp where they could both look good as opposed to being the victim in this circumstance," Nierman said. One idea? The fight started over a bird, so perhaps it should end with one. "The best possible outcome at this point would be to get her back to the store and find a way to get her a singing bird," Nierman continued. "That would tie this whole thing off very nicely, and everyone could move forward and deal with more important issues." You know what they say: It's not over 'til Molly the animatronic bird sings. events.title: Earnings beats are now the norm. What the stock market needs to keep rallying
events.summary: Analysts expect nearly 30% year-over-year earnings growth for the S&P 500, up from 26.7% on June 30th. Profits look robust below the Mag-7 surface, including 19% growth this year for S&P 400 MidCap operating earnings. Healthy beats are the new "status quo" while other forces could "gum up" a smooth earnings story. Will 30% profit growth and upbeat tech guidance be enough to keep the rally going? We'll soon find out. Third-quarter earnings season kicks into gear Tuesday with JPMorgan Chase and other big banks. Expectations are steep: consensus forecasts call for nearly 30% year-over-year growth, according to FactSet. That's up from around 27% three months ago. But 30% or more should be doable — S&P 500 profits have topped quarterly estimates by healthy margins since mid-2023. Tech will have to do its part at beating estimates and lifting guidance. For now, the sector shows no signs of slowing. Analysts expect 65% gains for tech profits, up from an estimated 57% growth three months ago. Upward revisions for Nvidia , Micron Technology and Dell Technologies are doing the heavy lifting, according to FactSet. Also positive, profit growth is broadening beyond the Mag 7. The other 493 stocks in the S&P 500 are forecast to deliver 27% year-over-year gains, topping the Mag-7 average, according to Russell Investments . S&P 400 MidCap operating earnings should rise 19% in 2026, notes Ed Yardeni, head of Yardeni Research. The first earnings test comes with the big banks. JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs , Citigroup , and Wells Fargo , reporting Tuesday, should reveal how steeper interest rates are impacting loan growth, balance sheets, M&A activity and the IPO pipeline. JPMorgan — the largest U.S. bank — will be critical, along with comments from CEO Jamie Dimon who tends to move markets with his outlook. Financials are on a knife's edge; the sector is hovering around its 200-day moving average, a key technical indicator, after falling 5% since August 31. Analysts see rising interest rates starting to sting loan growth and fixed-income securities held on balance sheets. The weakness could make for a relief rally, but earnings and guidance could go either way, pushing the stocks up or down, notes Julian Emanuel, senior managing director at Evercore ISI. "There will be volatility as investors hang on every word from the Big Banks this week," he said in a note. Emanuel remains bullish on the market, however, and tech in particular. Several other strategists concur. Goldman Sachs shifted to an "overweight" stance on equities Monday, saying "growth remains supportive." The bank's strategists see a favorable macro climate with low recession risk. And they expect inflation to ease in 2027 — all of which points to "more of a 'Goldilocks' backdrop," according to a note by Christian Mueller-Glissmann, head of asset allocation at Goldman Sachs Research. For positioning, he recommends a "barbell of AI beneficiaries and selective rate-sensitive, high-dividend and low-volatility stocks that could benefit from eventual rate relief." The setup also looks favorable because multiples have fallen, notes Lisa Shalett, chief investment officer for Morgan Stanley Wealth Management. Stocks are trading at 19 times forward earnings, down from 21 times over the summer, despite the fact that earnings growth has picked up. While rising bond yields have compressed multiples, "that's typical of a midcycle expansion when rate hikes have yet to truly bite," she points out. Shalett also takes solace in the market's growth drivers. "While many sectors will likely eventually be impacted by higher-for-longer rates, the key growth vectors for this boom — AI capex and wealth-linked consumption — have thus far proved rate-insensitive," she said in a note Monday. UBS sees gains for equities too. "Investors should remain positioned for market upside, and we forecast the S&P 500 to reach 8,400 by June next year," said Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, CIO Americas and Global Head of Equities for UBS Chief Investment Office in a recent note. More critical than bank earnings may be tech — a sector accounting for 40% of the S&P 500 and about a third of its estimated $800 billion in profits this quarter. Analysts will be looking for signals that AI chip and infrastructure demand are powering through a tough macro climate and higher energy prices, and the stocks will move on 2027 guidance. The first clues may come when Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company reports Thursday. Third-quarter profit estimates for TSM are up to $4.45 a share, from $3.42 in January, according to FactSet consensus forecasts. TSM has beaten forecasts in 19 of the last 20 quarters, including a 10.8% beat in the second quarter. Its outlook on chip demand will be a key indicator for Nvidia and other chipmakers. The Nasdaq 100 is sitting near record highs, however, thanks to a swath of AI companies issuing upbeat reports and new products — easing some of the consternation about the cycle topping out.

events.title: I broke into tech sales after working in construction. Here's how I landed a more flexible job with higher earning potential.
events.summary: Bryan Ruiz. Courtesy of Bryan Ruiz Bryan Ruiz transitioned from construction to tech sales for a higher earning potential. Ruiz used online courses such as CourseCareers to gain the skills needed for a career in tech sales. His perseverance led to a flexible and profitable career path at a SaaS company. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Bryan Ruiz, a 27-year-old tech sales representative based in Sioux Falls, South Dakota. It has been edited for length and clarity. I grew up in Puerto Rico, and about seven years ago, I moved to the US to look for construction work . After working in construction for a couple of years, I found it to be really back-breaking work. It didn't matter how hard I worked or how many skills I developed; there was always a cap on what I could earn because I was paid by the hour. I tried to get noticed and eventually get a raise, but it didn't work. I started thinking about pursuing a career where I'm really rewarded for the amount of work I put in. Within a year, I went from earning $18 an hour doing physical labor to a new career that put me on track to earn six figures. I decided to look into sales I was drawn to sales because it offered more upside than hourly work, and I liked the idea that strong performance could directly affect my earnings. I didn't know anything about sales. I watched a ton of YouTube videos trying to understand the space and what sales was about. I listened to podcasts on the job site, watched videos after work, and read books whenever I could. One podcast that helped me later on was " 30 Minutes to President's Club ." I also took a course through CourseCareers . The track I did was specifically for tech sales. I don't think you necessarily need a course to break into sales, but it helped me because it gave me a structured path to follow. It cost around $500, and I split it into a few payments. I finished the course in about a week because I desperately wanted to start my new career. I started applying to almost anything and everything I could find Landing interviews was a struggle at first, but eventually I got three interviews — and you only need one yes. I tried to schedule them during my breaks or see if I could get time off work to do them. My first interview completely destroyed my confidence. The hiring manager challenged me about not having any sales experience, and I reacted poorly. I started doubting whether this was for me. At the end of it, the hiring manager told me I should go sell cellphones, and then maybe we could talk. In my third interview, the manager really liked that I had reached out to him — that's exactly what you need to do on the job. He said he would give me a trial. I quit my construction job and, in January 2024, I started my first sales job. The money was a step back at first, but I wanted to focus entirely on proving I belonged. During my time there, I moved into an account executive role, and after about two years at that company, I moved to my current role at a SaaS company. Construction has a lot more in common with sales than I expected You deal with a lot of different people in construction: electricians, plumbers, and people from different walks of life. You learn social awareness skills that you might not realize you have. I was also already used to working long, hard hours. In every interview, when I mentioned my background in construction, the sales managers would say they knew I was used to working hard and that was not their concern. The hardest part about sales is accepting that most people won't be happy to hear from you You're interrupting someone's day. Even if what you're selling could genuinely help them, most people don't want to talk to you. It's something you have to accept and understand that you'll encounter this every day for the rest of your career. You just have to learn not to take it personally. I try to remind myself — and my team now — that this is work, not life. You spend eight or 10 hours doing your job, but that's not your whole identity. You leave work at work. Financially, I took a step back to take a big step forward In construction, I was earning around $50,000 a year. In my first year in sales, I made around $30,000. This year, I'm on track to pass six figures. In the tech sales roles I see, many base salaries are in the $60,000- $70,000 range, plus commission. It depends on the sales field you're in. Selling condos will have a very different structure from selling tech, but you should be earning a base salary of around $50,000 once you gain some experience. The best part of my new career is that I get to set my own schedule I work from home , so I can literally brush my teeth and sit down at the computer. I don't have to wake up early and drive to a job site anymore. Most days, I work a normal 9-to-5 schedule, but I also have flexibility. During the winter, I'll sometimes work from 7 a.m. to 3 p.m. to take advantage of the daylight and handle school pickup. My advice to anyone who wants to get into sales is to make the leap It doesn't really matter what job you're doing — some of the sales VPs at my company used to work in customer service. If you want to get into a career where you can earn more money by working harder, start watching some YouTube videos to learn the basics of sales. Prove that you can do the job, because sales managers are looking. It's not like other industries, where they only look at your résumé. If you can get in front of the people hiring and show that you can do the job, they'll be more willing to give you a shot. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Oil company wins tenders in Channel Country with supply to stay in Australia
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bridgeport Energy already has oil wells in the Cooper-Eromanga basin. ( Supplied: Bridgeport Energy ) An Australian oil company has won tenders to explore for more oil and gas in the Channel Country. Bridgeport Energy has been allocated 270,000 hectares of land with new supply to stay within the domestic market. Traditional owners and graziers want assurances that "significant" flood plains will not be damaged. The head of an Australian oil company says any fossil fuels taken from new land in Queensland's Channel Country will stay in Australia, but it could take years before oil or gas flows. Bridgeport Energy has been declared the preferred tenderer across an extra 270,000 hectares of land between Innamincka and Thargomindah along the South Australian-Queensland border. Bridgeport already has about 90,000 hectares of "oil-producing acreage" in the Cooper-Eromanga basin and processes oil at Queensland's only inland oil refinery in Eromanga. The land allocated for exploration is on the Queensland-South Australia border. ( Supplied: Google Maps ) The state government has been ramping up land allocations to mining companies since 2025. Bridgeport Energy chief executive Christian Lange said he wanted to work "very, very closely" with landholders including graziers and traditional owners before any exploration began. "We need to be cognisant that our disturbance on that land is zero effectively by the time we pack up and leave," he said. Agriculture-conservation alliance wants assurances Western Rivers Alliance is a cooperative between graziers, traditional owners and conservationists advocating to stop new oil and gas activities on Channel Country flood plains. The latest sites are not within the protected Channel Country flood plains where fracking was banned two years ago , but parts are within 5 to 10 kilometres of the boundary. Coordinator Riley Rocco said the alliance was "neutral" on mining outside the flood plains. "But the activity could come quite close to the flood plain and obviously we are keen to make sure that any oil and gas or any industrial activity stays managed well outside of the flood plain in order to not have an adverse impact on those significant river and flood plain areas." In May 2013, a major oil spill in the Channel Country at a Santos-owned well involved the loss of 250,000 litres of crude oil, which flowed for 2 kilometres before the leak was stopped. The Queensland Department of Environment did not prosecute Santos at the time but admitted damage could have been severe if the leak had occurred during floodtime. Mr Lange said impacts on groundwater, fauna, flora, roads and other "land disturbances" would be considered before new exploration begins. He said the small-scale company would use seismic waves to determine whether there were enough "commercial flows" of oil or gas underground. "I would anticipate that it's probably the best part of two years to obtain your authority to prospect, and then preparing to do seismic surveys, whether it's 2D, 3D or a combination of all those things," he said. Gas exploration was banned in some parts of the Channel Country in 2024. ( Supplied: Pew Charitable Trusts ) The latest round of tenders also included 62,500 hectares for the ASX-listed Vintage Energy in the Channel Country, while a four-business consortium won 30,600 hectares of land in the Taroom Trough. In a statement, Queensland Resources Minister Dale Last said increasing the supply of fuels was the "only solution to bring down the cost of energy". The state government has awarded 12 sites for oil or gas exploration since 2025.

events.title: I'm a working parent who's built over 150 AI agents to help run my life. I get digital overload, but I'm getting more time back.
events.summary: Tristen O'Brien has built over 150 AI agents, including an AI family assistant. Sarah Lutomski/Sarah Lu Photography Tristen O'Brien is a working dad who built over 150 AI agents to manage his life and get back time. O'Brien's family has mixed opinions on AI, but they all use the AI family bot he built. He built an AI video game to help manage his agents and reduce digital overload. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Tristen O'Brien, a 44-year-old AI educator and content creator who works in cybersecurity based in Indiana. His words have been edited for length and clarity. For a long time, I've felt like I can only focus on three things at a time without everything falling apart: family, work, and school. If I tried to add something else, one of those three things would fail. I've been in the tech industry for over 20 years, and I'm working toward my doctorate in AI . I'm also a YouTuber. I spent years learning the programming language Python because I wanted to create a world where I could automate parts of my life, giving me more time for hobbies and other things. Then ChatGPT came out , and I realized I had wasted about five years doing that. Since learning how to build AI agents , I've built over 150 of them to help me run my life. I'm now down to using around 70. I've always wanted to automate parts of my life There's a book about automating the boring parts of your life with the programming language Python. Years ago, I found this book and decided to learn it. Then, when ChatGPT came out, I quickly got into it. I'm not a developer; I do this by vibe coding. I first used ChatGPT to make funny songs and things like that. My interest kept growing, and I kept doing more with it. I've switched to Claude as my main model now, but I still use ChatGPT , Perplexity, and Gemini. Two years ago, I went to an AI conference where I learned about AI agents. I remember being so excited about what I had learned that I told myself that as soon as I got home, I was finally going to automate my life with AI. I use a specific prompting technique to build my agents The very first agent that I built after the conference was a Chipotle burrito agent that could order my burrito for me. I love Chipotle , and it was silly, but that agent helped me see the power of AI. When I build agents, I'm never just like, " OK, Claude , this is what I want you to do, do the whole thing." Claude has a command called "/goal" that keeps the agent going until it gets the goal right. I think it's helpful, but I've learned to be very clear, or it will mess up. I do what I call my BIP process: Braindump, interview, prompt. I brain-dump everything, explaining what I want it to do, then I have Claude ask me questions about anything unclear or that it thinks I didn't ask. Then it gives me this crazy long prompt. So I might've started with a 15-word prompt , but now I have a 500-word prompt on everything that I want the agent to do. I've built over 100 agents and stopped using some of them In total, I've built five research and education agents, four research and news agents, one agent that builds new products, 18 financial agents, 27 home and family agents , 26 inbox and communication agents, 42 agents for my YouTube channel, and another 27 agents for publicity and outreach. Not all of those agents run at once. For example, I only have 12 active home and family agents: Four run every day for reminders about birthdays, softball, the dog, and school paperwork. Four run weekly for groceries, meal planning, a Sunday family brief, and a weekly check-in coach. One runs monthly for house maintenance reminders, and three run only when something comes up, like travel, packing, or gift ideas. I also had an agent who looked at a Google Sheet with all of my friends' and family's birthdays. If it were two weeks before their birthday, the agent would go to a webpage for a service that would send them a birthday card with what looks like my handwriting, then postmark it from my address. But I stopped using that one because it didn't feel personal enough. AI is more powerful once you learn how to use plug-ins I have a wife and two kids. I think my daughter likes AI a lot, too, because we talk about it a lot, and my wife sometimes gets into it. But my son is an artist , so he's not as big a fan, and I agree that there's definitely a line with creative work and industries. However, one of my favorite agents I've built is our family AI bot, which we all use. I used the texting service Twilio with a Claude plug-in to create an AI agent that is a custom chatbot and assistant for our family. It pings us, and we're able to vote on things like what we want for dinner that week, or see our calendars side by side. This agent helps us organize our lives and stay on the same page. AI gets really powerful when you start using connectors. My Claude agents wouldn't be as powerful if it couldn't connect to my Gmail, my calendar, or Twilio. So, from a technical standpoint, I'd suggest learning how to sign in on those kinds of plug-ins first. I spend around $600 a month on my AI subscriptions, which also support my YouTube channel and other work. If I were just using this for my personal life, I'd probably scale back to the $200 Claude Max subscription. I created an agent hierarchy game I get digital overload sometimes, and there is a point where too much is digital. It was hard to keep up with all my agents, so, in addition to getting rid of some of them, I had to create a digital hierarchy. I'm the chief human officer. I have my AI chief of staff , who works with a handful of director-level AI agents, and those directors each have AI worker agents under them. My chief of staff will relay updates from other agents, so now I'm mainly communicating with one agent who's relaying updates to the rest, which helps with the overload. I also created an animated game world where I can see all my agents running around a village. The different levels of agents have different outfits, so I can tell which one's which. I can run around the game world with my chief of staff and go talk to one of my agents any time to check in on what it's doing. Tristen O'Brien's video game village for his AI agents Courtesy of Tristen O'Brien I can also press a button to call a meeting, and we all go to this meeting hall in the game. It's more of a visual way to see all of my agents, and talk to them individually if I want to. The AI agent meeting room inside O'Brien's AI agent village video game. events.title: Fortune’s AIQ Summit: The conversation has moved from experimentation to execution
events.summary: As companies race to adopt generative AI, agents, and new data tools, leaders face a more demanding question than whether to use the technology: How can they turn it into measurable value without creating new costs, risks, and organizational confusion? At the Fortune AIQ Summit at the New York Stock Exchange, executives from the technology, finance, industrial operations, travel, and human resources sectors explored what separates meaningful AI transformation from scattered pilots. The discussion made clear that the strongest companies are not simply distributing AI tools. They are redesigning workflows, developing talent, strengthening governance, and building the data and operating discipline needed to scale responsibly. Together, we explored these key trends: Moving from experimentation to enterprise transformation Building an AI-ready workforce Managing governance, trust, and risk Applying AI in physical and regulated environments Measuring ROI, controlling costs, and creating growth From AI adoption to AI transformation THE MOST IMPORTANT AI QUESTION IS NOT WHETHER A COMPANY HAS DEPLOYED TOOLS, BUT WHETHER IT HAS CHANGED HOW WORK GETS DONE. Speakers warned that widespread access to AI does not necessarily create productivity, business value, or organizational maturity. Diana David, director of futures at ServiceNow , said leading companies distinguish themselves through their commitment to people and operational discipline, not technology alone. In ServiceNow’s Enterprise AI Maturity Index, 57% of “pacesetters” invest in ongoing AI upskilling, compared with 4% of other organizations. The widest gap involves attracting, hiring, and retaining AI talent: 68% of pacesetters do so, compared with 10% of other companies. “Talent investment. That was the biggest gap,” David said. David cautioned against treating broad employee access to AI as proof of success: “95% of everybody has X, Y, Z,” she said. “But it is not translating into productivity, and it’s often not with training, and that doesn’t equal maturity.” The work, she argued, begins with leadership, a clear vision, transparent systems, the right data foundation, and iterative redesign of specific workflows. Paul Fipps, president of global customer operations at ServiceNow, made a related point: The greatest gains will not come from automating old processes faster, but from rebuilding them around new capabilities. “If I just automate or drive autonomous agents to drive the current processes I have, that’s a choice that might get some productivity bump,” Fipps said. “But the ones that are actually rethinking and reimagining the business processes … are really making the difference.” Fipps said companies should deploy AI horizontally, across employee-facing functions such as HR, legal, and technology, rather than isolating it in one department. He cited Standard Chartered , where AI has helped deflect 77% of employee requests. “If you get 25% to 30% deflection in those use cases, it’s game-changing,” he said. “If you get 75% to 80%, it is life-changing.” Amy Webb, founder and CEO of Future Today Strategy Group, was more blunt about the gap between ambition and readiness. “Let’s be fair, Fortune 500 companies are pretty late to the party on this,” she said. “Artificial intelligence didn’t just show up a couple of years ago.” Webb warned that companies are pouring significant capital into pilots without sufficient strategy, leadership, or planning—creating isolated projects that fail to produce durable value. Building the AI-ready workforce AI TRANSFORMATION IS A WORKFORCE TRANSFORMATION. The summit underscored that organizations need more than new software: They need employees and leaders willing to rethink established processes, learn new skills, and make room for new ways of working. Stacy Dillow, executive vice president and chief people officer at HPE , said companies must resist simply inserting AI into existing systems. “We’ve got to force ourselves to think differently, because if we’re not trying to change how we work, we’re just trying to retrofit and put AI in a process that isn’t going to give us a different answer,” she said. For senior executives, she added, AI adoption and transformation have become central management responsibilities. Danielle Gonzalez, chief people officer at Palo Alto Networks , described how AI is already changing the employee experience. A custom AI agent has reduced IT tickets by 83% and supports workflows across HR, finance, and legal. Instead of turning to a human HR partner or business contact, employees can increasingly ask an agent for answers tied to their role and location. Gonzalez said companies should hire and develop people who can adapt rapidly—not only learning new skills but questioning assumptions that no longer hold. “We’re looking for curiosity,” she said. “We’re looking for agency, and we’re looking for those people who can not only learn something at a fast rate … but also unlearn what they thought to be true, so that they can make space to move forward.” Drew Holler, chief human resources officer at Lennar, stressed that the responsibility is shared. “We’re going to give you all the tools, but it’s your responsibility to upskill yourself as well,” he said. “We’re going to give you trainings, but you, as an individual, have to upskill.” The workforce implications extend beyond reskilling. Francis Shanahan, chief technology officer at Peloton , warned that AI-enabled creation can create its own challenge. Employees are “inundated now because they can literally build anything,” he said, and “burnout” is becoming more of an issue. Michelle Kwon, chief operating officer at Runway, urged leaders not to mistake volume for productivity. “Just because you are using AI, that is not a proxy for your productivity or for doing a good job at work,” she said. AI should improve how people work, she argued, without generating additional work for colleagues or overwhelming them with output that has not been properly assessed and synthesized. Governance, trust, and control THE CASE FOR AI MUST BE MATCHED BY A CASE FOR OVERSIGHT. In regulated industries and high-stakes applications, leaders emphasized that successful deployment depends on selecting the right technology, understanding the risk, and keeping human judgment where it matters most. Hari Gopalkrishnan, chief technology and information officer at Bank of America , cautioned companies not to reach for AI reflexively. “One of the biggest mistakes we see ourselves and others doing is rushing to AI as a solution, when deterministic models do a plenty good job,” he said. Bank of America begins with client needs and a detailed inventory of the relevant process; sometimes a conventional mobile feature or real-time decision rule is the better tool. events.title: How to make economy feel like an upgrade, according to a travel expert who's spent 3,500 hours in premium cabins
events.summary: Flight expert Zach Griff shares how to bring the luxuries of first and business class to the economy cabin. Courtesy of Zach Griff Flying economy can feel crowded, cramped, and generally unpleasant. But it doesn't have to be. Here's how to give yourself an upgrade when you're stuck in economy. Economy seats may be smaller than those in upgraded classes, but that doesn't mean you have to be cramped between passengers. Economy tickets may not include a meal, but that doesn't mean you can't have a fine-dining experience. The economy cabin will never be as comfortable as first class , but that doesn't mean you can't make the most of it. Enter Zach Griff, travel expert and author of the travel newsletter From the Tray Table . Griff estimates he's spent 3,500 hours flying more than 1.8 million miles in business and first-class cabins . He flies 150,000 miles a year on average, including roughly 50,000 in economy. With so much experience in premium cabins , Griff has a few tips that make his economy flights feel like an upgrade. Start by booking a flight during an unpopular travel time. Joey Hadden/Business Insider One of the big perks of premium cabins is having more personal space. If you can avoid flying in a crowded economy cabin, you may be more likely to end up with an empty seat next to you, which can feel like an upgrade, Griff told Business Insider. According to Griff, the earliest and latest departures of the day tend to have the most empty seats. Aim for a Saturday or midweek booking, he added. Try to find a flight with two-seater rows. Chris Cooper/Bloomberg via Getty Images Griff said sitting in a row without a middle seat can make economy feel like an upgrade, too. There are rows like this on some wide-body planes, which have two aisles and are typically used for long-distance travel. So while you're searching for flights for your next international trip, take a look at the seat map before you book. Keep checking for open seats until boarding and move to the row with the most space. Joey Hadden/Business Insider When Griff flies economy, he starts checking the seat map for his trip two days before departure to see how full it is. "If it's looking like maybe another row has more space, I'd always move to that row to see if that may end up open," he said. "Monitor the seat map until the minute before boarding starts and move around to optimize your chances of finding an empty seat." You may even end up with your own row. Treat yourself to a nice meal. Courtesy of Zach Griff In many cases, business and first-class tickets come with the added perk of an in-flight meal. If you're in economy, Griff recommends bringing your own dish or getting some takeout on your way to the gate. "Treat yourself to something a little bit nicer because you're sitting in economy," he added. Make sure you're not missing out on any perks from airline status or credit cards. Lino Mirgeler/picture alliance via Getty Images Even if you're flying economy, having a credit card or elite status with the airline may make you eligible for free checked bags, earlier boarding, or possibly better seats, Griff said. Finally, pack your own amenities to stay comfortable. Courtesy of Zach Griff To make flying economy more comfortable, dress in athleisure and pack a sleep mask and noise-canceling headphones, Griff said. If you have a small massage gun, toss that in your carry-on, too, he added. With your mask on, earbuds in, a full belly, and an empty seat next to you, you may feel like you're on the other side of the cabin curtain. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Renewed mineral sands mine bid 'a turd in glitter', resident says
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Victorian government 'manipulating' planning laws to win critical minerals race, expert says Kane Busch and his family have been farming vegetables in the Lindenow Valley for 100 years. ( ABC Rural: Fiona Broom ) The Victorian government is assessing a mineral sands mine project it has already rejected. The global critical minerals race is behind the renewed attempt to green light the project, experts argue. The company behind the proposal says claims the project has not been altered since its previous rejection are "misleading and false". The Victorian government is "manipulating" its own planning system to fast track approval for a mining project it already rejected, a leading planning expert claims. The Fingerboards Mineral Sands Project proposed for eastern Victoria was knocked back by the government in 2021, because it would "pose a significant risk to the environment and valuable horticulture industry". But the government is now considering what it calls a "new and modified" bid to get the project off the ground, a description that RMIT emeritus professor of planning and environment Michael Buxton said was a "blatant deception". "The project is not a different project and it's not substantially altered," he said. Michael Buxton worked at the Victorian planning department for more than a decade. ( ABC News: Sean Warren ) Nearby residents who have spent years fighting the mine have a different description of the latest proposal. The company behind the project, Gippsland Critical Minerals (GCM), rejected these claims and said its new bid for approval included significant changes. GCM said the site was a rich source of a range of minerals, which had been deemed critical by the Australian government. Miners have been exploring the Lindenow Valley, 270 kilometres east of Melbourne, for mineral sands since the 1970s. Irrigated areas of the Lindenow flats. ( ABC Rural: Emma Field ) Between 2015 and 2023, global demand doubled for mineral sands, which contain concentrated amounts of heavy minerals such as rare-earth elements. Organisations from mining giants such as Rio Tinto to junior mining companies have had a stake in the region, but no project has ever been considered commercially or environmentally viable. After almost a decade of review, in November 2021 the Victorian government rejected a mining project proposed by Kalbar Resources, later Kalbar Operations. In 2023, Kalbar was renamed to Gippsland Critical Minerals (GCM) and submitted a "rescoped" proposal. Gippsland Critical Minerals has dug a test pit on its Fingerboards mineral sands site. ( ABC Rural: Fiona Broom ) Dr Buxton, who has been involved in planning for 50 years, including at the Environment Protection Authority and state planning department, said the government failed to follow proper process by accepting the Fingerboards project for a second review. "The minister could have just refused to consider this application — and in my view, should have," he said. Australia's strategic focus on critical minerals for economic and national security reasons was behind the renewed push for the East Gippsland mineral sands mine, he said. "This has provided companies with the opportunity to argue that it's a critical resource." Under the state government's critical minerals road map launched in December 2024, which outlines efforts to build a globally competitive critical minerals sector, eight mines are at various stages of approval. University of Sydney professor of global governance Susan Park said she was "not surprised at all" that rejected minerals projects were getting a second look. Dr Park said trade and security agreements between Australia and allies such as the United States were driving state and federal support for mining projects. The proposed Fingerboards mine site, 25 kilometres west of Bairnsdale. ( Supplied: Gippsland Critical Minerals ) In February, the Australian government gave the Fingerboards proposal Major Project Status, which gives "strategically significant projects" extra support to navigate regulatory approvals. GCM bills the project as a major source of "ex-China production" of the rare-earth oxides dysprosium and terbium, elements on Australia's critical minerals list. China controls almost all of the world's production and rare-earth refining. Terbium and dysprosium oxides, used in renewable energy and military technologies, are almost completely supplied by China. The Lindenow Valley is a highly fertile region known for its leafy salad vegetables, brassicas and sweet corn. Up to 2,000 workers harvest about 200,000 tonnes of food every year.

events.title: Losing your job after age 50 could derail your career
events.summary: Thomas Heep (left), Steven Fielding (center), and Jon McCarty (right) struggled to find work after losing their jobs later in life. Thomas Heep (left), Steven Fielding (center), and Jon McCarty (right) Some Americans who lose their jobs after age 50 spend years struggling to find comparable work. In September, the average unemployment duration for workers ages 55 to 64 was over eight months. Some older job seekers suspect age discrimination is hurting their chances of finding work. Cathy Valentine lost her job as a transformation lead in 2023. After three years struggling to find a comparable full-time job, the 61-year-old is now a prep cook at a cafe. She said she earns about an eighth of her previous salary. "It just feels like I tried to do everything right and I still am stuck," said Valentine, who lives in Florida. Some older workers who lose their jobs can afford to retire, while others find a comparable role fairly quickly. But those who don't risk getting stuck in a job search that drags on for months or even years — and is getting longer. On some metrics, older Americans are doing just fine in the job market . As of September, older workers had lower unemployment rates than younger workers, and when they were jobless, the median length of that unemployment was shorter. But those figures obscure a worse trend for older job seekers . While half of 55 to 64-year-olds were jobless for a relatively low three months, the group's average unemployment duration was more than eight months in September. That means some older workers have been unemployed for so long that they're pulling the average way up. The gap between the average and median has widened in recent months, suggesting the longest job searches may be growing even longer. In September, about 173,000 unemployed Americans ages 55 to 64 had been out of work for at least six months, and some are facing far longer stretches of unemployment. A Bureau of Labor Statistics analysis found that only 57% of workers ages 55 to 64 who lost their long-held jobs any time between 2023 and 2025 had found new jobs as of January 2026. By contrast, 73% of workers ages 25 to 54 who lost long-held jobs in that period had found new work. Some older workers may have taken their job loss as a sign they should retire. But for others, it marked the beginning of an uphill battle to find another job. The struggle to get hired after 50 As their searches drag on for months or years, older job seekers like Valentine often blame age discrimination for at least part of their struggles. Thomas Heep, a Denver resident in his 60s, has been searching for full-time work since losing his operations manager role in April 2025. He's struggled to pay his bills and filed for bankruptcy earlier this year. Heep suspects some employers may favor younger job seekers over someone his age because they worry he won't remain in the workforce much longer. "Even if a company loves my résumé, skill set, and work history, they're going to look at my age and go: How long is he going to stay? He's close to retirement age. It's too risky." he said. Thomas Heep has struggled to find full-time work since losing his job last year. Thomas Heep Other older workers suspect their salary expectations may be working against them. A former Big Tech employee in her early 60s who lost her job last year said she worries her years of experience may put her at a disadvantage compared with younger candidates willing to accept lower pay. "There's so many people getting laid off at this point who are younger, willing to take these ridiculously low salaries with no benefits," she said. While some research suggests age discrimination plays a role in hiring, proving it in any individual case can be extremely difficult. And for older job seekers who suspect their age is holding them back, there's often no clear path to addressing the problem. Jacob Zinkula writes about how workers are navigating their careers. Share your story with him by filling out this form , emailing him , or reaching out via Signal at jzinkula.29. Follow his work by clicking here . When finding another job feels out of reach For some older workers, a prolonged job search eventually leaves them with two options: settle for lower-paying work or give up looking altogether. Jon McCarty spent 18 months trying to find another software engineering job after losing his role in 2022. Earlier in his career, it typically took him about a month to find a new job. But he said that as he got older, his stretches without work grew longer. McCarty, who's in his early 60s and lives in Virginia, eventually took a part-time cashier job at Home Depot. He's come to believe he'll likely never return to his former career. Jon McCarty spent more than a year searching for another software engineering job. Jon McCarty Steven Fielding, 58, has been laid off more than five times during his career in tech communications. He's been looking for work since April and said the employment gaps over the course of his career have taken a toll on his finances, leaving him with little in savings. Fielding, who lives in Washington state, said he's trying to adapt to the changing job market, including by developing his AI skills . He suspects his age may be contributing to his difficult search, in part because he believes some employers prefer younger workers who are willing to accept lower salaries. Still, he's hoping his decades of experience can help him land another opportunity. "It's like my house is down to the foundation and I'm going to have to rebuild again," he said. "It's pretty daunting to think about." Do you have a story to share? Reach out to the reporter via email at jzinkula@businessinsider.com , or via Signal at jzinkula.29. events.title: One chart shows white-collar biz is thriving even as jobs dry up
events.summary: Employment in white-collar sectors has dipped, while output is surging. Maskot/Getty Images Employment has dropped in white-collar sectors, while output has continued to surge. AI and economic uncertainty are two likely reasons for the sluggish white-collar job market. Still, how productive AI makes companies remains a question. The white-collar sector is doing more with less. While the number of total jobs has slid in industries like finance, tech, and professional services, output has been on a tear. Gad Levanon, the chief economist at the Burning Glass Institute, examined how employment in white-collar-heavy sectors compares with real gross domestic product . He wrote in a Substack article that employment in finance, insurance, information, and professional and business services is collectively down roughly 2% since the end of 2022, while real output for these sectors has soared by 16%. The ongoing slow decline in employment for this group goes against historical patterns and highlights how workers and job seekers are facing a largely frozen, low-hire, low-fire job market . "A growing share of the work businesses used to get done by consultants, contractors, call centers and their own back-office staff is now delivered by software, cloud and IT firms, which produce far more per worker and add almost no staff," Levanon told Business Insider. "That is why the sector's output keeps rising while its hiring has stopped." The divergence also risks breaking the traditional link between economic growth and rising fortunes for everyday Americans. "Even a strong, continual growth in GDP may not translate into jobs for people, may not translate into a higher quality of life for people as well," said Cory Stahle, an economist at the Indeed Hiring Lab. People looking in these kinds of sectors may be having a challenging time. "It's important to remember for these job seekers that a career is not necessarily built over the course of two or three years," Stahle said. "It's usually built over the course of two or three decades. So what the pattern is now could easily shift a couple of years from now. So it's important to be reactive but not overreact to what we're seeing in the data, either." Have you been job searching in these white-collar sectors? Have you had to make a career pivot? Reach out to this reporter to share what that's been like at mhoff@businessinsider.com . Levanon said on Substack that there's demand in these white-collar fields, but firms can meet it with fewer workers. Part of that could be due to employers shifting their priorities toward leveraging AI . Levanon said "the back-office and junior tasks" that AI performs best at are concentrated in the white-collar sectors he looked at. Dante DeAntonio, senior director at Moody's Analytics, previously told Business Insider that the lack of hiring in white-collar fields is largely due to uncertainty around economic policy and AI. Other job market experts have noted that in Big Tech, employers pulled back after the pandemic-era hiring surge. The job market's woes can be especially difficult for people who lack years of experience. "Firms, I think, are certainly diving in with both feet, trying to find ways to gain efficiency from AI," DeAntonio said. "And certainly the first domino to fall is likely to be a pullback in hiring amongst younger workers, new college grads, positions where firms think they might be able to get some uptick from AI, and some sort of replacement value from AI." Whether companies are actually more productive because they're incorporating AI tools remains a question. Eric Kutcher, a senior partner and chair of McKinsey North America, recently said that there are individual productivity increases , rather than institutional-level gains. "You have people that are getting more productive as individuals, but they're just changing some of the work that they're doing," he said. Bureau of Labor Statistics data showed general labor productivity has increased, but not at a wildly accelerated clip. "We have seen that things have slowed down in the last few years, but output per worker and productivity was climbing even before we saw ChatGPT and AI starting to come onto the scene," Stahle said. "To me, that says that AI is part of the story here, but not the complete story. This is part of a longer-term trend." Have you been job searching in these white-collar sectors? events.title: Businesses blindly sending billions in profits to the tip with their food waste
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Food waste costing Australian businesses and the economy billions Topic: Recycling and Waste Management Karl Riseborough was shocked when he realised how much food was wasted at his brewery each week. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) Australia wastes about 7.6 million tonnes of food each year, costing the economy more than $36 billion. Less than a quarter of businesses regularly inspect their food waste, and operational methods mean it can go unnoticed. The federal government has committed to halving food waste by 2030, but some experts are concerned about progress. When Karl Riseborough realised how much food went to waste each week at his Sydney pub and brewery, he was shocked. Grain left over from the beer-making process was thrown out, as well as food waste from the kitchen. What surprised him most was the volume of waste on top of the spent grain. "The food scraps coming back, the plate waste, the kitchen prep waste … you don't really notice when it was all going straight into the bin," Mr Riseborough said. Food waste expert Belinda Chellingworth said many traders had no idea how much waste they were generating, or how much it was affecting their bottom line. The capacity of landfill is reaching a critical level in some areas. ( ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale/File photo ) Every year about 7.6 million tonnes of food is wasted in Australia at a cost of more than $36 billion to the economy . Of that wasted food, 70 per cent is edible and there are critical knock-on effects for landfill management, food security and the climate. With the support of Ms Chellingworth, who happily calls herself a "garbologist", Mr Riseborough has stopped throwing away 50 kilograms of spent grain from each batch of beer he brews. Karl Riseborough is saving thousands a year after some simple changes. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) "Now I have regular users who come and collect it once I've brewed and use it for the benefit of their gardens or their animals," Mr Riseborough said. "We had two 240-litre bins that were getting collected each week. We're now down to one bin collected each fortnight." He said that saved him about $5,000 a year. Australia's hospitality sector wastes 1.2 million tonnes of food each year, according to the Sustainable Restaurant Association. The economic impact of food waste in the food service sector is about $6.4 billion , averaging about $66,000 annually per business. Belinda Chellingworth says many businesses do not realise how much food they waste. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) Ms Chellingworth said less than a quarter of businesses regularly inspected their food waste. "Typically, many businesses, if they've got food left over at the end of their operations or the end of the day, then it will be landfilled," she said. "For many businesses, and particularly large businesses, the cost of food waste across their operations isn't fully realised because they incur it multiple times, but it's not obvious." Food waste will be a point of discussion at the COP31 conference. ( ABC South West WA: Jacqueline Lynch ) For example, over-ordering food is a cost to the kitchen. If it is not sold, that is a revenue cost, and then whatever goes into the bin also involves a cost for collection. "So they're paying for it multiple times, but they're different departments, different cost centres, and it's often not added together, so they don't understand the full cost across the whole business," Ms Chellingworth said. Landfills are nearing capacity in parts of Australia. ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) She said landfill capacity was reaching critical levels in many areas. Some tips in Perth are set to run out of space in two years and sites in New South Wales are set to reach capacity in four years . Victoria's capacity is expected to be reached in the next 10 years. To combat the economic and environmental impacts of food waste, the federal government has committed to halving food waste by 2030 . But UNSW food and health professor Johannes le Coutre does not believe the plan is on track. Johannes le Coutre says tackling food waste will help to ease food insecurity. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) "I'm not sure if that's attainable or achievable with the current landscape," he said. "In Australia we have a unique situation in that we are dealing with a big distance and that even in the food industry a lot of value-added manufacturing occurs overseas.
