events.title: Documents falsified to evade tax on Abramovich's wealth, BBC finds
events.summary: Watch: The documents that were falsified to allow Roman Abramovich to evade tax The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found. Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts. Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents. Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant". Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals. Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws". The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism. For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club. Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, £5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years. The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes". Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers. Chateau de la Croe (top left) in the south of France, Fyning Hill in Sussex and two superyachts vanished from company accounts The evidence is contained in a leak that includes thousands of documents about the oligarch's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies administered from Cyprus - which used to be a tax haven popular with Russians - between 1995 and 2022. The BBC and media partners including the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and the Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network - as well as the Bureau of Investigative Journalism , external - have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential , external investigation. In 2022, Panorama also reported on how Abramovich had made his fortune from a corrupt deal to buy a Russian state-owned oil company in the 1990s, selling it back to the government a decade later for billions in profit. He has previously said allegations of corruption in the deal are false. The profits from Abramovich's oil deals in Russia were funnelled into a web of offshore companies. They were administered from Cyprus by a corporate services firm called MeritServus, in Limassol, the island's second-largest city. Until 2005, Deloitte - now the biggest of the "big four" firms which dominate the accounting industry - owned MeritServus. After they split, the two companies worked closely together with Abramovich's associates to manage his global fortune. The leaked documents from MeritServus reveal some of their practices. Panorama - Roman Abramovich: How He Hid His Fortune He was the Russian oligarch who brought his wealth to the UK. But what’s the truth about Roman Abramovich’s fortune? Panorama investigates the documents that were falsified to hide his wealth and evade tax. Watch now on BBC iPlayer or on BBC One at 20:00 BST on Monday 12 October. Our first example of backdated paperwork comes in 2006, after a new law in Cyprus meant that company accounts had to be made public. The new transparency law threatened to expose the secrets of Abramovich's vast wealth. Deloitte Cyprus had prepared draft accounts for 2003 - but had not yet finalised them - for his Cypriot company Amiscan Investments. The accounts detailed $672m of luxury property. A mansion in West Sussex, a luxury flat in London and an estate in the south of France were all included - plus helicopters, private jets and a small fleet of boats the oligarch owned at the time, including the $147.5m Pelorus. Deloitte in Cyprus appears to have advised Abramovich's company on a scheme to evade tax To keep them secret, Abramovich's associates and Meritservus decided to rewrite history.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Redundancies likely at South 32's Groote Eylandt mine The Groote Eylandt Mining Company mine has begun redundancy consultations with staff. ( ABC News: Jano Gibson ) South 32 is likely to make redundancies at its manganese mine on Groote Eylandt in the Northern Territory. The company is looking to cut $129 million from the business and spend about $100 million on new water infrastructure. The company says it will make changes to strengthen its long-term viability. Job losses are likely at South 32's manganese mine on Groote Eylandt in the Northern Territory as the operation battles years of flooding impacts and skyrocketing production costs. The Groote Eylandt Mining Company (GEMCO) mine has begun consultations with staff. The ABC understands it needs to cut $129 million from the business in response to costs increasing by more than 80 per cent in recent years. The island and mine site were hit hard by Tropical Cyclone Megan in March 2024, but it is understood multiple wet seasons and persistent seepage of groundwater into the pits are also responsible. Mining pits on Groote Eylandt filled with water after Cyclone Megan in 2024. ( Supplied ) A South32 spokesperson said in a statement the company would make changes to strengthen its long-term viability and was speaking to workers. "GEMCO has completed an internal review in response to a more challenging operating environment and increased cost pressures, and has begun implementing changes designed to strengthen the long-term sustainability of the business," the spokesperson said. "The review forms part of a program focused on improving structures, systems and processes and ensuring GEMCO is well positioned to operate successfully into the future. As part of this work, GEMCO has reviewed its workforce requirements and commenced consultation with employees and contractors who will potentially be impacted. Officials from two separate unions representing workers at GEMCO told the ABC they believed office staff would likely be the target of redundancies . A spokesperson for the NT branch of the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union said it was closely monitoring the situation to see if blue-collar workers were affected. Union officials were told South 32 management would provide staff with more information about the redundancies by the end of the week. According to GEMCO's enterprise bargaining agreement, the company must consult with workers before making any significant organisational changes. The bargaining agreement is due to expire at the end of 2027. The MV Anikitos was loaded with 41,000 tonnes of manganese ore when it crashed into a loading wharf on Groote Eylandt. ( Supplied ) The island's wharf was destroyed in 2024 when Tropical Cyclone Megan pushed a loaded bulk carrier into the structure during high tides . Heavy rainfall damaged the mine's pits, a critical bridge and several roads. Exports from the island did not restart until 2025. Mining is expected to conclude on the island within the next 10 years, according to the local Aboriginal land council. events.title: Kaniva wants to be known as an EV charging hub
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tesla applies to nearly double the number of chargers in Kaniva Kaniva could soon become one of the biggest EV charging sites in Australia. ( Supplied: Bale Farming ) Tesla hopes to nearly double the number of fast chargers it has in the country town of Kaniva from 10 to 18. Experts say more investment is required to ensure EV charging infrastructure keeps up with vehicle sales. Residents have until next Monday to object to the company's plans. On a long stretch of highway roughly halfway between Melbourne and Adelaide is a farming town hoping to cement its reputation as an electric vehicle (EV) charging must-see. The western Victorian farming town of Kaniva, with a population of roughly 800 people, already has 10 Tesla Superchargers behind its quaint country pub. The global tech giant has submitted plans to the local council to install another eight, and publican Bob Cane couldn't be happier. Kaniva is home to 10 EV charging sites, with plans to install another eight. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) "It's about bringing people to Kaniva, connecting them with a classic, quintessential Australian classic town," Mr Cane said. Painted sheep have adorned the streets of Kaniva since 2012. ( ABC News: Martin Boulton ) Kaniva currently markets itself as the first and last highway town in Victoria, the gateway to the Wimmera Mallee Silo Art Trail and the "home of Sheep Art". Mr Cane said the chargers were invigorating the town and adding another string to its economy. "When they plug in their car, what are they going to do? [They will] go for a walk into town, get a coffee, grab a hamburger," he said. Bob Cane is hoping the new Supercharger stations will be up and running before Christmas. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) The Windmill Cafe owner Jemma Hill said the chargers had been a boon for the town. "They [travellers] stop, they come over, they grab their lunch and their coffee, they come into town," she said. "It's creating extra foot traffic within the town, which is fantastic, makes it feel very alive." Jemma Hill says the current EV chargers have helped her business. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) The existing chargers are a lifesaver for some travellers already tackling the trek between Melbourne and Adelaide. "We do this trip a few times a year … If we didn't have this, we couldn't get [to Melbourne]," Tom Beresford said. Kaniva is home to about 800 people. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) West Wimmera Shire Council deputy mayor Helen Hobbs said the site, which has been open for about nine months, had already made a difference in the town. "That has actually given people like the bakery confidence to invest," Cr Hobbs said. "To have a brand new bakery with seating for 100 people, it's beyond anything I could have imagined." Helen Hobbs says the EV chargers have brought outside investment into the town. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) EV sales doubled in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, according to the Electric Vehicle Council of Australia. The council's Aman Gaur attributed the jump to cheaper EVs, rising fuel costs and improved charging networks. "We're now up to 4,200 charging locations across Australia and over 11,000 connectors," Mr Gaur said. "Charging stations have definitely been increasing in Victoria and the number of connectors has also been following suit." Ampol this month paid $225 million to buy Evie, one of the country's largest charging networks. Milad Haghani says if EV demand continues to grow at the same pace, charging infrastructure will have to catch up. ( ABC News: Patrick Stone ) University of Melbourne associate professor of urban resilience and mobility Milad Haghani said charging infrastructure would have a serious job keeping up if the EV sales boom continued. "It's hard to predict whether or not the spike in demand that we have observed this year is going to be sustainable," he said. "But if even a fraction of this demand continues into the future, that means that the infrastructure has some catching up to do." Public chargers have rarely had queues, he said, but that could change as more people buy EVs. The West Wimmera Shire Council has published Tesla's planning application online while it assesses the proposal. The application says the upgrade would cost $250,000 and that the existing 10-stall site, open for about nine months, has exceeded the company's expectations. A traffic report filed with the application says 10 to 20 EVs charge at the site each day, with holidays a natural peak period. Residents have until next Monday to lodge an objection to Tesla's plans.

events.title: UAE Property: 'Can my tenant legally list my apartment as a holiday rental without my consent?'
events.summary: Question: I own an apartment in Dubai Marina, which I've rented to the same tenant for two years. A neighbour recently contacted me because different people appear to be entering the apartment every few days with suitcases. I checked one of the holiday rental websites and, to my surprise, found what appears to be my apartment being advertised for short-term stays . I never agreed to this and my tenancy contract says the property is for residential use by the tenant. The tenant is paying the rent on time, so financially, I haven't lost anything, but I'm uncomfortable with strangers continually using a property I'm responsible for. Can a tenant legally do this without my permission, and could I as the owner face problems if something happens? Ahmed, Abu Dhabi Answer: I wouldn't ignore this simply because the rent continues to arrive on time. There's an important distinction between a tenant occasionally having friends or family stay and somebody commercially offering another person's property as short-term accommodation. Dubai's holiday-home sector is regulated, and properties being used for this purpose need to comply with the relevant licensing and registration requirements. Separately, your tenancy agreement determines what your tenant is permitted to do with the apartment. Subletting in Dubai is not illegal; however, the landlord must be informed and agree to the subleasing. Since you were not informed, his actions are illegal and he cannot simply decide to turn your property into his own short-term rental business. Before taking any action I suggest you document what you've discovered. Save screenshots of the advertisement, including photographs that clearly identify your apartment and keep any messages from neighbours or building management. I would then write to the tenant and ask for an explanation rather than immediately making accusations. I'd also establish whether the apartment has actually been registered as a holiday home and, if so, how this was done without your knowledge. There's another practical concern: short-term occupation can mean considerably more wear and tear than a conventional tenancy, as well as possible issues with access cards, building security and insurance. For landlords, this is a useful reminder that receiving the rent doesn't necessarily mean everything is fine with the property. Sensible asset management means knowing how your investment is actually being used. Q: My former partner and I bought a villa in Dubai several years ago in both our names. We have now separated. I want to sell the property so we can both move on financially, but my ex refuses. He says that because he owns half of the villa I cannot force him to sell his share. Neither of us can realistically afford to buy the other person out, and there is still a mortgage on the property. What happens when two people jointly own a Dubai property but one wants to sell and the other simply refuses? Are we effectively stuck owning it together indefinitely? Emma, Dubai A: This is unfortunately one of the complications of joint property ownership that people rarely think about when they're happily buying together. You cannot ordinarily sell your former partner's ownership interest simply because you want the whole property sold. Equally, however, joint ownership doesn't necessarily mean two people must remain financially tied together indefinitely. The first thing I'd establish is exactly how ownership is recorded on the title deed and the respective ownership percentages. Then have the property independently valued. Once you know the realistic selling price, deduct the outstanding mortgage and likely selling costs so both parties can see what equity would actually be available. Sometimes having a real number on the table makes negotiations considerably easier. Possible solutions include one party refinancing and purchasing the other's interest, an agreed sale on the open market or another mutually acceptable transfer arrangement, subject of course to the lender and Dubai Land Department requirements. I'd also check who has been paying the mortgage , service charges and other property expenses since the separation because those contributions may need to be considered when the financial position is ultimately resolved. If agreement genuinely cannot be reached, this moves beyond estate agency advice. You should speak to a Dubai lawyer experienced in property and co-ownership disputes about the legal mechanisms available to bring the joint ownership to an end. The wider lesson for unmarried couples, friends and relatives buying together is simple: discuss the break-up before the purchase. A written co-ownership agreement setting out what happens if one person wants to sell can prevent an enormous amount of difficulty later. The opinions expressed do not constitute legal advice and are provided for information only. Please send any questions to mario@evadxb.com

events.title: The extra stripe that's landed Australian retailer White Fox in court
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Adidas sues White Fox Boutique over its trademark three-stripe design A pair of Adidas shorts with its trademark three-stripe design next to White Fox Boutique shorts with four stripes. ( Supplied ) German sportswear brand Adidas has accused Australian fashion retailer White Fox Boutique of infringing its trademark three-stripe design with garments featuring four stripes. Legal experts say the case could test the trademark registration. The matter is set down for hearing in early 2027. When is a stripe not a stripe? According to sportswear brand Adidas, when it is part of its trademark. The global sportswear giant is suing Australian online fashion retailer White Fox Boutique for selling items allegedly "deceptively similar" to its three-stripe logo, in a case experts say could test the trademark's registration. The German-based brand has filed a trademark infringement claim against the Sydney-based company, popular with teenagers, in the Federal Court of Australia. According to court documents, Adidas accuses White Fox of replicating its trademark across multiple clothing items and advertising content that feature four parallel stripes of equal width in a colour contrasting with the colour of the clothing. Adidas claims this design is "deceptively similar" to its three-stripe trademark, which it has used in Australia for more than 65 years and globally for more than 75 years. White Fox is defending the case, which will play out in court hearings next year. A White Fox Boutique advertisement seen on the back of a bus. ( Supplied ) According to the documents, White Fox Boutique has promoted and supplied clothing with four parallel stripes on it since March this year, including advertisements on buses, bus stops and on social media. Adidas said it asked White Fox to remove the garments from sale in March and to stop using the four-stripe design, which White Fox declined to do. Adidas further claimed White Fox used genuine Adidas shoes, in the same colours as its clothing, in some promotional material, which it said took advantage of the brand's reputation and may lead consumers to draw an association between the two companies. An Instagram post advertising a White Fox Boutique outfit paired with genuine Adidas shoes. ( Supplied ) It alleges White Fox's actions are likely to cause damage to its reputation. In court on Friday, White Fox's barrister Ed Heerey KC said the online fashion retailer would argue the four stripes emblazoned on the label's clothing were simply decorative rather than a trademark. He highlighted similar items bearing the four stripes from other brands, including fast-fashion labels Princess Polly, Glassons and Shein. Intellectual property law expert Muhammad Abbas said this case was not just about a fourth stripe. "Adding a stripe is neither a complete answer to a trademark claim nor automatically an infringement," Dr Abbas, a Queensland University of Technology lecturer, said. He explained a 2023 High Court decision considered the impression a notional buyer, "allowing for imperfect recollection", would have of the registered trademark, compared to the impression created by the sign used. The three-stripe design dates back to the brand's foundation in 1949, but was not trademarked until 1952 after Adidas discovered a Finnish brand Karhu had trademarked the same logo. Founder Adolf Dassler struck a deal and traded two bottles of whiskey and the equivalent of 1,600 euros ($AUD2,500) for the logo, which it has extensively protected ever since. In 2013, it successfully sued Pacific Brands over its use of a four-stripe design on some of its Dunlop and Grosby shoe designs, with the court ruling that three of the 12 designs in question were "deceptively similar". However, University of Technology Sydney School of Law senior lecturer Sarah Hook said challenges overseas had led to Adidas losing its trademark registration in some jurisdictions. In the US, Adidas unsuccessfully took high-end designer Thom Browne to court over a four-stripe design. Thom Browne wore socks with the four-stripe design to court in New York. ( Reuters: Eduardo Munoz ) Thom Browne then challenged the trademark registration in the UK, and the High Court ultimately ruled the trademark was invalid. Fashion designer Thom Browne emerges from a New York courthouse victorious over sportswear giant Adidas. University of Melbourne intellectual property law studies director Benjamin Hopper said distinctiveness was a core doctrine of trademark law, meaning it had to be distinguishable from other goods or services from other traders in the same marketplace.

events.title: Judge halts Trump administration's taxpayer-funded ads
events.summary: A federal judge on Sunday ordered the Trump administration to immediately halt taxpayer-funded ads featuring President Trump. Why it matters: The ruling temporarily blocks the ads weeks before November's midterm elections as multiple lawsuits challenging the Trump administration's use of taxpayer money play out in court. Sunday's ruling stems from a suit filed in the Southern District of New York by Washington, D.C.-based watchdog Common Cause, non-profit Democracy Forward and other plaintiffs. A similar lawsuit , filed by the Democratic National Committee, was filed in D.C. federal court earlier this month. The big picture: The Trump administration maintains that the ads are public service announcements and that previous Republican and Democratic administrations have used taxpayer-funded advertising to promote government policies. Trump pledged to pay for the ads himself after both lawsuits were filed, though the White House told Axios there were no plans to reimburse the government for millions already spent on the ads. Driving the news: The plaintiffs in the New York lawsuit allege that the Trump administration exceeded congressional authorization and violated restrictions on publicity and propaganda. In a brief order , U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon found that a motion filed by the coalition was "not moot." She found they had "demonstrated that they are likely to succeed on the merits, will suffer irreparable harm in the absence of an injunction, the balance of the equities tips in their favor, and an injunction serves the public interest," according to the order. The suit names the Department of Homeland Security, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought, and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles as defendants. What they're saying: The coalition said in a statement emailed by Democracy Forward it was "pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda." The statement added, "There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda." Representatives for the White House and DHS did not immediately respond to Axios' Sunday evening request for comment. What's next: A hearing is scheduled for Oct. 13 to discuss next steps in the case. Editor's note: This story was updated with a statement from the plaintiffs.

events.title: Beyond AI: How HKICC 2026 Develops Judgement, Resilience and Global Leadership
events.summary: As technology transforms how business problems are analysed and solved, the HKUST International Case Competition 2026 challenges students to develop the human capabilities that remain essential to leadership. [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] AI can generate an answer in seconds. Knowing which answer to trust—and how to act on it—still requires human judgement. The HKUST International Case Competition (HKICC) 2026 put that distinction to the test, bringing together twelve elite undergraduate teams from leading business schools around the world to navigate ambiguity, defend complex decisions and work across cultures under pressure. The University of British Columbia Sauder School of Business emerged as champion after a week of competition focused on the innovation and application of artificial intelligence. As businesses navigate technological disruption and growing complexity, future leaders must look beyond fast answers. They must use technology to strengthen analysis while retaining responsibility for context, trade-offs and long-term value. Supported by HSBC for the fourth consecutive year, HKICC brings together high-performing teams from universities across Australia, Canada, Hong Kong SAR, Hungary, the Netherlands, Singapore, South Korea, Spain, Thailand, and the United States. Participants tackle real-world business challenges while collaborating across cultures and perspectives. “At HSBC, we are committed to nurturing the next generation of business leaders,” said Mr. David GRIMME, Chief Operating Officer, Asia and Middle East, HSBC. “HKICC is an exceptional platform for talented students to tackle real-world business challenges while sharpening strategic judgement, strengthening creative problem-solving, and building collaboration skills.” Turning AI-Enabled Analysis into Decisions Business challenges rarely have a single correct answer. Leaders must still evaluate assumptions, weigh risks and make decisions under uncertainty. Leaders must decide which assumptions to test, which risks to accept and where limited resources can have the greatest impact. At HKICC, participants developed practical strategies related to the innovation and application of artificial intelligence. Working within tight timelines, teams adjusted their strategies as new information emerged and defended their reasoning before experienced industry judges. Liron SAEDI of the University of Southern California Marshall School of Business, who received the Best Presenter Award, said: "AI can help with the research behind a case, but at the end of the day, we are the ones recommending and implementing the solutions.” While participants spent much of the week analysing cases, their learning also extended beyond the competition room. A highlight of this year's programme was the HSBC Student Engagement Event, where participants engaged directly with senior leaders and gained insights into leadership and career development. After a week of intense competition, the University of British Columbia Sauder School of Business emerged as Champion of HKICC 2026. The University of Southern California Marshall School of Business and the National University of Singapore secured the first and second Runner-up titles respectively. UBC Sauder also received the Outstanding Business Concept Award for its innovative and compelling solution. Beyond the case analyses and final presentations, participants practised the behaviours that effective teamwork requires: managing time, testing assumptions and ensuring different perspectives were heard. Anjana SRINIVASAN, Chief Administrative Officer Asia & Middle East and COO Asia International Markets at HSBC, who served as one of the final judges, said: "Great teamwork is more than simply sharing the work. It means listening as much as contributing, challenging ideas respectfully, and ensuring every voice is heard and valued. The ability to collaborate across different perspectives while working under pressure is a skill that will serve these students well throughout their studies and careers.” For participants, those principles were tested in practice. Boin KANG from the National University of Singapore said: "It's really about time management, working under pressure, stress-testing our knowledge and rationale, and explaining our thinking to one another." Together, these experiences required teams to move beyond dividing tasks. They had to challenge ideas constructively, reconcile different viewpoints and maintain a coherent recommendation under pressure. The Capabilities Future Leaders Will Need Through HKICC, HKUST Business School and HSBC share a commitment to developing leaders who can navigate uncertainty, adapt to change and work across cultures and markets.

This year’s Disrupt isn’t about predicting the future of AI; it’s about building companies in it. Across six editorially curated stages, founders will hear practical lessons from the CEOs, investors, engineers, and operators shaping the next decade of technology. Whether you’re raising your first round, scaling your team, or deciding how AI changes your product, every session is designed to answer one question: “What can I take back to my company on Monday morning?” Disrupt works a bit differently, depending on where you are in your founding journey, with different tracks you can follow to make the most of the three days: You’re here to pressure-test your thesis, meet your first angel or pre-seed investors, and figure out who else is building in your space. Scaling, hiring, in search of partnerships You’re here in search of talent, strategic partners, and market visibility. events.title: Fox stays positive on data centers even as public backlash grows
events.summary: The News Despite increasingly critical media coverage of AI and the spread of data centers across the US, one news network has been painting a more positive picture. More than half of the references to data centers on Fox News over the last two years would have left viewers with a favorable impression, compared to less than 10% on CNN and 5% on MS NOW, according to a new Semafor analysis of mentions of data centers on each network. The mentions were pulled from closed captions preserved by the Internet Archive, which keeps a digital, searchable library of recorded TV news. A pair of AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI scored each reference on its content, with the network’s name removed. Mentions of data centers have, predictably, shot up across all three networks in recent months as political backlash against AI swells and the data centers themselves have become a salient issue ahead of the midterms. But Fox’s opinion and morning shows, including, , and leaned on the promise of AI, economic investment and the race with China, skewing Fox’s coverage more favorably, the analysis showed. The network’s news shows were more measured. In an Aug. 23 monologue that at one point featured a chyron reading “The case for data centers,” Fox host Brian Kilmeade acknowledged “real concerns,” but argued that “saying no to data centers nationwide also means saying no to the tax dollars that can flow into a community. … If Americans don’t build the infrastructure to meet the demand, somebody else will.” On CNN and MS NOW, the criticism focused as much on the facilities’ political toxicity as on harms like power bills or water use, casting them as unpopular with voters and a liability for politicians who back them heading into the midterms. Data centers “are driving up energy costs, sucking up water supplies, wiping out rather than creating jobs,” MS NOW’s Katy Tur said in May. “Politicians beware.” Polling shows that across demographic groups, Americans hold increasingly negative views of data centers: More than half of Americans say data centers are mostly bad for the environment , Pew Research Center found last month, compared with 39% in January. Fox News did not comment for this story. Max’s view The pro-data center programming on Fox News comes as the right tries to define its positions in an AI-fueled, post-Donald Trump future. Fox’s favorable data center coverage mirrors Trump’s position on their growth and the need for AI companies to help fuel the US economy. “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in August. “If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame.” But anger about data centers and the rapid advancement of AI represents a faultline within the MAGA coalition that swept Trump back into office. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., have questioned some data centers in their states, while Texas Gov. Greg Abbott seems to have flipped from supporting data centers to looking to slow their growth in his state amid a tougher-than-expected reelection campaign. Some on the right I have talked to in the last several months worry that Fox News, which Trump watches religiously, and other pro-data center voices are encouraging the president to take positions that are broadly unpopular with his rural and suburban base. “The Big Tech oligarchs, the guys driving AI, did a terrible job,” Steve Bannon, a staunchly anti-AI Trump ally, told the Daily Signal in September. “They came in to try to muscle local communities, and particularly since President Trump’s strongest base is in exurban and rural communities, that’s where they were really the ugliest, and they haven’t made their case, and they particularly haven’t made their case at the local level about the economics of this, and the energy of this, and the water of this, and the manifestation of what these things are going to be used for.” Room for Disagreement Not all of Fox’s data center coverage has been rosy; its tenor grew slightly less favorable in 2026 compared to last year. “It’s taxing our system way too much on water, agriculture land, or electricity. We’re gonna implode,” the Texas agriculture commissioner said in an interview on a weekend Fox show in August. “We just can’t do it. There’s not enough.

events.title: Hack reveals Netanyahu campaign's media ties
events.summary: The News Hacked messages from an adviser to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu are providing a glimpse of his aides’ close ties to the media. The incumbent prime minister’s reelection campaign has been repeatedly rocked by hacked and leaked documents, part of broad attempts to destabilize a wildly divisive leader both inside and outside his country ahead of Oct. 27 elections. The latest breach comes from the WhatsApp account of Netanyahu aide Jonatan Urich, who appears to have exposed sensitive information through a vibe-coded media-monitoring app. Haaretz reported Sunday that it had “verified” the leak. The messages include conversations between Urich and Amit Segal, a central media figure who is chief political analyst for Channel 12 News, the country’s leading broadcaster, and host of the program , an analogue of the US show of that name. In the exchanges, Segal offers advice about the campaign’s videos and its messaging: Netanyahu’s management of the aftermath of the October 7 attack is his core political advantage, he suggests. Segal mentions he offered the same advice to Netanyahu’s campaign spokeswoman. In another message, Urich shares a speech Netanyahu is planning to give. Segal declined to discuss the messages on the record. Urich, who is also enmeshed in a scandal over payments from Qatar, didn’t respond to an inquiry, but in a lawyers’ statement posted to X confirmed that he had been hacked and threatened legal consequences against anyone who published the content of the leaks. Israel’s Privacy Protection Law prohibits republishing content obtained through illegal means. Ben’s view Hacks and leaks are challenging to cover. The most important story in most hacks — including this one — is the hack itself; this is part of the broad internationalization of the Israeli political campaign, in which actors across the region and in the US line up for and, mostly against, the leader who led his country’s response to the October 7 attacks. But Israeli commentators also professed shock, if not surprise, Sunday at how closely aligned the journalist and spin doctor appeared to be. Segal is a center-right figure broadly aligned with Netanyahu — but he’s also a top journalist who appears on international platforms, like the American political figure Dan Senor’s widely-followed podcast, as an independent analyst. One Israeli journalist compared Segal’s role in Israel to that of Fox News host Bret Baier, who maintains journalistic independence despite working for a right-wing platform. The messages put a dent in Segal’s version of that image, and offer a glimpse at parts of an Israeli media that has grown very close to its prime minister. Room for Disagreement Segal addressed the controversy on News 12, describing the messages as part of a “very delicate tango between the journalist and the subject of their coverage.” He added that “any people I’ve covered over the years gave me drafts of speeches, saying, ‘This will be our campaign, what are your thoughts?’” Notable The region’s politics have been buffeted — and illuminated — repeatedly by aggressive cyber campaigns for years. Semafor reported in 2023 on extensive, leaked Iranian government communications that revealed Iranian attempts to influence US politics.

events.title: ABC News offers contradictory explanation for vanishing Anduril story
events.summary: The News When ABC News removed a story about Donald Trump’s sons from its website without explanation on Thursday, an unnamed company source told media reporters the article had been published “prematurely.” Nathan Lee, the investigative reporter who wrote the original piece , used the same language in emails to Powerus and Anduril, two of the companies at the center of the piece. But emails between ABC News and its subjects, provided to Semafor, show the network seeking to downplay its errors by misrepresenting its own processes. On Oct. 7, ABC News published an investigation into a new $6.6 billion deal between defense contractor Anduril and the US Navy to build a new high-tech submarine shipyard in Maryland. The piece largely focused on the financial ties between President Donald Trump’s son and defense companies, noting that Donald Trump Jr. is a partner at investment firm 1789 Capital, which “claimed a major stake in Anduril in June 2025 from a $2.5 billion investment into the company.” After the piece was published, a spokesperson for Anduril reached out to Lee with several urgent requests for correction. The company — which had not responded to ABC News’ inquiries prior to its publication, according to an Anduril source — wanted the network to clarify connections between Anduril and 1789, noting that the firm had invested $50 million in Anduril’s latest round, a small percentage of the $2.5 billion total. “Today, 1789 owns approximately 0.13% of Anduril and has no major investor rights. Any suggestion that 1789 financed the round or holds significant ownership, governance position or ‘major stake’ in Anduril is inaccurate,” Anduril’s spokesperson wrote to Lee, according to emails obtained by Semafor. After the story was published on Wednesday, Lee told Anduril that the network was slightly tweaking the language in its piece, but it was otherwise standing by its story. “I have spoken to my editors and we have updated the story for accuracy,” Lee said in a note. “We had pulled the ‘major stake’ language from previous reporting. 1789 Capital did claim a stake from the $2.5 billion investment your company received, so we are standing by our language to that extent.” Anduril’s PR team was not satisfied, and continued to press the network to clarify its story, saying that the piece misstated 1789 Capital’s investment in Anduril’s fundraising round. “It’s still not clear. I read your text and it reads as if they invested the full $2.5b. Would be much more accurate to list their actual investment of $50m and even more accurate to share that they own less than a percentage point in Anduril,” a spokesperson wrote. In another email later Wednesday afternoon, Lee said ABC News’ editors had reviewed the language and were standing by the piece. “Apologies, but my editors said we are standing by the language. I’ll make sure to reach out to both of you directly for any future stories,” Lee said. But by Thursday, the network had changed its mind. The network removed the piece without explanation, and Peter Charalambous, an ABC News producer in New York, reached out to Anduril and Powerus, a drone contractor mentioned in the story, saying the story had been “published prematurely and removed from our website.” On Friday evening, ABC News republished a new version of the story re-reported by Charalambous, now without a byline . An editor’s note did not include language that the initial piece was published early. “Editor’s Note: CORRECTION: A version of this story published on Oct. 7 contained errors in the description of certain company investments, government contracts and event chronologies. After subsequent reporting, this version contains corrected information and additional context regarding some of those investments, contracts and events.” A network source told Semafor: “We always review every situation in a thorough and thoughtful manner and will not be providing further comment at this time.” The source also noted that it was extremely rare for ABC News to remove a story. Status reported Sunday that the article was mentioned during the network’s regular 9 am editorial call the day it was published, “suggesting at least some staffers were aware of its publication,” and it “circulated it through its usual email distribution without raising any immediate alarms.” Max’s view ABC News’ suggestion that its initial story was published prematurely is familiar spin to anyone who has dealt with crisis PR. It minimized the company’s mistakes and made the situation seem like an accident. But at a time when distrust in the news media continues to rise, deflections like this can damage the credibility of mainstream, nonpartisan American journalism. Tellingly, the network seemed to know the difference in its official response, acknowledging that the original piece contained errors. Brett Velicovich, co-founder of Powerus, another company mentioned in ABC News’ initial piece, complained that the network’s handling of the story reinforced his frustration with much of the media coverage of his company and the president’s administration. “It’s destroying the integrity of what reporting is all about,” Velicovich said. “The damage is already done.” The Trump family’s mix of business and governing, unprecedented in recent history, is an important reporting target, as journalists attempt to understand how companies and countries are attempting to influence policy by investing in Trump businesses or bringing the Trumps on as partners themselves. But ABC News’ decision to remove its story without explanation while misleadingly telegraphing that it was simply published on accident gave the president’s son and many on the right another opening to criticize mainstream news outlets. If more and more people continue to believe that news organizations are willing to mislead or fail to take full accountability for mistakes, will they listen when outlets have legitimate stories? Room for Disagreement Remove the numbers, and the most basic version of the story — the Pentagon is paying very large sums to a defense contractor in which the president’s sons have invested, and whose co-founder, Palmer Luckey, is a high-dollar Trump donor — is correct . It also follows a pattern congressional Democrats have promised to investigate should they retake power after the midterms.

events.title: Roofing scammers con homeowners out of thousands of pounds
events.summary: Scammers pretending to be legitimate workmen are charging homeowners thousands of pounds for roofing work that is not completed, done badly or not necessary, according to Citizens Advice. The consumer advice charity says one in 10 of all the scams it recorded over the past year were related to roofing, making it the most common type of scam brought to them. It can leave victims like Crystal, from the Midlands, thousands of pounds out of pocket. The 68-year-old was frightened and found it hard to sleep after a rogue builder left her roof with dislodged bricks and blocked gutters. She said she felt pressured into agreeing to having her roof re-done and paid a total of £5,500, only for the original contractor to send his son instead, who left work in the eaves incomplete. "We had heavy rain a couple of weeks after he did the job, and it ended up like a waterfall coming down the wall," she said. Her neighbour's house was also damaged. "They took the lead off my neighbour's side of the chimney, which caused bricks to fall into his attic and the rain to go into his house," she told the BBC. The experience still haunts her: "I can't sleep. I don't eat properly." In the year to August the Citizens Advice Consumer Service received 9,000 complaints about roofing work, including problems with construction, repairs and weatherproofing. Of those 2,205, or about one in four complaints, were suspected scams, up from 2,098 the year before. Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice, urged consumers to carry out thorough checks on traders before agreeing to hire them. "Scammers exploit the fact that roofs are out of sight and reach, knowing most people can't easily inspect the work themselves," she said. Victims also reported aggressive and intimidating behaviour, with three quarters of fraudsters using "doorstep" sales tactics. Citizens Advice cited the case of Charlotte, 65, who lives alone in north eastern England. Tradesmen she found online initially offered to fix her leaking gutter for £250. The two men then said there was further work that needed to be done, that would cost £2,500. "An hour later they said it was sorted, but they'd found another problem," she said. It was dark and Charlotte felt afraid. "They knew I was alone, I didn't feel like I could deal with anything that might happen after, so I paid £3,500," she said. But the next day she could see no sign of any work having been done, she said. To avoid falling victim to roofing scams, Citizens Advice suggests: Be alert: Always ask for references and for everything to be in writing. Be wary of unsolicited doorknockers and callers Gather evidence: If a trader causes problems, be sure to take photos and gather the necessary paperwork and receipts Know your rights: Traders must give you the information about your right to cancel in writing. If the job is not done with "reasonable care and skill," the Consumer Rights Act 2015 also entitles you to ask for the problem to be fixed or a refund Lord Bichard, chair of National Trading Standards, said rogue traders were "criminals deliberately preying on people in their own homes". He described roofing fraud as "particularly cruel", and said Trading Standards would pursue fraudsters through legal routes. "Victims can lose life savings in a matter of hours and be left with damaged homes, financial hardship and a profound sense of vulnerability long after the criminals have gone," he said. events.title: Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia
events.summary: Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February US President Donald Trump is facing a growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia as the Iran war continues to impact global energy prices. Trump on Friday announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by several other shipments. That is despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks ago. The move has been criticised by some Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who believe the deal violates US laws. As well as the initial release of 300,000 tonnes of diesel, Trump said Russia would then supply 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that. This would be followed by a further three million tonnes, which would be delivered "within a short period" dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine during the ongoing war between the two countries. "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed these numbers to Tass, the country's state-owned news agency, saying the export volume could reach three million tonnes per month in future. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended". It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen. A group of seven senators - four Republicans and three Democrats – on Sunday said the deal violated US laws, urging Trump to "reverse course". "The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the lawmakers said. They added that Congress had "explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine". The statement was signed by Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden. Trump's 'energy ceasefire' claim welcomed by Zelensky but Russia silent Published 1 day ago Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work? Published 3 days ago Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices Published 3 days ago Not everyone is opposed to the deal. Republican Thomas Massie, who has sparred with Trump a number of issues, said the US should lift sanctions on all petroleum products. Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News the agreement would work through existing legal channels the US has to help bring prices down and that anyone in Congress who said it would not was wrong. Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February, with the fighting severely disrupting supplies of crude oil - a key ingredient in petrol and diesel. The rising prices have become a key issue for Americans ahead of next month's midterms elections, which will determine if Trump's Republican Party maintains control of Congress. Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy and the war in Iran and he has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain. The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market. The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September. Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers. The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tonnes this month, it amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption. It is not only at home that Trump is facing opposition to his diesel deal with Russia. A number of international leaders have criticised it, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who said the US and other allies of Ukraine should focus on ramping up pressure on Russia to end the war. Meanwhile, Trump announced in Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had reached an "energy ceasefire" but did not give more details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed this but there was no response from Moscow.

The agreement slashes Chinese imports by millions of cars over four years, the EU’s trade commissioner said, calling it “ only a first step .” The deal leaves untouched the vast majority of Brussels’ $1 billion-a-day trade deficit with Beijing. Chinese brands accounted for one in four European hybrid sales in August, swamping Europe’s legacy automakers. Volkswagen recently announced 100,000 job cuts . Beijing is playing for time, a Trivium China analyst suggested: “In exchange for reviews, dialogue, and ‘understandings,’ it has conceded little on the structural drivers of the EU’s massive trade deficit .” — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Environmental watchdog to review new Kimberley gas project
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Buru Energy sends gas project for EPA approval, saying it could power northern WA by 2029 Buru Energy's proposed Rafael conventional gas project in the Canning Basin. ( Suplied: Buru Energy ) Buru Energy has referred its Rafael conventional gas project to WA's Environmental Protection Authority for assessment. Environmentalists claim it could be a "Trojan horse for fracking" — something the company rejects. Buru expects a decision from the EPA by the end of the year. The company behind a proposed gas project in Western Australia's Kimberley says it could meet the region's power demands with locally produced energy for the first time. Buru Energy referred its Rafael conventional gas project to WA's Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) for review in early October. The proposal involves developing a facility at the project site, located in the Kimberley's Canning Basin about 85 kilometres south of Derby, to process conventional gas from two co-located production wells. Conventional gas is natural gas extracted using simple drilling and pumping methods, as opposed to unconventional extraction methods like hydraulic fracturing, or fracking. Well testing underway at Buru Energy's Rafael conventional gas project. ( Supplied: Buru Energy ) Buru executive chairman David Maxwell said the Rafael project was the only proven conventional gas and liquids resource in the greater Kimberley region. "At the moment, the Kimberley relies on imported energy … from Karratha, Perth, Darwin, and Asia," he said. He said the Rafael project would improve energy security and be cost-effective, with reduced road traffic another potential benefit. Up to 300 tonnes of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) would be produced at the Rafael plant per day — the equivalent of about 16 or 17 terajoules of energy — alongside LPG and condensate. Mr Maxwell said the Kimberley used between six and 13 terajoules per day for power generation, with the amount varying based on the time of year. "We'll also supply beyond the Kimberley into, for example, the northern Pilbara. "In the case of LPG, we would be supplying in the order of a quarter to a third of the Kimberley's LPG demand." The West Australian government has banned fracking in over 98 per cent of the state, but this does not include parts of the Kimberley including the Canning Basin. Earlier this year, WA's EPA recommended a fracking proposal by Black Mountain Energy subsidiary Bennett Resources go ahead subject to conditions. The Valhalla Gas Exploration and Appraisal Program would see up to 20 exploration and appraisal wells drilled in the basin. A record 8,000 appeals were lodged against the project. Community members gather in Broome to protest the Valhalla fracking proposal. ( ABC Kimberley: Dunja Karagic ) When asked about the fracking proposal in Broome this month, WA Mines Minister Daniel Pastorelli said the method had drawn varied perspectives. "I understand everyone has differing views on these types of things and I respect that completely," he said. "Obviously our policy and our approach is based on science, and that is what we're doing when it comes to hydraulic fracturing." Daniel Pastorelli acknowledges fracking is a controversial topic. ( ABC News: Keane Bourke ) Environmentalists have expressed concern Buru's Rafael project, although a conventional gas project, could pave the way for fracking to occur in the future. Environs Kimberley executive director Martin Pritchard said Rafael "could be a Trojan horse for fracking". "They (Buru) might be saying right now that they're not intending on fracking, but their statements to the ASX clearly say that they want to undertake fracking in the future," he said. Buru's David Maxwell rejected the accusation. "It's got nothing to do with fracking at all," he said. "And if there was any fracking involved — and I stress there is not — that would be a separate [EPA] referral, a separate application and a separate approval process and we're not in that process at all." Buru Energy's Yulleroo 2 wellhead 60 kilometres east of Broome was fracked in 2010. ( ABC Kimberley: Ben Collins ) The company previously used the hydraulic fracturing technique at its Yulleroo gas field also in the Canning Basin, but Mr Maxwell said it no longer did so. "We do not currently practice hydraulic fracturing," he said. "In the past Buru has, but Buru has put that on the shelf, and at the moment we have no plans for fracture stimulation." Mr Pritchard said solar and batteries, rather than gas fields, were the way forward for cheaper and cleaner electricity in the Kimberley.

events.title: Six senators call for Trump administration to 'immediately reverse course' on Russian diesel plan
events.summary: A bipartisan group of six senators are calling on President Donald Trump’s administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices WASHINGTON -- A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump's administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices. Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote. Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute. “The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” they wrote. The Republican senators who signed onto the statement are Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut. Tillis, in an interview that aired Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” said there's a legitimate case for saying the president is not following the law if the administration goes through with its diesel purchase plan. “We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied,” Tillis said. Trump's announcement came just a few weeks after Congress passed legislation that directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. The congressional effort was aimed at cutting the flow of money Russia receives from oil and gas sales to finance its war against Ukraine. The lawmakers also noted that Congress explicitly banned Russia energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war. “Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies,” the six lawmakers wrote in their statement. “President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law.” Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said Trump is focused on reducing the cost of energy when asked whether the president's action would be in violation of U.S. law. Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded 8 people, including 2 kids, pregnant woman, killed at home: Police District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' “The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions,” Barrasso said on CBS's “Face the Nation.” He also encouraged Trump to enforce the sanctions law that Congress passed last month. “This is just another point of leverage for the president to use against Putin in an effort to get a long-term solution in that part of the world,” Barrasso said. Energy experts say the Russia deal is unlikely to make a dent in high prices at the pump. Richard Nephew, a senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy, noted that the total amount of diesel appears to be less than what the U.S. uses in a day. Nephew argued that Iran and Russia might benefit more than the U.S. “The Iranians are probably very excited because it shows that there’s a lot of pressure still on the U.S. And the Russians are excited because it puts a big hole in the sanctions regime,” he said. Trump has recently sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran , which has elevated world energy prices. events.title: Buttigieg gambles on a different path for 2028
events.summary: Pete Buttigieg has been able to campaign for Democrats across the country more than many of his potential 2028 rivals this past year. One reason: He doesn't have a job. That's by choice. Buttigieg said no when top Democrats urged him to run for governor or the U.S. Senate in Michigan this year. Why it matters: That decision is a gamble for Buttigieg's presidential ambitions. He's been able to build a national network over the last two years but hasn't added to his relatively thin resume as a former mayor of South Bend, Ind., and Joe Biden's transportation secretary. Buttigieg, 44, became a national political figure without following the typical path. He ran for president in 2020 as a small-town mayor and won the Iowa caucus by offering an optimistic vision and impressing voters with his communication skills — including in hostile environments. Driving the news: In early 2025, Democratic lawmakers and strategists including New York Sen. Chuck Schumer and former Michigan Sen. Debbie Stabenow urged Buttigieg — who had moved to Michigan — to run for office in his new state. Winning such an office, they argued, would help Buttigieg build his resume for a future White House run and give him a chance to distance himself from the unpopular Biden administration. Buttigieg passed, citing both a desire to stay home more with his husband and young twins, and figuring that he could still get his message out without being in the Senate. Instead, he set about building a larger national network among Democrats — particularly with Black voters in the South, where he had struggled in the 2020 Democratic primary. Buttigieg has traveled to 37 states since he left the Biden administration, Politico reported last week. Democratic candidates in vital swing districts and states have welcomed him to campaign for them this year while resisting offers from other potential presidential candidates such as former Vice President Kamala Harris , New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and California Gov. Gavin Newsom. In Buttigieg, many Democrats see a surrogate who can draw attention and crowds without the degree of negative attention that other prominent Democrats attract. Buttigieg also will campaign in key races in the final weeks before the Nov. 3 election. He's scheduled to be in Michigan and Virginia — which happen to hold early contests in the 2028 presidential primary. Between the lines: Buttigieg has tried to position himself as a candidate of the next generation who also has enough experience in the executive branch to be able to deliver. He's betting that the traditional ladder of running for president — becoming a senator, governor, or vice president first — no longer applies, especially after the Trump era. What they're saying: Buttigieg "knows what no one else on the Democratic side does, which is what it's actually like to run for this office — the pacing, the pressures and imperatives," David Axelrod, a former senior aide to President Obama and an outside adviser to Buttigieg in the past, told Axios. "At a time when the party and country will be searching for youth and forward-looking vision, he has the capacity to articulate one in a powerful way," Axelrod added. Axelrod said that if Buttigieg runs, "it will be because he feels the timing is right for someone like him, and the big mission is more compelling than the statewide races on which he took a pass." A Buttigieg spokesperson said that "when Pete decided not to run for office in Michigan, he promised he would still get to work to help candidates everywhere. He's been doing just that."

events.title: Aaron Sorkin’s ‘The Social Reckoning’ is off to a weak start
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. “The Social Reckoning,” Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to “The Social Network,” is on track to make only $5.5 million at the domestic box office this weekend, according to Sunday estimates. That’s below the already underwhelming $7 million to $8 million the studio had projected, and it means Sorkin’s new movie is unlikely to become a “Social Network”-sized hit. The earlier film had a $22 million opening weekend and made a total of $97 million domestically (and that’s at 2010 ticket prices). It also won Sorkin an Oscar and became one of most influential on-screen depictions of Silicon Valley and startup culture. Beyond the fate of a single film, the weekend box office could also offer hints about audience excitement, or lack thereof, as we kick off a fall full of movies starring villainous, real-world tech CEOs . There’s Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary “Musk” (which also opened this weekend), Nathan Fielder’s apparently uncategorizable Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” (coming next weekend!), and the OpenAI boardroom drama “Artificial” (which has a new distributor after being dropped by Amazon). Outside of theaters, Netflix also has a series called “The Altruists” coming in November , telling the story of Sam Bankman-Fried and the collapse of FTX. As for “The Social Reckoning,” while “The Social Network” was a notable success, the theatrical landscape has changed significantly in the last 16 years. And where the first film focused on the excitement and drama of Facebook’s early days, the sequel is darker and heavier — it’s all about whistleblower Frances Haugen’s decision to leak what became known as the Facebook files. So maybe a movie about Senate hearings and algorithm changes was never going to be a big hit. Or maybe the real audience is among older moviegoers who have only returned sporadically to theaters . And I wonder if critiquing Facebook feels a bit less urgent to audiences who are more likely to be losing sleep over AI. Maybe just as importantly, the new movie’s reviews just aren’t very good . (For what it’s worth, I enjoyed “The Social Reckoning” but will fully admit that it’s overloaded with Sorkin’s trademark speechifying. events.title: Mildura and South Australia connected by bus service after six-year hiatus
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts New bus service re-establishes link between Mildura and South Australia The Monty Express can drop Mildura residents off in South Australia, and SA residents off in Mildura. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) The Monty Express coach will re-establish a direct road transport link between Mildura, Renmark and Adelaide. The route has not been serviced in almost six years. The service will make its first interstate journey on October 12. A new bus service has launched connecting Mildura in Victoria's north-west to South Australia. From this week, a bus named The Monty Express will be travelling the Sturt Highway between Sunraysia and Adelaide via Renmark. It has been nearly six years since the route was serviced, with Greyhound Australia canning its Mildura to Adelaide coaches in 2016 , and another bus company ceasing its operations in 2020, in the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic. The lone direct flight between Mildura and Adelaide also no longer exists, with Rex Airlines terminating the service in May 2023. Ever since, getting into the festival state from Mildura involved detours via Ouyen, Horsham or Broken Hill, or at greater cost, flying to Adelaide via Melbourne or Sydney. The Monty Express will start taking passengers from October 12. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) Former Sunraysia resident Stuart Saunders ran a survey six months ago to gauge interest in restoring a Mildura to Adelaide bus service. He said support was overwhelming, and he soon prepared to pivot from his information technology career to become a bus driver. He purchased a 36-seat bus, which he named The Monty Express after the family's pet Cavoodle, Monty. "There's very much a sense of community in the coach industry," he said. Stuart Saunders and his family in front of their new business venture. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) The Mildura–Renmark–Adelaide service begins today. It will initially run twice a week, departing Adelaide on Mondays and Thursdays and returning on Tuesdays and Fridays. It will run as an express service with pick-ups at Mildura, Renmark, Adelaide Airport and the Adelaide Central Bus Station. Under a service agreement with the SA government, The Monty Express cannot pick up South Australian residents unless they go to Mildura. Stuart Saunders with his children, Matilda and Gabriel, wife, Melody and dog, Monty. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) The agreement exists to avoid impacting passenger numbers on the existing Stateliner coach service route between the Riverland and Adelaide. Mildura man Steven Haby describes himself as a transport enthusiast. The former Melburnian is a member of the Bus and Coach Society of Victoria and the Australian Timetable Association. He will be travelling from Mildura to Adelaide to experience the first service of The Monty Express on Monday. Steven Haby has booked his ticket on The Monty Express. ( Supplied: Steven Haby ) "I'm very much an advocate and supporter of public transport," Mr Haby says. "I thought this was a really good opportunity to support the service going forward and be one of the first passengers on the run. "You can have a sustainable public transport network in a city like Mildura … making it frequent, reliable, cheap, and to places where people want to go." Mr Saunders hopes The Monty Express will not only benefit Mildura residents, but will connect people in the Riverland with Sunraysia's V/Line bus services and flights. "Not only are we trying to give an express service into Adelaide from Mildura, but the challenges for the Riverland people trying to get into Mildura, I'm hoping we can solve some of their problems as well," he said. Tamille Hunter is a resident of Cobdogla, a South Australian town less than two hours from Mildura by car. Ms Hunter is unable to drive and has occasionally used existing transport options to get to Mildura. The journey she took involved catching a bus to Adelaide, a flight to Melbourne, a train to Swan Hill and a bus to Mildura. The Monty Express can seat as many as 36 passengers. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) "At the moment, for us to go to Mildura it takes us 24 hours and over $600," Ms Hunter said. She said getting The Monty Express to Mildura would open up lots of opportunities for her. "From there, I could visit my family and friends in Melbourne on the V/Line," she said.

events.title: Trump bears down on Zelensky as Russia keeps up attacks on Ukraine
events.summary: President Trump's announcement Sunday about an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine referred to a potential deal that includes each side stopping attacks on oil refineries — and he expects Volodymyr Zelensky to abide by it, a White House official said. The official said if attacks on oil refineries cease, a deal to stop hitting power plants and energy grids could come next. Why it matters: Trump appears to be singlehandedly trying to will a partial ceasefire into existence. But for now Russia hasn't accepted any kind of ceasefire — and Ukraine wants one that forbids attacks on power plants. Reality check: The "refinery for refinery" proposal, as the official dubbed it, is lopsided. A Ukrainian official told Axios that the country has a single oil refinery which the Russians have attacked multiple times and isn't fully functional. Russia, by contrast, has a vast network of refineries. "We import diesel and gas. What we need is for the Russians to stop attacking our electricity grid," the Ukrainian official said. "The Russians are thinking about" it, the White House official said. "We will know soon if they are ready." Case in point: Hours after Trump's announcement, Russia conducted strikes on power plants in Ukraine, according to Ukrainian media. What he said: Trump's Truth Social post sounded at first like a major breakthrough. "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" he wrote. It appears much more tenuous than that. Zelensky said the announced ceasefire "was news for me." State of play: After reaching a deal with Russia Friday to lift diesel sanctions, Trump remains focused on stopping Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. He believes the strikes are driving up U.S. gas prices. White House officials warn that Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries are hurting Zelensky's relationship with Trump more than they're damaging Russia. "Trump is really mad. He feels Zelensky is taking the U.S. for granted," the White House official said. Zoom in: Amid the crisis with Ukraine, presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have put their planned trip to Moscow on hold, at least until they get clarity on whether Ukraine and the Europeans are ready to agree to a new unified proposal for Putin. A Ukrainian official told Axios on Friday that during a meeting with U.S. negotiators in Miami on Friday, Witkoff and Kushner threatened that Trump could stop sharing U.S. intelligence if it continued to ignore his requests. A U.S. official denied that, saying Witkoff and Kushner told the Ukrainians that the U.S. was a strong partner, providing munitions and intelligence. Ukraine therefore shouldn't take actions that hurt American consumers, the two said. On Sunday, the Financial Times reported that the U.S. told European countries it might stop selling weapons to Ukraine through NATO if Ukraine continues to strike Russian refineries.
